## About the Editor

Hamid Jahankhani

*([Hamid.jahankhani@northumbria.ac.uk](mailto:Hamid.jahankhani@northumbria.ac.uk))*

Professor Hamid Jahankhani gained his PhD from the Queen Mary College, University of London. In 1999 he moved to the University of East London (UEL) to become the first Professor of Information Security and Cyber Criminology at the university in 2010. Over the last 15 years Hamid has also been involved in developing new and innovative programmes and introducing the “block mode” delivery approach at UEL. The programmes he has developed include an MSc in Information Security and Computer Forensics, and a Professional Doctorate in Information Security.

Hamid’s principal research areas for a number of years have been the fields of cyber security, information security and digital forensics. In partnership with the key industrial sectors, he has examined and established several innovative research projects that are of direct relevance to the needs of UK and European information security professionals, digital forensics industries, Critical National Infrastructure and law enforcement agencies. Hamid has planned, proposed and managed several collaborative projects, and secured a substantial research income of several million Euros.

Under Hamid’s supervision, 13 PhD and Professional Doctorate students in information security have completed their theses. Hamid has also been leading international and national research projects in a number of areas.

Professor Jahankhani is the Editor-in-Chief of the *International Journal of Electronic Security and Digital Forensics* ([www.inderscience.com/ijesdf](http://www.inderscience.com/ijesdf)), published by Inderscience, and general chair of the annual International Conference on Global Security, Safety and Sustainability (ICGS3). Hamid has edited and contributed to over 15 books and has over 150 conference and journal publications. In the summer of 2017, Hamid was trained as a GCHQ “cyberist” to train the next generation of cyber security experts through the GCHQ CyberFirst initiative. Professor Jahankhani has a number of books forthcoming, namely, Cyber Criminology, Blockchain and Clinical Trials — Securing Patient’s Data, Cyber Security Practitioner’s Guide, Digital Twins Technologies and Smart Cities.

## Introduction

## It’s Time to Make the Case for Ethics

Ali G. Hessami

*Vega Systems, London, United Kingdom  
[Hessami@vegaglobalsystems.com](mailto:Hessami@vegaglobalsystems.com)*

Since the days of man as hunter gatherers, the success and prosperity of humanity has been associated with one key differentiator against other species, i.e. the invention of tools and artefacts. This inventiveness was inevitably driven by the need to generate a differential advantage against adversity in order to survive. The advent of agriculture brought the use of manmade tools to a higher level. Such tools gave mankind the ability to cultivate land, produce surplus food and transcend beyond the daily challenges of subsistence and survival. Whilst the invention of tools and artefacts bore testament to man’s superior cognitive powers, these arose in response to man’s needs to complement his feeble physique and powers in a harsh eco-system, and played a largely functional role in the advancement of the species. In this spirit, the quality, efficacy and diversity of tools and artefacts increased to enhance performance. However, the performance of tools, products and services has often been viewed narrowly through a utilitarian perspective often focused on the market mechanisms of price, functionality and desirability/quality. This has held true largely due to the limited impact of products and services on the society at large. This is a condition that is no longer tenable given our overt dependence on technological tools, products, services and artefacts that are transforming our lives and making us dependent on them without giving us the ability to influence their design, production, or functionality or to hold the supply chain accountable. In this setting, a new paradigm is called for that goes beyond concerns over commercial and functional performance and encourages the providers of products, services and systems towards transparency, accountability, explainability and the observance of higher ethical values in their increasingly global roles. This is the era of ethics and moral considerations for all enterprises, public or private, for or not-for-profit. Strangely but not unexpectedly, this also applies to the safety as well as the security of products, services and systems. We will explore the rationale, necessity and the attainment of this laudable emergent property in this introduction.

### Facets of Performance

A purposeful aggregate of interconnected parts performing one or a suite of functions is regarded as a system. A system generally resides in an environment (larger eco-system) or as part of a larger system (system of systems) and manifests properties and behaviours that are not attributable to its individual constituents but to their inter-working. This is referred to as emergence or the emergent property of a system. Apart from emergence, a system can also be viewed from specific stakeholder perspectives that constitute nine inter-related facets of performance, comprising the following:

•Technical and functional.

•Commercial, cost and profitability.

•Environmental.

•Integrity (reliability, availability and maintainability).

•Resilience.

•Safety and security.

•Sustainability.

•Quality.

•Social and individual perceived value and preference.

These facets of system performance are inter-related and their individual desired level of attainment often involves a degree of trade-off and the discretion of the stakeholders regarding an acceptable level for each attribute. A desirable product, service or system delivers an optimal blend of these in a given context and at a crosssection in time.

One particular aspect of performance or behaviour that is traditionally not analysed or treated systematically and comprehensively is the value aspect. By default, it is regarded as the forte of the marketing department to cater for consumer preferences and choices to maximise sales opportunities. One key aspect of value is the social/ethical value that is concerned with the cultural, social moral norms of good/decent behaviour and the impact of products, services or systems on the ethical values held in the stakeholders’ community or the whole society. This implies that design decisions and structural and behavioural aspects require stakeholder consultation and that the identification of ethical values that may be affected by the system of interest’s concept of operation is crucial, in addition to all the other requirements relating to other facets of performance cited earlier.

### The Need for a New Dimension

We have finally moved beyond focussing on safety after two millennia, and new concerns over the protection of life and property have emerged in the physical and cyber security contexts. Whilst safety is regarded as freedom from unacceptable levels of human harm that arise from unintended random or systematic errors and failures, security can be broadly defined as freedom from the unacceptable risks of human harm or loss of property arising from intentional acts and causes. The assurance of safety and security is broadly approached from the perspective of the risk of human harm and property loss to the direct users and stakeholders of a product, service or system. The well-being, happiness and overall quality of life in the social context is the next dimension of interest, largely driven by the emergence and advancement of digital technologies that pervade our lives and that may progress further to have an impact on many aspects of our lives normally considered private and personal. This is rather unprecedented in human history and requires urgent review, an evaluation of the existing and emerging social hazards, and the formulation of proactive strategies to preserve and protect moral and ethical values that have evolved over millennia for the advancement and prosperity of human societies.

### *Ethics and morals*

Ethics is the branch of knowledge that deals with moral principles that govern human behaviour. Morals are the measures of right and wrong in the judgements and decisions that we face in life.

### *The principal ethical philosophies*

There are a number of predominant ethical canons and philosophies that offer competing views of human behaviour. The choices a person makes in all walks of human endeavour depend very much on the philosophies he follows. The oldest school is attributed to Aristotle, and it is known as Virtue Ethics. This is largely concerned with individual qualities (virtues) that underpin our behaviours and promote well-being. The focus is largely on virtues rather than the negative individual traits that are referred to as vices. In this individual and bottom-up perspective, the promotion and upholding of individual virtues are considered instrumental to the collective societal well-being and the quality of interactions and relationships. This is analogous to quality ingredients being essential to integrative virtue from the total system/societal perspective. Whilst this approach has its virtues, it evidently lacks the systems perspective in that the emergence of a virtuous society at peace and happy with itself is not necessarily and entirely conditioned on moral choices made by the individual members.

The second school of philosophy regarding ethics is the Consequentialist school, which is more concerned with the systemlevel emergence of happiness and well-being from the integral of actions, choices and decisions made by the human agents, sub-systems and components of a system of interest. This regards any choice or decision ethical/moral so long as it contributes or is perceived to contribute to maximising the satisfaction, fulfilment and happiness for the largest number of beneficiaries. This is analogous to an economic utility function and the desire for maximisation of return on an investment as a rational course of action. There are many challenges in utilitarianism, least of all estimating, anticipating or rationalising a system-level effect from a component level course of action. This is as much an issue with human affairs as it is with complex technological systems. The nearest analogy with technological systems is a systems analysis technique known as Failure Mode, Effects and Criticality Analysis (FMECA) that strives to identify critical component level failures that have a major impact on system-level reliability, safety and availability.

The third established perspective on ethics emphasises the importance of leadership and stewardship. The Deontological or Duty Ethics proposed by Immanuel Kant explores the ramifications of choices, options and decisions by those who occupy the positions of responsibility, authority and leadership. This is driven by the realisation that senior decision makers’ choices and decisions are more influential/impactful and more significant in terms of their effects on the stakeholders, hence the necessity for moral considerations. One key criteria for the morality of a duty holder’s decisions and choices is to ensure that all the others impacted by the decisions made are treated fairly and with dignity, and not used as means to the decision makers’ ends and objectives. The influential decision makers are also encouraged to consider circumstances in which their decisions could become universal laws and whether they would be willing to endure life influenced and shaped by those laws. Duty ethics demands moral scrutiny, considerations and judgements by those in a position of authority that would impose limits on their choices. In this way, those in a position of authority strive to ensure that every critical decision is made empathetically in an informed moral context.

The three schools of ethical philosophy endeavour to scrutinise the morality of human choices and decisions from the perspectives of individual virtue (component), consequence/utility (systemlevel) and duty holders (governance). From a holistic systems analytical viewpoint, the three canons of ethical philosophy provide an encompassing framework for understanding, analysing and proactively addressing ethical concerns arising from our choices, decisions and actions from a personal, corporate and collective perspective. However, this ethical framework is drawn from the Western world’s philosophical paradigm. The ethical values that underpin our cultural, historical and social morals may also originate from a multitude of other rich and equally pertinent ecosystems that have their origins in ethnic beliefs, behavioural codes, creed and culture. A universal ethical framework should additionally factor in values that are not necessarily traceable to personal virtues, duty holders’ maxims or pure utilitarianism. Ancient human societies and associated cultures have largely evolved in relative isolation, each developing their own ethical values and moral codes. These will additionally provide a potent landscape for the exploration of ethical values and moral implications in the design of products, services and systems alongside the three philosophies cited earlier.

### The Emerging Reality

The widescale emerging pattern of cyber attacks globally poses an unprecedented threat to governance, economic activities, and the peace and stability of the largely digitally-transformed lifestyle. The recent cyber attacks on the USA power grid and power companies, also known as the so-called grid hacking — a spree of attacks on over 300 universities and some private companies in the USA and beyond resulting in the loss of 31 terabytes of private data estimated to amount to an equivalent of $3 billion worth of intellectual property and a whole host of data breaches including one which yielded 2 terabytes of private information on hundreds of millions of American adults — are illustrative of the unabating current trends. Apart from the colossal economic, strategic and geopolitical impact such breaches have, many of the security breaches of state and private sector enterprises have major ethical dimensions relating to privacy, trust, duty of care/protection and accountability.

Alongside the current concerns over security, there are other technological developments that bring great promise and at the same time pose major risks to mankind if not understood, analysed and mitigated proactively. The emergence of autonomous and smart products, systems and services, and the vast potential of Artificial Intelligence (AI) comprise the most notable and impactful innovations over the horizon — although they already pervade our lives to some degree.

In this dynamic, exciting, promising as well as potentially disruptive setting, the need to focus on the societal macro perspective is more urgent than it has ever been.

### *Ethics now*

On 1 November 2018, thousands of Google employees staged a mass protest against the corporate’s sexual misconduct allegations. This protest took the form of a walkout, which was held across Google offices from Tokyo to California to demonstrate against workplace culture. This Walkout for Real Change followed an earlier employee reaction to a large military contract in 2018 in which employees objected to the company’s involvement in non-civilian and militaristic projects. The campaigners in the walkout put forward a five point list of demands that comprised issues from i) putting an end to forced arbitration in harassment and discrimination cases, ii) commitment to equal pay and opportunity, iii) transparency over disclosure of sexual harassment, iv) a globally inclusive process for reporting sexual misconduct and v) the appointment of an employee representative on the Board.

These anecdotal cases paint a newly emerging picture in the hierarchical corporate world even for colossal multinational enterprises that dominate many aspects of global transactions with online services. In this newly emerging paradigm, the passive employees of a large enterprise attempted to awaken a sense of social responsibility and to promote ethical and moral behaviour in an otherwise commercial corporation with impact and partial success. This hopefully heralds the emergence of a socially responsive perspective on all business activities, invariably supported by the power of social media and the instant communication of ideals, including cases of abuse and soft power by the technocrats and scientists who do not sit at the pinnacle of power in large corporations and multi-national enterprises.

### *The need for pragmatism*

The legal framework in most developed countries places a duty of care on people and all public and private enterprises regarding the health, safety and welfare of employees, customers, stakeholders and the general public. Physical and cyber security are increasingly regarded as an extension of the duty of care towards the general public but the general public are not yet subject to the same level of protection by laws and regulations in these areas. Interestingly, safety and security are both facets of the ethical values pertaining to a product, service or system. The importance of safety and security necessitates a new pragmatism towards social/public good that transcends mere compliance with legal duty of care imperatives. This demands a new codified ethical framework to enable public and private enterprises to factor in social sensitivities and ethical values in the design and deployment of their products and services. In this new paradigm, the power of the employees and the consumers are brought to bear as a form of highly responsive and effective market regulation, especially in the absence of adequate legal instruments. The development of legal instruments seems to trail behind the fast-paced technological innovations, but the reality is that many immoral and unethical activities are not necessarily illegal. This new form of social soft power is the antidote to the pure private motive and accountability towards shareholders that dominate the current corporate and legal landscape.

### What Next?

There are a number of developments that herald a ray of hope in this dynamic, fast paced and often confusing scene. They are largely driven by current necessities and the initiatives of a number of international standardisation and professional institutions.

Within the context of cyber security, a large-scale effort has been under way to develop a global standard for the cyber protection of Industrial Automation and Control Systems (IACS). The ISA-64223 suite, comprising a 14-part series of standards and technical reports that covers models, concepts and processes for the security of industrial automation and control systems, has been developed by the International Society of Automation (ISA) with the goal of uniformity of approach in the field of instrumentation. Each part of the ISA-62443 suite covers a specific aspect of IACS Cyber Security and is aimed at a particular audience — from the designers and developers of complete systems to the suppliers of components and system integrators, operators and maintainers. The 14 parts are grouped in four key categories addressing general principles, policies and procedures and system and component level processes as illustrated in the overview diagram ([Fig. 1](#introduction.xhtml#fig1)).

It is worth noting that due to its extensive scale and scope, the ISA-62443 suite is still undergoing further updates and enhancements.

![image](images/fig1.jpg)

**Fig. 1.**Overview of the ISA-62443 suite of IACS cyber security standards.

In the larger context of social good and societal impact, the International Institution of Electrical and Electronic Engineers (IEEE) has recently embarked on an ambitious programme of developing standards for Ethically Aligned Design. Apart from giving generic guidance on the Ethically Aligned Design standards, now in second revision, the IEEE Standards Association currently hosts 14 working groups focussed on various aspects of the design and behavioural features of smart, autonomous and AI technologies, products, services and systems. The whole initiative is under the IEEE P7000™ series of standards projects, which was under development at the time this book was written, and which represents a departure from the 1300 IEEE global standards on technology, interoperability and safety. It currently comprises the following:

1.**IEEE P7000**™ — Model Process for Addressing Ethical Concerns During System Design

2.**IEEE P7001**™ — Transparency of Autonomous Systems

3.**IEEE P7002**™ — Data Privacy Process

4.**IEEE P7003**™ — Algorithmic Bias Considerations

5.**IEEE P7004**™ — Standard on Child and Student Data Governance

6.**IEEE P7005**™ — Standard on Employer Data Governance

7.**IEEE P7006**™ — Standard on Personal Data AI Agent Working Group

8.**IEEE P7007**™ — Ontological Standard for Ethically-Driven Robotics and Automation Systems

9.**IEEE P7008**™ — Standard for Ethically-Driven Nudging for Robotic, Intelligent and Autonomous Systems.

10.**IEEE P7009**™ — Standard for Fail-Safe Design of Autonomous and Semi-Autonomous Systems

11.**IEEE P7010**™ — Wellbeing Metrics Standard for Ethical Artificial Intelligence and Autonomous Systems

12.**IEEE P7011**™ — Standard for the Process of Identifying and Rating the Trustworthiness of News Sources

13.**IEEE P7012**™ — Standard for Machine Readable Personal Privacy Terms

14.**IEEE P7013**™ — Inclusion and Application Standards for Automated Facial Analysis Technology

The current concerns over safety, reliability, security and even ethics require an integrated framework that guides, empowers and supports an inclusive approach to the development of products, services and systems and does not treat each dimension of performance as an independent facet of self-serving significance. This holistic framework is likely to be sustainable in the sense that a product, service or system that does not embody a judicious blend of all the performance requirements cited would fail to be sustainable technically, commercially, environmentally or from a societal point of view. This will pose a challenge but offer the promise of going beyond individual concerns, ethics, safety, security and localism whilst taking a macro perspective. In this new paradigm, the laws and regulations will be supplemented by an agile, responsive and informed global community.
