### 4.5.Anomaly Detection

Anomaly detection can refer to the problem of finding patterns in data that do not conform to expected behaviour (Chandola *et al.,* 2009). Nonconforming patterns can be described as anomalies, peculiarities or exceptions. Anomaly detection is used in a variety of applications such as credit card & banking fraud, insurance claims and security surveillance.

The detection of an anomaly within a dataset has been studied as early as the 19th century (Edgeworth, 1887). This has led to numerous research studies carried out to analyse a variety of anomaly techniques that have been developed for specific applications.

Anomaly detection can be described as the translation of data into categories based on specific criteria. For example, spurious data travelling through a computer network could be considered an anomaly that has been caused by a malicious intruder, malware or a software bug. This event may subsequently trigger an alert or initiate a workflow dependent on the activity and how it is categorised. Anomalies in credit card transaction data could indicate credit card or identity theft (Aleskerov *et al.*, 1997), or anomalous readings from a space craft sensor could signify a fault in some component of the space craft (Fujimaki *et al.*, 2005).

### 4.5.1.*Data noise*

Rousseeuw *et al.* (1987) and Teng *et al.* (1990) both describe the relevance of data noise when determining anomalies. Noise can be defined as a phenomenon in data that is of no interest and which becomes an impediment when analysing data. Noise removal is driven by the need to remove the unwanted objects before any data analysis is performed. Noise accommodation refers to immunising a statistical model estimation against anomalous observations (Huber, 1974).

Within Dakota, data noise can be described as crossover zones that contractors enter on their way to their destination. The intersection of zones could also be identified as data noise that should be eliminated from the detection algorithm. The data derived from the crossover area between two zones has been identified within the dataset. This can be observed as flickering between two zones over a prolonged period.

To eliminate the crossover effect and data retrieved when contractors are in transit between zones, a minimal time period has been incorporated into the security model. As an example, the researcher identified the time taken by contractors when walking between zones by analysing the time they entered and exited fields within the data stream. To improve accuracy the researcher also physically monitored human movement patterns within the Dakota environment to cross-reference the Bluetooth data with observation data (see the section on physical monitoring).

It was evident from the data retrieved from the proximity monitoring solution, in addition to the observation data, that a 10-second limit should be set within any zone to eliminate data noise.

### 4.5.2.*Detecting anomalies*

At an abstract level, an anomaly is defined as a pattern that does not conform to expected normal behaviour (Chandola *et al*., 2009). Therefore, in its basic form, anomaly detection can be described as the identification of normal behaviour, and, within a specific environment, observing any changes that are different from the normal pattern.

The anomaly identification process can be very challenging as there are many factors that need to be taken into consideration:

•Understanding normal behaviour and identifying the nuances of how humans integrate with others within a working environment.

•Determining the boundaries between normal and abnormal behaviour may not be an exact science. There are potentially an infinite number of contributing factors that may alter the perceived normal behaviour pattern.

•Individuals with malicious intentions can adapt and attempt to disguise their actions to look normal.

•As what is defined as normal behaviour will potentially evolve over time, continuous realignment will be required to prevent false positives.

•The definition of an anomaly may be different depending on the role and even the specific individual within an organisation.

•Noise within the data can alter the perception of the threat and trigger an alert. The environment will need to be explored and superfluous data ignored.

### 4.5.3.*Classification*

The primary purpose of this research paper is to construct a security model that incorporates an algorithm that will detect a potential threat through an anomaly detection process. An important aspect of the detection process is the classification of an anomaly once the anomaly is detected.

The research has classified the anomalies into the following groups, classes or sets.

### 4.5.4.**Point-based anomalies**

Based on data collected over a period of time, an individual whose movement patterns are considered anomalous in relation to the baseline data would represent an anomaly. Chandola *et al.* (2009) describe anomaly detection as the problem of finding patterns in data that do not conform to expected behaviour. They define the term anomaly as identifiable patterns in data that do not conform to a well-defined notion of normal within a twodimensional dataset.

This can be visualised in [Fig. 4.7](#chapter4.xhtml#fig4.7) which depicts a typical pointbased anomaly approach.

N1 and N2 represent the baseline data areas that have been identified as normal behaviour. T1, T2, T3 and T4 are classed as anomalies (potential threats) as they fall outside of the boundaries of the baseline areas denoted by N1 and N2.

![image](images/fig4.7.jpg)

**Fig. 4.7.**Point-based anomaly approach (source: Chandola *et al*. (2009)).

A simple example of a point-based anomaly could be a bank account, where N1 and N2 represent normal spending patterns. T1, T2, T3 and T4 represent abnormally high spending patterns, or spending outside of normal geographical locations.

Whilst this could be considered a simple example, it does demonstrate how pattern analysis can be used to detect spurious patterns and how it has real-life applications. The detection of anomalies in credit card transaction data could indicate credit card or identity theft (Aleskerov *et al*., 1997). The anomalous patterns within an MRI image may indicate the presence of malignant tumours (Spence *et al.*, 2001).

### 4.5.5.*Contextual-based anomalies*

Contextual or conditional (Song *et al.*, 2007) data is anomalous but only in a specific context. In other ways the data may conform to normal behaviour. The contextual attribute of the data will determine if it represents abnormal or normal behaviour.

Contextual anomalies are defined through two attributes:

•Contextual

![image](images/cir.jpg)Determines the context or location of that instance. As an example, in geospatial data, latitude and longitude could be used as contextual attributes.

•Behavioural

![image](images/cir.jpg)The behavioural attributes of a data set could be defined as the non-contextual characteristics of each specific instance. As an example, in a spatial data set representing global average temperatures, the temperature of a city would be considered behavioural.

[Figure 4.8](#chapter4.xhtml#fig4.8) depicts a graph demonstrating contextual abnormality within a temperature time period.

The temperature (data) is the same in T1 and T2; the context of that data within the different time periods has an impact when determining if the data is abnormal for the season. T1 is normal but T2 can be seen as an anomaly for the time of year.

![image](images/fig4.8.jpg)

**Fig. 4.8.**Contextual anomaly approach.

### 4.5.6.**Collective anomalies**

If a collection of related data instances is anomalous with respect to the entire data set, it is termed a collective anomaly. The individual data instances in a collective anomaly may not be anomalies by themselves, but their occurrence together as a collection is anomalous (Chandola *et al.*, 2009). This does not imply that individual data sets are anomalies, but that their occurrence collectively with other data sets can be classified as an anomaly.

As an example, during August 2017, Dakota’s access control logs displayed an unusual increase in staff located on the 3^(rd) floor visiting other floors, and in particular the floor directly below. The data was analysed and the entry point used by the vast majority of staff was to the right of the elevator. Under closer inspection the log data also appeared to only affect male members of staff.

The issue was quickly identified. The male toilets on the 3^(rd) floor were unavailable for 24 hours so staff had to use the facilities on other floors. The toilet was also located to the right of the elevator, so staff used this access point.

A single observation (member of staff) visiting another floor is not unusual, but a collective data set (multiple staff) could be considered anomalous and can be classed as a collective anomaly.

### 4.6.Threat Model and Algorithm

The primary objective of this research paper is to reduce the risk posed by an insider through the development of a robust threat detection model which incorporates an effective and tested algorithm.

Dakota’s recently implemented proximity monitoring solution provides a constant stream of human movement data that is interpreted and processed within a dedicated security server.

Whilst Dakota security personnel are able to selectively monitor movement of the Bluetooth security badges, Dakota senior management believe it is not cost-effective to deploy a team of dedicated security staff to permanently monitor the movement of 50 separate individual contractors. It is also believed impractical for security personnel to understand the regular movement patterns of contract staff, their working practises and the specific zones in which they operate.

Leveraging data obtained from the Bluetooth proximity monitoring solution, a purpose-built application has been constructed to process the data using an algorithm that determines the threat posture of each individual contractor.

### 4.6.1.*Extracting the data*

The proximity solution is provided by Zonith, a Danish-based security solution provider who specialises in security, alarm handling and notification solutions (Zonith, 2018). Zonith’s proximity solution is based around generic hardware components that are not vendorspecific.

The Zonith solution comprises adapted Bluetooth Beacons, Bluetooth enabled devices (including Bluetooth security badges) and the Zonith application. The Zonith application is known as the Real Time Location Solution (RTLS), and incorporates customised schematics of the client office space. Dakota have preloaded a plan for each of the floors it occupies within its London headquarters.

RTLS is hosted on a single dedicated security server, running Windows 2016. The front-end application is delivered through an Internet browser environment using an Apache Tomcat server. The data is stored on a dedicated proprietary database, which is located on the same server (Project, 2018).

![image](images/fig4.9.jpg)

**Fig. 4.9.**Zonith RTLS.

Data is fed from the Bluetooth-enabled ID badge to the beacon. This is then sent to the RTLS server and stored onto the embedded database. [Figure 4.9](#chapter4.xhtml#fig4.9) outlines this process.

After analysis of the data provided by the RTLS system, it was discovered that in its native format the data was not sufficient to construct time analysis. Additionally, the native data set did not provide the sequence number that would be required for time calculation or movement profiling.

Sufficient data from all the job roles was therefore required to provide a baseline for the algorithm. To achieve this an extraction of two months’ historic data was analysed to determine recognised movement patterns and anomalies within the data set.

The data was reassembled, and a sequence number was added at the beginning of each data set. To reduce the length of the data processed, a unique User ID field was also added. This associated the Media Access Control (MAC) address of the Bluetooth proximity ID pass with a simple, much smaller numerical value. An entry and exit flag was then included as this would indicate if the Bluetooth ID pass entered or exited a zone.

To identify the time spent in each zone, two data sets were required for the calculation, one made up of instances when the Bluetooth ID badge entered a zone (or beacon) and one made up of instances when it left a zone. By default, each beacon sends a signal when the Bluetooth ID badge enters a zone and a second signal when it leaves a zone. To connect these two data sets together an Enter ID flag was inserted. As the Bluetooth ID badge enters a zone, a null value is added to the data set, but when the badge leaves the zone, the Enter ID flag is set to the sequence number associated with entering that zone. [Table 4.5](#chapter4.xhtml#tab4.5) depicts how the two fields and data sets are connected, thus identifying the time spent within each zone.

By calculating the difference between the entry and exit time stamp fields (connected by the entry/exit flag and the enter ID field), the time spent in each location was calculated and displayed within the Timing field.

Using [Fig. 4.9](#chapter4.xhtml#fig4.9) as an example, the individual entered the zone and generated the REC ID ‘1’ at 13:46:20 (time stamp), the entry/exit flag was set to ‘1’ (denoting an entry) and the enter ID field was set to null (no connection with another data set). When the individual left the zone, a second data set was created, sequence no ‘2’ (within the rec ID field) at 13:46:25.

**Table 4.5.**Typical data set manipulated for the algorithm.

![image](images/tab4.5.jpg)

The entry/exit flag was set to ‘0’ (exit indicator) and the enter ID was set to ‘1’ as this refers to the sequence number depicted in the rec ID field.

### 4.6.2.**Threat detection application**

To build a threat detection system that could identify anomalies from movement data retrieved via the RTLS system, a threat detection application was created, named Shadow Guard.

Shadow Guard was written as a progressive web based application using Hypertext Mark-up Language (HTML), Cascading Style Sheets (CSS) and PHP: Hypertext Pre-processor (PHP). A MySQL database was embedded within the threat detection server to store and process the data.

[Figure 4.10](#chapter4.xhtml#fig4.10) depicts how movement data is detected and passed from the ID badge to the beacon (using Bluetooth) and then into the RTLS server through an Ethernet connection.

Once the data was written into the Zonith proprietary database, a trigger was created (within RTLS) that copies data from the RTLS database into the Shadow Guard server where the data is reconstructed and stored in the new format.

### 4.6.3.*Baseline behaviour*

Once the data collection method was constructed and the data sorted into a readable format within the Shadow Cloud application a series of baselines was constructed to determine the normal working patterns of Dakota’s contractors.

Extensive testing was undertaken by the researcher, who was assisted by Dakota’s facilities staff. Each security pass was checked to ensure each of the beacons was able to detect the badges and the zoning was correct with minimal bleedover.

Referencing the job roles outlined in [Table 4.5](#chapter4.xhtml#tab4.5), Dakota’s security personnel staff were engaged and each of the Bluetooth access cards was activated and handed to each of the contractors working within the office area of Dakota’s head office in London.

![image](images/fig4.10.jpg)

**Fig. 4.10.**Data stream between RTLS and Shadow Guard.

The 3^(rd) party contracts were scrutinised by lawyers to ensure the advanced monitoring required for anomaly-based threat detection did not breach any privacy laws or contractual concerns.

Each of the Bluetooth badges was charged and permanently attached to the building RFID access control card (see Appendix B).

To ensure sufficent data was collected to provide an effective baseline, an initial two-month collection period was implemented. As the amount of data collected would be dependent on the specific job role, the researcher decided to concentrate the analysis on one specific role within the organisation.

Using the data contained in [Table 4.5](#chapter4.xhtml#tab4.5), which outlines the access required by each of the contractor roles and the standard operating times, it was evident that the cleaners would provide the level of data required to build a baseline. Whilst data from all contract staff was collected, the initial baseline analysis was concentrated on the 9 cleaning contractors employed by Dakota.

Data was collected from November 2017 until January 2018; this included the Christmas holiday period. The data was then reconstructed into the new format that included a unique sequence number, user ID (to replace the ID badge MAC code), entry/exit flag, zone (based on the beacon MAC code) and the timing field, see [Fig. 4.10](#chapter4.xhtml#fig4.10).

### 4.6.4.*Analysing data*

Once sufficient data was collected the analysis process could take place. The data was separated into individual floors. To detect abnormal behaviour patterns it was evident that there could be multiple determining factors that indicate potential malicious intentions. To understand and analyse the risk factor, the data was separated into different sections.

### 4.6.5.*Entry points*

As each floor had its own unique characteristics, including specific hotzones, critical areas and entry/exit points. It was considered important to analyse each floor’s entry point as this could indicate an anomaly.

As an example Dakota’s 3^(rd) floor has four separate entry points, these are as follows:

•Elevator A

•Elevator B

•Stairwell A

•Stairwell B (fire escape)

As the three elevators that service each of the floors are communal, there was a risk of unauthorised access to Dakota’s private floorspace. To reduce this risk Dakota installed two glass doors on either side of the exit/entry path from the elevators.

[Figure 4.11](#chapter4.xhtml#fig4.11) depicts Dakota’s 3^(rd) floor layout, incorporating two security doors. Note that each access point requires RFID access control to enter and triggers separate beacons (zones) at each entry point.

![image](images/fig4.11.jpg)

**Fig. 4.11.** Typical Dakota office access point.

Two stairwells also service the 3^(rd) floor and are located at separate areas of the open plan office. These extry/exit points also require access control and trigger separate Bluetooth beacons.

As the contractors must enter the zone using their respective RFID access control cards (which are attached to the Bluetooth badges), they will be picked up by a beacon as they enter the office area.

Although the specific entry point may be considered less important when determining the threat level, it can still represent anomalous behaviour that may impact the threat detection algorithm.

A key aspect of any anomaly detection technique is the nature of the input data ( Chandola *et al.*, 2018). It can therefore be considered important to determine the relevance of the data collected and its importance when defining the algorithm.

As an example, based on the data collected over the two-month baseline period, it was clearly evident that the cleaners accessed the floor through the same entry point 90% of the time. This can be explained using the chart in [Fig. 4.12](#chapter4.xhtml#fig4.12).

![image](images/fig4.12.jpg)

**Fig. 4.12.**Entry point statistics for the 3^(rd) floor.

These results were cross-referenced and verified using RFID access control data. Whilst there may be legitimate reasons to use different access points, the evidence indicates a clear pattern forming.

The rationale for using the elevator access point A is also clear, as the cleaners regularly start their shift at the small kitchenette area, which is located nearest to the elevator access point A.

As an additional layer of assurance and based on the times each cleaner visited the 3^(rd) floor, the researcher was able to verify the theory that the kitchenette and potentially the toilet (which is located adjacent to the kitchenette) were the targets of the cleaners each time they visited the 3^(rd) floor.

### 4.6.6.*Time of day*

Using the data acquired through the access control logs and the Bluetooth beacon data, the next process to be measured was the specified time the cleaner accessed the floor.

Using the data within [Table 4.2](#chapter4.xhtml#tab4.2), it is straightforward to calculate the time of entry against the contractual agreements. The data can be verified and cross-referenced using the access control and beacon logs.

It is worth noting that whilst an individual can gain access to a floor using tailgating techniques, it would be considerably more difficult to prevent the beacon detecting the Bluetooth ID badge.

Dakota’s cleaners’ specific operating hours are regimented and are mostly based outside of normal business hours.

As Dakota are a financial services organisation, their operational hours are based on the London Stock Exchange’s (LSE) trading hours. The cleaners visit the office from 5am–7am, 12–2pm and 5pm–7pm from Monday to Friday.

There may be specific occasions where cleaning staff are authorised to work over the weekend and lunchtime, but this is for specific tasks that are not included in their regular duties. The extra hours worked are not considered normal working hours.

It is evident that the identification of anomolous activity requires careful consideration and analysis of 3^(rd) party contracts and historical data collected by the proximity monitoring solution. This element of the overall anomaly detection process could be considered subjective and dependent on the role of the people being tracked.

As an example, cleaners usually work contracted hours that may be specific to the business, so it is easier to measure and detect discrepancies in their working patterns. The working patterns of electricians or specific maintenance staff who may have sporadic working patterns, on the other hand, could prove challenging to analyse.

### 4.6.7.*Time spent in a zone*

Once an individual has entered a secure area that has no further access control barriers, zone analysis must then be incorporated into the anomaly algorithm. Using historic movement data, it is possible to detect routes taken within an open plan office based on the sequence of zones the proximity sensor has entered. However, routes are subjective and may be difficult to quantify.

Using baseline data, specific patterns can be detected based on the time spent within each zone. Using the cleaners’ data as an example, [Fig. 4.13](#chapter4.xhtml#fig4.13) depicts the data collected over the baseline period for a single zone.

The cleaners are assigned specific areas and supported by other cleaners where necessary. Cleaners are also expected to cover an alternate floor when another cleaner falls sick or goes on holiday. As an example, Cleaner 8 is the primary cleaner for the 3^(rd) floor. However, other cleaners will provide support where necessary. For example, they might help to collect the refuse once the individual desk bins have been emptied.

Using a point-based anomaly approach, [Fig. 4.13](#chapter4.xhtml#fig4.13) analyses the cleaners’ access data for Zone 1 on the 3^(rd) floor (over the baseline period).

The data highlights an interesting pattern: The regular cleaner (Cleaner 8), spends more time in the zone and visits the zone more frequently.

![image](images/fig4.13.jpg)

**Fig. 4.13.**Average daily activity in a single zone.

The non-regular cleaners’ data is clearly grouped, they collectively spend a shorter period of time within the zone under analysis.

This pattern is reflected across the entire floor, showing the primary cleaner spending considerably more time within each zone, whilst the supporting cleaners enter the zones less frequently and for a shorter period. Based on the working practices of the job role this could be considered normal behaviour.

Using the same point-based anomaly approach, a single zone was analysed over a 7-day period. The purpose was to identify normal and abnormal activity.

[Figure 4.14](#chapter4.xhtml#fig4.14) uses a point-based anomaly approach, detailing the time each cleaner spent within a typical zone.

Using the data provided, there is a clear demarcation point between standard and unusual activity.

This data set is typical across all the zones, except when a cleaner was at a hotspot. In that case, the time spent within that area increased.

![image](images/fig4.14.jpg)

**Fig. 4.14.**Typical zone activity.

When determining threat metrics, it is important to understand the thresholds for normal, unusual and anomalous behaviour.

[Figure 4.15](#chapter4.xhtml#fig4.15) references the demarcation point as a percentage of normal operating activity that includes a margin of error based on the data collected. The chart includes a detailed breakdown of user activity within one zone over a 7-day period.

Activity has been correlated into three bands — normal, unusual and abnormal activity. It is evident that the normal time spent within this specific zone by one job role accounts for 95.5% of all activity. It can therefore be assumed that this data group represents normal activity.

The data defines a much smaller grouping that can be identified as unusual behaviour (3.5%). The last recorded data point for this zone was between 7–8 minutes (1.5%) and this has been designated as abnormal.

Data recorded beyond this demarcation point would be considered a potential threat and an alert would be generated.

The snapshot of data detected within Zone 3/1 is typical of other zones within the target organisation. Whilst each zone may have differing time values, which can be dependent on the specific zone or the job role, the percentages stay constant.

![image](images/fig4.15.jpg)

**Fig. 4.15.**Point-based anomaly chart detailing user activity (source: Dakota).

Novikova and Murenin observe that making note of the duration each employee stays in the controlled zone allows one to identify anomalies and potential malicious behaviour (Novikova and Murenin, 2017).

### 4.6.8.*Zone metrics*

Once the individual leaves a specific floor, their activity can be analysed and appropriate metrics applied through the algorithm. When the individual leaves a controlled zone, it can be detected as the data set will have no corresponding data set on that floor, see [Table 4.6](#chapter4.xhtml#tab4.6).

[Figure 4.16](#chapter4.xhtml#fig4.16) depicts zone data extracted from the proximity solution and confirms the working practices of selected job functions. Using [Fig. 4.16](#chapter4.xhtml#fig4.16) as a reference, it is possible to determine in which floors a cleaner predominately operates.

![image](images/fig4.16.jpg)

**Fig. 4.16.** Average zones visited.

This can provide a baseline metric to highlight significant changes to the work patterns that might indicate unusual behaviour. Determining thresholds can be challenging as it may be necessary to temporarily reassign staff to different floors.

Working on the same metrics used when determining anomalies within zone activity, a similar threshold can be applied when determining significant pattern changes.

Using a single individual as an example, [Fig. 4.16](#chapter4.xhtml#fig4.16) details the average number of zones visited by Cleaner 5. The metrics are taken from the proximity monitoring solution and confirm the floors in which the cleaner is a regular visitor.

Data was collected and processed over a two-month period and used to construct a baseline; however, once the Shadow Cloud application is fully deployed this metric will be updated in real-time.

Using the 2^(nd) Floor as an example within [Fig. 4.17](#chapter4.xhtml#fig4.17), one can see that Cleaner 5 has a daily average of 75 zone hits. Using the same margin-of-error metric previously employed when measuring the zone activity, behaviour is considered unusual if the number of visits in a particular day ≥50% of the average day’s zone visits.

![image](images/fig4.17.jpg)

**Fig. 4.17.** Zones visited by Cleaner 5.

Again, using the same methodology, behaviour can be considered an anomaly when the threshold reaches ≥100%. If daily zone visits are ≥200% then an immediate alert is triggered.

### 4.6.9.*Pattern triggers*

The final analysis phase of the anomaly detection process could be considered the most complex. Movement analysis through an open plan office, with limited physical controls, can be challenging.

![image](images/fig4.18.jpg)

**Fig. 4.18.**Movement patterns of Cleaner 8 through multiple zones.

Data recorded by the proximity monitoring solution movement was analysed over a period of two months to identify specific patterns based on the job role and other mitigating factors such as hotspots or desk configurations.

The cleaners were used as an example as they provide a regular stream of data that can be analysed over the baseline period. [Figure 4.18](#chapter4.xhtml#fig4.18) details an extract of data recorded on the proximity monitoring solution over a period of an hour. Movement patterns appear to be controlled, following a predictable path. The cleaner entered the floor at the expected entry point and stayed within adjacent zones until the three spikes in the movement pattern were identified and highlighted. Cross referencing these zones with the floor map can provide some clarity and explains the slight deviations in movement. These do not represent and may not indicate anomalous behaviour.

Using historic pattern analysis, one can detect anomalies that can affect the baseline data. However, subtle changes need to be accommodated so that the risk of false positives is reduced. Historic pattern analysis may not be possible for some roles as the data may not be available due to the nature of the task.

As an example, a plumber may not visit the premises regularly, potentially only when an emergency occurs. They may also require access to all areas within the building to address a water leak.

As part of the experiment, where there was sufficient data available to construct a baseline pattern of movement analysis, data was analysed in an attempt to identify a standard pattern for each role on each floor. [Figure 4.19](#chapter4.xhtml#fig4.19) depicts the movements within three separate days at the same time. It is evident the movement pattern was too random for accurate pattern analysis and could cause too many false positives as there were potentially too many variables to consider when constructing an effective threat model. This was evident when analysing the cleaners, whose movement can be erratic and who may have a legitimate excuse to move freely around an open plan office area.

![image](images/fig4.19.jpg)

**Fig. 4.19.**Pattern analysis over three separate dates.

However, it is possible to construct triggers based on historic pattern analysis when analysing other job functions whose movement is dictated by the task. As an example, air conditioning engineers will operate in or around the airflow extractor fans on each floor. These are located at specific locations within an office, so a trigger could be incorporated if they moved to other areas without legitimate reason.

[Figure 4.20](#chapter4.xhtml#fig4.20) outlines data captured over two days of tracking the same individual. This allows one to visualise how movement patterns can be completely different on a daily basis and illustrates how an anomaly can be detected within a complex movement pattern.

A single event may not indicate anomalous behaviour and could cause false positives. The threat anomaly solution is not based solely on a single method to detect anomalous behaviour. It relies on multiple factors and processes. Each has the potential to raise an alert or increase the risk counter until a combination of events triggers an alert. Murenin *et al.* (2017) describes how anomalous behaviour can be detected through the analysis of human movement trajectories and anomalies in routes using uncommon controlled zones.

![image](images/fig4.20.jpg)

**Fig. 4.20.**Movement patterns that incorporate a trigger.

### 4.7.The Algorithm

One of the primary objectives of this research paper is the construction of a robust and effective algorithm that leverages data retrieved from the recently deployed proximity monitoring solution. The algorithm is an integral part of the Shadow Cloud application that was created for this research project. The algorithm is constructed from active elements, each with the ability to alert and increase a running threat counter. As the contractor enters Dakota’s controlled office space a counter is reset to ‘0’ (zero).

The main elements of the algorithm are as follows:

•Entry point

•Date

•Time of day

•Time spent in each zone

•Number of zones entered

•Zone pattern anomaly

[Figure 4.21](#chapter4.xhtml#fig4.21) depicts the algorithm as a process flow.

### 4.7.1.**Verification process**

Once the proximity solution had been fully integrated within the working practices of Dakota and its 3^(rd) party contractors, a verification process was initiated. With the assistance of the facilities department and the security staff, the algorithm, which formed part of the Shadow Cloud application, was tested to determine any anomalies and false positives.

Triggers were configured at each stage of the algorithm and triggers were analysed to ensure the metrics fell within an acceptable margin of error.

[Figure 4.22](#chapter4.xhtml#fig4.22) depicts each stage of the algorithm and the average percentage of triggers within each stage over a two-month period. As an example, the time spent by each cleaner within each zone was within the permitted parameters 95% of the time. This is visualised in [Fig. 4.15](#chapter4.xhtml#fig4.15), which can be seen as indicative of normal behaviour.

The algorithm has been designed to incorporate some false positives. These would allow a margin of error to be incorporated. As an example, the threat threshold for Dakota has been set to ‘3’. This is based on the analysis of the targets and the data collected. The threshold for another organisation may be higher or lower depending on the risk appetite, the job functions or the physical attributes of the building.

### 4.7.2.*False positives*

The initial testing phase of the threat model produced some false positives that needed to be addressed. Detailed analysis was undertaken at each stage of the algorithm process to ensure the appropriate controls were incorporated into the design.

![image](images/fig4.21.jpg)

**Fig. 4.21.**The algorithm as a process.

![image](images/fig4.22.jpg)

**Fig. 4.22.**Algorithm triggers.

Focussing on the 8 cleaners, [Fig. 4.22](#chapter4.xhtml#fig4.22) depicts the number of triggers as a percentage over the two-month baseline period and through the various phases of the algorithm. [Table 4.6](#chapter4.xhtml#tab4.6) details the number of instances when each specific cleaner activated a trigger over the baseline period.

Each trigger was investigated to ensure the threshold values were sufficient to prevent unnecessary false positives within the overall algorithm. To ensure the experiment did not create false working patterns the data subjects were not directly approached. Facilities and security were questioned to ensure the cleaners’ activity was normal. There were two methods that could be used to set the threshold levels. One of these could be carried out at the algorithmic function stage and the other required changes to be made to the overall threat detection level. To provide the most flexibility, each stage of the algorithm was adjusted to allow a margin of error based on the false detection rate.

**Table 4.6.**False positive triggers over a two-month baseline period from December 2017 to January 2018.

![image](images/tab4.6.jpg)

### 4.7.3.*Experiment validation*

Whilst it can be argued that historic data analysis can determine trigger thresholds, an independent test of the parameters can provide additional assurance. Dakota regularly engages independent cyber and physical security specialists to conduct social engineering tests against the organisation. Once the proximity solution was implemented and Shadow Cloud configured to accept data, a physical penetration test was conducted against Dakota’s London headquarters. A team of two ethical social engineers gained access to Dakota’s London office using social engineering techniques. They posed as sensitive waste disposal contractors, using bogus identification to gain access. They obtained two security passes, with Bluetooth tracking embedded. They gained access to three of the five floors within Dakota’s private office space, as sensitive waste disposal contract staff are only permitted to access selected floors within the building. Due to the time they arrived, tailgating was not an option as no staff were present. The social engineers gained access to the three floors where sensitive waste bins were located, as their access passes permitted them to do.

[Figure 4.23](#chapter4.xhtml#fig4.23) details the expected floor entry point and the zones visited. It also depicts the actual entry points and the floors visited by the social engineers.

![image](images/fig4.23.jpg)

**Fig. 4.23.**Social engineer movement and triggers.

**Table 4.7.**Social engineer proximity data.

![image](images/tab4.7.jpg)

*Source*: Dakota.

The algorithm triggered numerous times during the period the social engineers visited the 3^(rd) floor. [Table 4.7](#chapter4.xhtml#tab4.7) outlines the data collected and the specific triggers.

The threshold value for Dakota was set to ≥3. The social engineers triggered an alert due to the zones they visited and the time spent within those zones. This was prior to the ‘zones visited’ and ‘pattern offset’ elements being processed. Whilst this could be considered an extreme example as social engineers were used, it validates the algorithm based on the thresholds set using baseline data.

### 4.8.Regulations and Legal Considerations

### 4.8.1.**GDPR**

The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), which comes into effect on 25^(th) May 2018, will impact all EU organisations that collect, store and process personal or sensitive data (Ico.org.uk, 2017). To provide an effective threat mitigation solution, Shadow Cloud will record and process human movement data that is not anonymised. As part of its GDPR preparation process Dakota enhanced its privacy and data protection policies, seeking legal advice to ensure the data recorded was lawful and met the ICO’s regulatory requirements.

### 4.8.2.*Privacy laws*

Bruce Schneier (Schneier, 2016) describes surveillance as a technical and a legal problem. A key project deliverable is the identification of threats based on data collected on human behavior patterns.

As Shadow Cloud requires the tracking of individuals it will inevitably pose privacy questions. Whilst it could be argued that analysing data to prevent threats is ethically acceptable, using the data to target individuals for other purposes, which may include discriminating against the target, could breach privacy and human rights law.

To ensure Dakota comply to privacy regulation a clear and concise agreement with all 3^(rd) party organisations was reviewed by the Data Protection Officer and the organisation’s legal representative to ensure the enhanced proximity monitoring process did not infringe on the individual rights of its contract staff. Law professor Eben Moglen once wrote ‘if people are doing nothing wrong then they have the right to maintain a balance between the individual and the power that is monitoring’.

### 4.9.Conclusions and Recommendations

This research project has explored the relationship between human movement patterns and the potential threat posed by an insider with malicious intentions. The real challenge perhaps is to understand how employees navigate a specific environment, how they process physical obstacles and how they interact with co-workers.

Whilst it can be argued that humans have distinctive movement traits, such as using the same entry point, it is evident that trajectories within an open plan office environment can be influenced by a complex set of variables.

Understanding the characteristics of the building and including areas where staff congregate, such as the water cooler, were considered integral when designing a threat model.

The primary focus of the project was the creation of an algorithm that would form part of an overall threat detection solution. The algorithm would initially leverage the data supplied from the target organisation but could be adaptive and used by other human monitoring solutions.

As the target data was analysed it was evident that the algorithm could not rely on a single trigger as this would produce too many false positives. It was clear that a multi-dimensional approach measuring a set of contrasting variables was required.

The algorithm was dissected into seven components, each able to process the specific characteristics of the targets, analysing the time, the date and their movement patterns. The research had intended to identify specific movement patterns that were evident within other research papers that focused on door entry data.

The data provided from the proximity monitoring solution highlighted the complexity of the human decision-making process. When a binary decision had to be made between different access points, the targets would invariably choose the same option; this was evident when entering a floor, as 90% chose the same entry point. However, when presented with multiple options the patterns were far less predictable.

This is why the algorithm could not rely on one measurement metric and incorporated a variety of data sets to determine an anomaly, ultimately reducing the risk of false positives.
