## ABSTRACT

In this modern era, malware has emerged as a malicious cyber threat to critical information and communication infrastructure. Ransomware is a type of malware which holds the victim’s computer hostage by encrypting the data available on it, which makes the data unusable and inaccessible to its legitimate user. The attacker demands that the user pay before the decryption key is released to reverse the attack. This chapter explains about ransomware and its classification, how it impacts different platforms, the severity of ransomware, the methodology used by ransomware to penetrate target machines, the attack vectors used, the latest ransomware attacks, the most common targets of ransomware attacks, how to prevent ransomware attacks, and ways to recover.

*Keywords* : malware, ransomware, botnets, cryptography, bitcoins, crypto-lockers, attack vectors, exploit kits, RSA public key, MD5 algorithm, AES, symmetric key, WannaCry, Petya, SimpleLocker, TeslaCrypt, NotPetya, IoT

### 5.1.Introduction

According to Kapersky, as computers evolved from floppy-disk bootable machines into more sophisticated workstation devices such as laptops and smartphones, malicious software technology or ***malware*** as it is most commonly known evolved along with them (Kaspersky, 2018a). Kaspersky also suggests that malware was existent from information technology’s infancy but that the use of malware only bloomed when personal computers began to be accessible to everyone. The first malware was called the **“Elk Cloner Virus”** (Tasril *et al*., 2017). Examining the features of the Elk Cloner Virus, we see that this malicious technology, which once used simple motifs and techniques, has become more sophisticated and now does more serious damage to computer devices. The Elk Cloner Virus was formed as a “prank” and did not do much harm. Its self-spreading feature relied on social engineering techniques such as floppy-disk insertions (Touchette, 2016). Cyber criminals built upon these foundations until they formed the cyber crime industry as it exists today.

Cyber crime, which has cost industries approximately 100 billion USD, is classified according to the types of malware that the industry produces. Research done by Kapersky has identified the types of malware in a diagram in [Fig. 5.1](#chapter5.xhtml#fig5.1) called the “Malware Classification Tree” (Kaspersky, 2018b).

According to the same report, the classified malwares are considered “specific function” malwares, which means that these malwares are only capable of designated damage and do not produce a complex effect on devices. In contrast, cyber criminals have devised multi-dimensional and multi-functioning malwares. 65.32% of these are *botnets* which affect devices worldwide, and 34.68% of these are a combination of trojans and worms as shown in [Fig. 5.2](#chapter5.xhtml#fig5.2) (Soni, 2018).

![image](images/fig5.1.jpg)

**Fig. 5.1.**Malware classification tree.

![image](images/fig5.2.jpg)

**Fig. 5.2.**Pie chart of multi-functional malware vs. single-function malware (Trojans).

Cisco has classified these versatile malwares as “Advanced Malwares” and has identified the most prominent advanced malwares as the following: riskware, spyware, adware and ransomware with *ransomware* being the deadliest due to its capabilities (Cisco, 2018). Esset defines riskware as a type of malware which increases security risk by using encryption methods to identify user procedures and diverting the procedures into digital transactions (e.g. using a credit card) without the user’s permission (Esset, 2018). Spywares are types of malware which, as can be deduced from their name, collect data about a device, encrypt the information and send the data back to the origin of the malware. These data are used illegally to blackmail the people from whom the data is collected (Stavrou *et al*., 2010). Avast, an anti-virus company, adds that spywares are usually accompanied by adwares, which bombard the user with inappropriate and unwanted pop-ups or advertisements which are harmful to the device (Avast, 2018). Finally, when these features are combined and tailored for a bigger purpose, ***ransomware*** is produced.

An observation can be made that most of the advanced malwares were enhanced by the development of encryption and of new ways to cipher text. The field of **cryptovirology** was developed when researchers realised how these cryptographic techniques could be used to develop malware (Young, 2017).

### 5.2.Ransomware and How It Impacts Different Platforms

Ransomware has affected several companies worldwide by making it necessary for them to pay a large amount of money to their attackers without actually gaining anything beneficial. For instance, Arran Brewery, a brewing company in Scotland, recently paid 2 Bitcoins worth 9,600 GBP to a group of anonymous hackers just to restore the company’s system after all the computers of the company had been locked down (BBC, 2018). A similar incident also happened to the United States government when the Pennsylvania Senate Democratic Caucus had to pay Microsoft to reconstruct the senate’s IT Framework after it was breached on March 3, 2017 (Cimpanu, 2019). The same report states that hackers were demanding 28 Bitcoins as payment, which comes up to 30,000 USD, but instead the government decided to reconstruct for the hefty price of 700,000 USD in order to discourage future attacks to government offices. As these incidents start to increase, attacks are reportedly getting worse.

**Ransomware** is a type of advanced malware where the victim is held at ransom for infected files or documents. The files will not be made available to the victim unless payment is given to the attacker, at which point the attacker will remove the malware from the system (Young, 2017). Ransomware is believed to be one of the most effective malwares for the year 2017, with a total amount of more than 12 million malware counts. The number of malware counts increased by 36% in the last quarter of 2017 (McAfee, 2017). The fact that ransomware accounted for 5 billion US dollars lost globally in the year 2017 led Europol to conclude that ransomware was the most dangerous malware threat, and to say so at their conference entitled “Internet Organised Crime Threat Assessment (IOCTA) 2018” (Walker, 2018).

As ransomware has turned into a booming business, ransomware authors have devised two types of ransomwares: *locker ransomware* and *crypto ransomware* (Deloitte, 2016).

**Locker ransomwares** are the types of ransomwares which do less damage since these ransomwares do not encrypt the files of the victim. Locker ransomware is used to terrorise the victim by prompting the victim to pay for a fine charged for misusing the internet (i.e. watching pornography or downloading illegal programs from torrents). These ransomwares usually come with an interface credible enough for the victim to believe that the warrant is legitimate. Attackers may include the targeted user’s sensitive data, such as their IP address and their last viewed malicious website, to make the warrant more convincing (Deloitte, 2016).

**Crypto ransomwares (crypto-locker ransomwares)** are the types of ransomwares which do more damage to the device and to the financial stability of the victim. Crypto-lockers are a type of ransomware which infects a device and ***encrypts*** the victim’s files until the ransom has been paid. Some of these crypto-lockers even delete the back-up from the system, making it harder to recover the victim’s files (Richet, 2016).

### 5.3.Methodology of Ransomware

The word ransomware comes from the words “ransom” and “malware”. One could define the word ransom as a payment or acquiescence to certain demands in exchange for the release of a hostage or of something held hostage (Merriam-Webster, 2018). So, understanding the criticality of a malware capable of holding virtual platforms to ransom and how the procedure is undertaken is deemed essential.

Much research related to ransomware has pointed out that different ransomwares can have different approaches of propagation, but all ransomwares follow a pattern of propagation that has five phases beginning from the point when the victim’s system is compromised. The five phases are as follows (Brewer, 2016):

1.***First Phase: Acquisition, Utilisation and Infection***

The process of acquiring ransomware is similar to the process of acquiring any other type of malware (Ali, 2017). Norton by Symantec suggests that ransomware and other forms of malware can be categorised into five types depending on how they are acquired, and these are as follows (Norton, 2018):

•Software-integrated malwares: This is when a user downloads a software which is tagged as “free” but which actually comes with the hefty price of having one’s system infected by malware.

•Peer-to-peer virtual sharing: This is when a user shares files electronically by using BitTorrent, uTorrent etc. This does not only refer to file sharing between familiar peers but also refers to the ***illegal*** download of applications via anonymous uploads.

•Removable media: This is the most common method of malware acquisition. Malware is transferred to the victim via electronic devices such as USBs, CDs, External HDDs, etc.

•Network acquisition: This happens when a device connected to the internet comes across a website which has malicious cookies or pop-ups and the victim falls into the trap by exploring the links integrated into these digital platforms.

•General lack of protection: This happens when a device is not kept secure by software which offers protection from malwares.

**Attack Vectors of Ransomware**

Although there are plenty of ways to be infected by malwares, researchers have identified that ***fortunately***, there are only a few ways of acquiring ransomware. These vectors could be divided into those which are acquired through virtual means and those which are acquired through physical means.

*Virtual Means of Ransomware Acquisition*:

a)**Emails** are the main source of ransomware attacks. Statistics show that there are approximately 354.5 billion emails delivered daily worldwide and 85.35 percent of these emails are spam, which means only 14.64 percent of emails are legitimate (Cisco Talos, 2018). IBM estimates that there was a 350 percent increase in spam mails from January 2015 to December 2016 and, alarmingly, despite the fact that not all spam mails contain malwares, the total malware content in spam mails by percentage is increasing. Malware-containing spam mails made up approximately 10 percent of 100 percent of spam mails sent in January 2015. By 2016, spam mails had increased by 450 percent, and malware-containing spam mails made up 210 percent of the 450 percent (IBM, 2016) as shown in [Fig. 5.3](#chapter5.xhtml#fig5.3).

Symantec suggests that these malwares are spreading largely due to a botnet named Necrus which was established just to send out spam mails worldwide (O'Brien, 2017). Symantec also states that ransomware, if acquired through email, can be activated through one of the following steps (O'Brien, 2017):

•Malicious attachments being opened

•Malicious attachments initiating third party JavaScript or PowerShell commands

•Malicious attachments initiating the download of **exploit kits**

![image](images/fig5.3.jpg)

**Fig. 5.3.**Volumes of malicious and non-malicious spam.

b)**Exploit Kits** literally exploit the vulnerabilities of a computer. Exploit kits are used to take advantage of a particular device’s weaknesses via web browsers, programs or operating systems. Most exploit kits are integrated into websites, and once a user visits that particular site, the kit is activated in the user’s device. The kit will then scan for vulnerabilities in the device used to navigate the website and, subsequently, it will implement the malware into the device in question. The infected website is not necessarily a malicious website since legitimate websites like BBC or Yahoo could be infested through advertisements as well (Monrose *et al*., 2015). According to a study done by Malwarebytes, as shown in [Fig. 5.4](#chapter5.xhtml#fig5.4), 61 percent of all exploit kits contain exploit payloads for ransomware (Malwarebytes Labs, 2016).

*Physical Means of Ransomware Acquisition*

**Social Engineering** is used as a sure but risky way to spread malware. Social Engineering is the manipulation of human psychology in order to persuade a person to perform a behaviour which may have a devastating effect on that person, another person or a group of individuals. Researchers may refer to it as “hacking” a human for an intended purpose (Mann, 2008).

![image](images/fig5.4.jpg)

**Fig. 5.4.**Exploit payload summary.

*Kevin Mitnick’s Proposed Social Engineering Methodology* (Gallegos-Segovia, 2017):

•**Information Gathering:** This is the step where details of the victim are gathered by certain individuals.

•**Trust:** This is the step where the attacker establishes a deeper connection with the victim. By doing so, an appropriate attack vector could be identified by the attacker.

•**Exploitation:** This is where the attacker executes the plan of exploitation and the ransomware infects the device.

•**Reach:** This is where the system is finally compromised. Usually the attacker is not in contact with the victim at this point.

The *December 2015 Ukraine Power Grid Cyber Attack* is an example of how these methods have been used. Numerous reports suggest that the incident was a well-planned attack on Ukraine’s power company named Ukrenergo (BBC, 2017). Most investigators were amazed by how well the information and trust gathering was executed and further blamed the Russians for devising a way into the Ukraine’s SCADA system then manipulating the system through an infection caused by a USB (Zetter, 2016).

These proposed methods of social engineering can be further used to identify the different types of attacks that can be established. These are as follows (Gallegos-Segovia, 2017):

•**Ego Attacks:** The attacker tries to create a personal connection with the victim by offering help and proving the reliability of the attacker’s intelligence to the victim. Once the victim falls for a transparent manipulation, the attacker executes the ransomware on the system.

•**Sympathy Attacks:** The attacker uses emotional means to create a connection with the victim. When the victim starts trusting the attacker, the attacker executes the ransomware on the system.

•**Bullying Attacks:** The attacker uses force, dominance or black-mailing to gather information. This is the most common and most effective type of social engineering attack.

2.***Second Phase: Consignment and Implementation***

The next step is the process of installing the malware on the system, encrypting the ransomware program inside the device and further establishing a secure platform for the **upcoming** command and control network.

The ransomware uses a simple RSA asymmetric public key (Emsisoft, 2018) that will call a **GET** or **POST** request at some point (Securonix, 2018). The **GET** or **POST** request would consist of the following parameters to be collected (Emsisoft, 2018; Securonix, 2018):

•computer name

•processor information

•volume serial

•operating system

•active drives

•Public IP in a pattern of: { ipv4bot\[.\]whatismyipaddress\[.\] com}

•disk space

Researchers (Emsisoft, 2018) have identified the reasons why ransomware developers use RSA public keys in coding ransomwares and these are the following:

•They take up lesser space in memory and can be easily transported.

•Third parties or malware analysts surveying the network would only see plain texts and scrambled encrypted network traffic.

•This gives the malware authors a chance to use their own server during the communication with the deployed ransomware.

After identifying the victim through their unique hashed identity (using the MD5 Algorithm), the ransomware would identify whether the process was running via **root or admin access** (Rajpal and Kotov, 2014). If the ransomware was running through either root or admin access, then further installation of the ransomware would take place through the following steps (Rajpal and Kotov, 2014):

As shown in the flowchart, the ransomware would unpack itself to the memory of the device or the hard disk and then would execute itself. The software would then create multiple copies of a stage dropper and inject the payload into explorer.exe and svchost.exe. In the next *phases*, the ransomware would also delete all shadow copies and back-up files and finally disable the device’s ability to restore the system.

![image](images/fig5.5.jpg)

**Fig. 5.5.**Ransomware installation procedures.

These processes normally take only a few seconds to execute and usually are executed without the user’s knowledge (Brewer, 2016), as shown in [Fig. 5.5](#chapter5.xhtml#fig5.5).

3.***Third Phase: File Encryption and Command and Control (C2)***

*Command and Control Establishment*

This phase is the most important phase of a ransomware since, in this phase, a ransomware will do whatever it has been coded to do. After making sure that all packages of the ransomware have been successfully injected into the system, the ransomware platform in the device would now communicate to the command centre (host) via an RSA key pair (Brewer, 2016). A .bit namecoin would then be used to query.bit domain-friendly DNS servers through the code: {ns1.crop\[.\]corpservers\[.\]ru; a\[.\]dsnpod\[.\] com}. Once the connection is established, this is where the information gathered via a **GET** or **POST** request would be sent to the host in the Base64 encoding format \[31\].

Researchers have (Rajpal and Kotov, 2014) identified that over the past few years, ransomware developers have shifted from using HTTP to using TOR and SSL during the communication phase of command and control establishment. The simplest reason is that it is more complex to decrypt TOR and SSL data in contrast to HTTP data. Data encrypted with RC4 encryption, which is the most commonly used method to encrypt HTTP data, can be decrypted and fingerprinted using the simple *mathematical expression* \[a – z\]\\ = \[z – z 0 – 9\]+, also called *Regrex* (Kaspersky, 2016)*.* TOR and SSL’s full encryption makes it difficult for developers to code a network signature for initial stage detection; however, TOR is less used due to multiple network restrictions (Rajpal and Kotov, 2014).

*File Encryption Process*

The following files and folders are excluded from encryption:

•desktop.ini

•autorun.ini

•nuser.ini

•GDCB-DECRYPT.txt

These are excluded to allow the command server to connect to the device controlled (NJCCIC, 2018).

The encryption of files is done through a combination of RSA 2048bit (public key) and AES 256bit (victim data) encryption. After data encryption, the ransomware is expected to encrypt the files by assigning a public-private key for the randomly generated symmetric key. This process is shown in [Fig. 5.6](#chapter5.xhtml#fig5.6).

This type of encryption does not need any shared secret key, which makes it easier for the attacker to keep the ciphered text and only allow the victim access once ransom is paid (Emsisoft, 2018).

![image](images/fig5.6.jpg)

**Fig. 5.6.**Process of encryption used by ransomware.

In most ransomwares, Virlock is commonly used for encryption. Virlock consists of two layers of encryption in which the **first layer** is a combination of XOR and ROL encryption which is backed up by a **second layer** of XOR encryption (Lindskog and Zavarskya, 2016). All the encrypted files are converted into .GDCB or .KRAB files which then prompt a report back to the command centre using the same **GET** or **POST** request (Rajpal and Kotov, 2014).

4.***Fourth Phase: Back-Up Corruption***

Unlike most malwares which are usually designed just to implement the infection that the program is designed to spread, most ransomwares are designed to delete the back-up of the victim’s files or at least the back-up of the ransomware (Brewer, 2016).

Ransomwares usually end by deleting the shadow copies of the victim’s files by either of two available methods: the VSSAdmin service or the WMI service. The two methods are identified in (Securonix, 2018), which also shows the exact code used by the ransomware to delete all the shadow copies. This code can be seen below.

5.***Fifth Phase: User Detection, Payment and Clean-Up***

The FBI has claimed that the Barack Obama Blue Blackmail Virus has been one of the biggest issues faced by the USA. The virus resulted in numerous people logging in to their devices and suddenly seeing President Obama’s face along with an FBI notice asking them to pay a certain fine (Osborne, 2018). This news is a perfect example of the aftermath of a ransomware attack. Attackers demand a certain amount of pecuniary reimbursement for the locked files, which should be paid within a certain period of time.

Due to the advancement of technology, most attackers require victims to pay using bitcoins but there are other viable means of payment like credit or debit card payments, etc. (Rajpal and Kotov, 2014).

[Table 5.1](#chapter5.xhtml#tab5.1) suggests that most ransomware attackers require victims to pay from a range of 100 USD to 500 USD or from 0.5 BTC (3,280 USD) to 0.8 BTC (5,250 USD).

Usually these instructions are saved in the hard drive with file names such as “HELP\_DECRYPT” for CryptoWall V3 or “HELP\_YOUR\_FILES” for CryptoWall V4. Once payment is given to the attacker, the attacker will decrypt the files and the ransomware will clean up by itself (Brewer, 2016).

**Table 5.1.**Payment options.

 
| Family || Payment Options || Price of Decrypting |
| --- | --- | --- |
| TeslaCrypt || Bitcoin Payments are normally required but developers also accepted credit or debit card payments in the earlier variations. || 500 USD — increased to 1000 USD if not paid within the time frame (Kaspersky, 2018c) |
| CryptoLocker || Started off with more options but eventually these options were narrowed down to Bitcoin || 300 USD (Cannell, 2018) |
| Petya or NotPetya || At this point only Bitcoin is accepted by the criminals (Fruhlinger, 2017). || 0.3–0.5 BTC |
| WannaCry || Payments must be made in Bitcoin || Between $300 (£228) and $600 (Gibbs, 2017) |
| SimpleLocker || Payments must be made via the Ukrainian MoneXy cash transfer system. || 260 hryvnias ($22, £13) (NJCCIC, 2016) |
| GandCrab || Dash or Bitcoin || 1200 USD — increased to 2400 USD if not paid within the time frame (Abrams, 2018) |

### 5.4.Latest and Most Prominent Ransomwares

As explained before, ransomware is an evolving business with malware developers as its vendors and cyber criminals as its customers. Due to this “booming” trend, many variations of ransomwares have become available in the market. The following are the top five strongest ransomwares in the last five years, as identified by an organisation of security decision makers called CSO.

Top Five Strongest Ransomwares (Fruhlinger, 2017):

1.**CryptoLocker**: considered the most generic variation of ransomware due to its ability to encrypt all the files inside the victim’s device. These ransomwares use law enforcement-themed GUIs to threaten the victim into paying the ransom, which they must do since decryption is near to impossible. All back-up files are deleted as soon as the infection starts (Cannell, 2018). CryptoLocker is usually called the “primitive ransomware” since the developers have not updated the features of the said ransomware (Fruhlinger, 2017).

2.**TeslaCrypt**: considered a subvariant of CryptoLocker; this ransomware started claiming victims in 2015. This ransomware used gaming websites to spread itself and to infect devices, which is why those affected by this ransomware were mostly gamers. This ransomware only encrypted files with a file size lower than 268 MB (Osborne, 2018). The developers of the ransomware have decided to shut down operations and upon doing so, the developers also posted the universal decryption key which helped infected devices to recover successfully (Koller, 2016).

The final message of TeslaCrypt, which included the master decryption key, read as follows:

*“Project closed! Master key for decrypt: 440A241DD80FCC5664E861989DB 716E08CE627D8D40C7EA360AE855C727A49EE. Wait for other people make universal decrypt software. We are sorry!”*

3.**SimpleLocker**: a ransomware effective on the Android platform which gathers the IMEI, the model number and the manufacturer details for the command and control centre. Encryption is done via the AES encryption method and the ransomware also accesses the camera to take a picture of the victim. This picture is used to further threaten the victim into paying the ransom (NJCCIC, 2016).

4.**WannaCry**: considered one of the deadliest ransomwares to be developed. This ransomware shut down multiple hospitals across the United Kingdom and Ukraine. The developers of WannaCry were able to detect vulnerabilities in Windows which were first discovered by the United States National Security Agency. Symantec later on began to suspect that the developers originated from a North Korean-linked group called Lazarus (Fruhlinger, 2017). This ransomware is also one of the latest. 6,912 appointments were cancelled and 19,000 affected when WannaCry affected NHS operations in the year 2017. This attack, despite being “unsophisticated” as Kingsley Manning suggests, became so successful due to the fact that the different NHS offices were “intertwined” with each other, thus quickening the spread of the ransomware (BBC, 2017).

5.**Petya** and **NotPetya**: launched a week after the WannaCry outbreak, this ransomware is confirmation that a new age of ransomwares has begun (Fruhlinger, 2017). Petya or NotPetya was spread by attackers who sent a job application document via email in the PDF file format. When the PDF file was accessed by the company, the ransomware was unleashed. NotPetya is the very first ransomware which does not need any spam emails to be sent or social engineering to be carried out in order for infection to occur and administrative access to be gained. As long as there is a network connection in between two devices, Petya or NotPetya can move from one to the other (Fruhlinger, 2017).

Aside from these famous ransomware attacks, there are a few other ransomwares making their name in the market. One of the most prominent in recent years is GandCrab which just released their latest version, Version 4, in July 2018. GandCrab acts exactly like CryptoLocker and is also considered deadly since the ransomware converts files to .KRAB extension files once encrypted (Abram, 2018).

### 5.5.Platforms Affected by Ransomware Attacks

Malwares in general can affect multiple technological platforms, but recent studies have shown that ransomware has only affected three technological platforms so far. During the height of the *WannaCry* ransomware attacks, banks and bank users in India were falsely warned through circulating *Whatsapp* messages that the ransomware had actually breached ATM machines throughout the country. These allegations were proven to be hoaxes upon deeper investigation by one of the leading banks of India, called the Rural Bank of India (NDTV, 2017). Had this been true, ransomware could have been considered a deadly terrorism weapon by governments around the world.

Researchers have identified that ransomware has affected mobile platforms, computing platforms, and IoT and cloud computing platforms. Out of these three types of platform, it is most vital to keep IoT and cloud computing platforms secure.

a)**Computing Platform:** Computing platforms have always been those most affected by ransomwares. As previously discussed, ransomwares act on computers by infecting the system and encrypting the files in the system until a certain amount of ransom is paid. A large number of ransomware attacks on computing platforms — 86.87 percent of total ransomware attacks in 2016 — are directed at home users (Walton, 2017).

b)**Mobile Platform:** Due to people spending more time on their mobile phones, doctors have concluded that most people are suffering from mobile addiction (SC Magazine, 2017). Having this in mind, cyber criminals have taken advantage of people who are “addicted” to mobile phones.

*Android —* This has been the biggest target of ransomware attacks on mobile platforms. This is mainly due to the “openness” of the Android platform. With mobile ransomware increasing by 137.8% from the first to the second quarter of 2017, SC Magazine predicted that there would be a spike in mobile ransomware in 2018 (Snow, 2016). However, in Android ransomware and in mobile ransomware overall, cryptolockers are less common since file encryption would be useless on mobile platforms due to the cloud backup feature that most mobile devices have. This is the reason why most Android ransomwares lock applications with a coded GUI which shows the details of the ransomware once the application is opened (Norton, 2018). The newest mobile ransomware, specifically dedicated for Android, is better implemented. This ransomware, which is tagged as *Android.Lockroid.E*, locks the whole mobile device instead of just locking the specific applications inside the mobile device. This way, the user’s mobile device would be locked and unusable until the ransom had been paid (Savage *et al*., 2015).

*iOS —* According to a report released by Symantec, iOS devices are mostly secure due to Apple’s Technological and Security Ecosystem Structure. The only way that an iPhone can be vulnerable to ransomware is when the mobile device in question has undergone the process called “jailbreaking” (Ismail, 2018). Despite all the protection that Apple offers for iOS phones, researchers suggest that Proton Remote Access Trojan (RAT) has affected plenty of iPhones worldwide (Snow, 2016).

c)**IoT and Cloud Computing Platforms**

As previously discussed, the invention of NotPetya paved the way for a type of ransomware which does not need third party connections like spam mails or social engineering to infect and gain administrative access to any device. This led developers and researchers to think of the next step that ransomware would become capable of. Although there has been no reported ransomware attack on any IoT or cloud computing platform, the implementation of this idea is not too far away, especially now that IoT is being plagued by DDoS attacks such as Mirai (Cobb, 2017). Since ransomware developers can now understand and create ransomwares which can multiply by themselves on a shared network, IoT technologies are not safe any more since all IoTs share a common network, that is, the cloud (Budd, 2016). Although speculation about Microsoft 365’s cloud-based technology being attacked by a ransomware named CERBER or RANSOM\_CERBER. CAD has not been fully proven, TrendMicro researchers have stated that the ransomware in question can encrypt 442 file types using AES 265 and RSA encryption techniques. However, it seems like the coding of cloud ransomware is just in its initial stages since the only command that the ransomware can successfully deliver is to play an audio message in a computer-generated (creepy) voice (Sneed, 2016). These incidents may actually hint at a growth of ransomware in the IoT and cloud industries.

d)**Industries**

Ransomwares are not only built for the sole purpose of affecting regular citizens but are also built for a larger cause. Since malware development can be used for money making and has already become a booming business, malware developers have concentrated attacks on industries where more benefit could be derived. A report by Scientific American Magazine states that cyber criminals have been targeting and crippling important “institutions that everybody relies on” through different types of ransomware (Martin, 2017). According to a report by CSO, the three industries which have been most affected by ransomware attacks are the following: healthcare, government and education. Out of these, *healthcare* has been the most affected of all (Osborne, 2018). These industries are targeted more since they run 24/7 and thus need their updated files all the time. Serious threats can arise when institutional or organisational data from these industries is leaked or sold on the dark web. This is why these industries tend to pay for the ransom quicker than the other ransomware victims (Cylance, 2018).

Alarmingly, it has been made clear in a report by Cylance (called the 2017 Threat Report) that healthcare has obviously been targeted the most, and that law enforcement and/or ICT developers within the healthcare industry do not seem to have any methods to overcome these threats.

The pie charts below show the ransomware attacks performed on each type of industry over the span of a year (Kidron, 2017). Whilst there was a significant drop in the percentage of total ransomware attacks affecting almost every industry from 2016 to 2017, as shown in [Fig. 5.7](#chapter5.xhtml#fig5.7), the percentage of total ransomware attacks affecting the healthcare and food industries increased (by 24 percent for the healthcare industry). Scientific American Magazine (Martin, 2017) has reported that, aside from the Pennsylvania Senate incident, police stations such as the Swansea Police Department (2013) and Fire Departments in Maryland (2015) have been struck by ransomwares due to the simple fact that these organisations hold sensitive and important data about citizens which is vital for the proper functioning of the government. The police department of Swansea had to pay 750 USD just to recover their files but the Fire Department of Maryland opted not to pay in order to discourage further attacks.

![image](images/fig5.7.jpg)

**Fig. 5.7.**Industries impacted by ransomware (Kidron, 2017).

Scientific American Magazine’s report (Martin, 2017), delivered a clear warning to those in charge of law enforcement and cyber security. These cyber attacks are happening to the health industry and the government now, but a day will come when these malicious attacks could become worse. Critical infrastructures such as dams, power grids or worse could be attacked. Supervisory Control And Data Acquisition (SCADA) systems, which must be frequent users of the internet in order to function, could also be attacked. A report suggests cyber criminals have coded a ransomware which is dedicated to infecting SCADA systems and this ransomware is named LogicLocker (Kidron, 2017). This ransomware uses socket APIs and manipulates weak credential-authentication mechanisms into infecting the workstation. After infection, the ransomware does not encrypt the files but instead deletes all current authentication passwords and lets the command and control centre change the password to one of the attacker’s choice. This way, the company affected needs to pay the ransom for the new authentication details (Turpin and Harmsworth, 2001).

### 5.6.Preventing Ransomware Attacks

Different companies, different researchers and different anti-virus brands have different suggestions for preventing ransomware infection and spreading. Although different research studies have yielded different and sometimes opposing opinions on how to prevent ransomware, the general approach to preventing ransomware is always the same. Prevention can be done in two ways, which we call human prevention and advanced prevention.

a)**Human Prevention**

**Information Dissemination:** With the advancement of technology, people are now expected to gather information, be vigilant and ***educate*** themselves about the latest news in the digital society (Ali, 2017). Information about harmful software, not just *ransomware*, should be disseminated on different platforms so that they reach a wider audience. These platforms are as follows (Carbon Black, 2018):

•**Mail** (Physical Mail or Email)

•**Newsletters**

•**Company or educational briefings**

•**Websites**

•**Reports**

•**Conferences**

•**Workshops**

•**Other media** (Social Media etc.)

Although people can learn plenty from these sources, they should be wise enough to choose credible sources like the government or IEEE. Websites accessed for information regarding malwares should ideally be from anti-virus company blogs such as Kaspersky, Avast, Esset, etc.

b) **Technical Prevention:** A few technical but simple steps are suggested by multiple research studies in the field of malware. These steps are subcategorised by different digital vectors and most of these steps can be found online.

**Back-up, Back-up, Back-up!** (Rajpal and Kotov, 2014)**:**

•*Regularly Back-up Data*: Back-up could be done in two different ways. Since there is a minimal chance of being hit by ransomware on both your device as well as a selected cloud application, users are advised to use a cloud back-up for important and sensitive files. This is the same reason why mobile ransomware does not encrypt files inside the mobile device but just locks the whole system instead.

•*External Hard Disk Back-up:* An external hard disk can also be suggested as a back-up measure, but researchers suggest that after back-up, external hard disks should be unplugged from the computers (Ali, 2017).

•*Deploy User Account Control:* This will help limit the access of ransomwares since most ransomware procedures require administrative permissions.

**Email Security** (O'Brien, 2017)**:**

•Prevent downloads of unknown attachment files.

•Do not open spam mails if the mail is sent by an unknown user.

•Install special email defender applications that have real-time link following.

•Disable macro scripts on the files received via emails (O'Brien, 2017)*.*

**Anti-Virus:**

•Anti-virus software should always be updated (Ali, 2017)*.*

**Other Important Preventive Measures:**

•Disable remote services if not in use.

•Disable Bluetooth services if not in use.

•Limit access to unreliable websites (i.e. porn sites).

•Limit clicking on links provided by colleagues; instead, type the full address into the link bar.

**Prevention for Mobile Users** (Ismail, 2018)**:**

•Apps should only be installed from trusted application stores.

•Check the permissions of the application being downloaded to see if the permissions are appropriate for the use of the application.

•Try as much as possible not to jailbreak iOS platforms

**c)Advanced Prevention**

Multiple research studies online have given suggestions for different approaches that bigger companies can use in preventing ransomware attacks. A few of the most effective advanced prevention techniques are (Zetter, 2016):

•Key back-up

•Process monitoring on Android platforms

•Using a connection monitor and connection breaker

•Honeypot techniques

**Ways to Recover from Ransomware Attacks**

An incomplete ransom attack is when the user gets to know that there is a possible ransomware attack due to appearances of .KRAB and/or GDCB-DECRYPT.txt files but the files are not yet encrypted. In order to recover from an incomplete ransom attack, the user is advised to automatically run the anti-virus application, which will do a virus scan of the system. It is also suggested that all devices infected with the ransomware should be disconnected from the network to protect cloud based or external back-up files (Brewer, 2016).

It is much harder to recover from a **successful** ransom attack. Organisations and researchers always ask a common question: **To Pay or NOT To Pay?** There is a good reason why researchers and organisations ask the question and it all has to do with the rate of success of file recovery and the eradication of the ransomware. Even when the ransom has been paid and the files decrypted, the user can never be sure that there are no more residual files from the ransomware left in the system (Brewer, 2016). The ransomware residual files can actually hide in mailboxes or directories without the user knowing and these files can be triggered at any time that the user is logged in to the computer. If the user opts to pay for the ransom, as previously stated, the ransomware **should** delete itself and hostage files should be returned without any alterations. The article (Brewer, 2016) finally suggests that buying a newer device is wiser especially if files are backed up online since this would help reduce the likelihood that the ransomware developer will produce more ransomware applications.

### 5.7.Conclusion

Although ransomwares are ranked as only the sixth most prominent malware in most cyber crime reports, ransomware is still a deadly malware. This is due to the fact that ransomware has the capability to do damage by means of infecting a user’s device and encrypting either all the files or the whole device. The damage will only stop when the victim has paid the ransom, and in most cases, the length of time given for the victim to pay the ransom is limited. If the deadline passes, multiple research studies have suggested that the victim would then be obliged to pay double the original ransom price. Multiple research studies also suggest that despite the victim being able to pay the ransom price, there is no guarantee of his files being returned and/or the ransomware being eradicated completely from the system.

Most of the prominent ransomwares such as WannaCry, CryptoLocker, TeslaCrypt, SimpleLocker, GandCrab, Petya and NotPetya use RSA 2048-bit encryption for the public key and AES 256-bit encryption to encrypt the victim’s data. Ransomware’s most prominent feature aside from encryption is the command and control feature which actually gave birth to a new type of malware. This step made Kaspersky predict that the new trend for 2018 is for a shift from ransomwares to ***cryptomining*** to occur. Cryptomining is a term that describes an attacker’s use of better ransomware.

**Human Involvement**

Human involvement in an attack is key since ransomware as a simple hard-coded software is **useless.** Ransomware cannot spread and infect devices **on its own.** Human involvement actually gives life to ransomware and the way ransomware infects devices. Humans create the ransomware software and humans spread the virus. As previously stated, most acquisitions of ransomwares occur due to a human falling for the spam email trick set by hackers. Social engineering, which was previously discussed, also plays a vital part since social engineers use psychology to achieve illegal ends. Humans are also responsible for activating the malware since most ransomware activation happens when .exe files disguised as PDF or Word files are executed. Cyber criminals are also responsible for the encryption of files inside the victim’s device. Finally, once the trap is set, humans are also responsible for choosing whether **to pay** or **not to pay.**

Human empowerment, along with the proper dissemination of information, is key, as it is important for the public to know what ransomwares are and how to fight the attacks. With proper education about this topic, humans can actually reduce the likelihood of these types of cyber attacks by means of early-stage prevention. Finally, ransomware attacks can only be prevented if the **humans** in the computing environment are willing to critically educate themselves about the digital advancements in different computing industries.

## Chapter 6

## Protecting and Securing Data Through Blockchain Across Industries

Stefan Kendzierskyj\* and Hamid Jahankhani^†

*Northumbria University London, UK*

\*[*stefan.kendzierskyj@northumbria.ac.uk*](mailto:stefan.kendzierskyj@northumbria.ac.uk)

^†*[Hamid.jahankhani@northumbria.ac.uk](mailto:Hamid.jahankhani@northumbria.ac.uk)*

## ABSTRACT

Blockchain is being viewed as a mechanism that can further protect and enhance the security of data due to its properties of immutability, auditability and encryption, whilst providing transparency between parties who may not know each other and who therefore are operating in a trustless environment. It’s true that blockchain has its roots in cryptocurrency applications and is still evolving for that purpose in the financial sector, but many other organisations across different industries are beginning to see the non-crypto use cases in which this mechanism can be used to record data that cannot be changed or reversed or as smart contracts (as a way to time-stamp transactions between parties). Consequently, blockchain is becoming extremely relevant and purposeful. Organisations have various options. They can run blockchain as permissionless (anyone can join), permissioned (invitations are required) or hybrid (like a consortium). They can also choose whether data should be held on-chain or off-chain in data lakes. With industry entering its fourth industrial revolution (Industry 4.0), the addition of blockchain as a complementary technology has its place; there are some industries very suited to the significant impact it may bring. Also, the advances made in areas such as Internet of Things and Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence may have considerable impact on the amount of data we collect for analysis and the ways in which we store, manage and analyse it. They may also increase the likelihood of cyber attacks and the ripple effects they cause. This has also become complicated, as cyber attacks have become much more sophisticated in recent years. Cyber attacks come in different configurations, and various industry sectors have suffered from a range of these different attack vectors, resulting in some devastating outcomes. These cyber attacks have manifested in the shape of ransomware, malware, manipulation methods, phishing and spear-phishing. Whilst data breaches are a serious incident, there is a growing concern in most organisations regarding attacks that are designed to have a more destructive effect, such as the Ukraine cyber attack in 2015 that resulted in a shutdown of the power grid, or the WannaCry ransomware attack in 2017 that caused widespread chaos with healthcare institutions unable to carry out any tasks since access to data/systems was unavailable.

*Keywords*: blockchain, Industry 4.0, smart contracts, cyber attacks, IoT, AI, ML, WannaCry, immutability, auditability

### 6.1. Introduction

With the fast-growing development of cloud-based architecture, smart technology such as Internet of Things (IoT) and many other new developments of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) have caused a large increase in data volumes and more complexities to arise during the process of finding a more secure and efficient way to handle and manage the data. This is heightened by the increasing cyber attacks and the wide range of attack vectors. Cyber attacks have become a lucrative and more organised criminal behaviour with the availability of ransomwareas-a-service, as an example. It’s becoming apparent that even with attention to the various business structures and methods to mitigate cyber security risks, such as continual review of policies/compliance, training, patching, deploying Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems (IDPS), etc., the cyber security breach effect has not been lessened. In fact, more diverse types of cyber attacks are increasing and growing year on year at a faster and faster rate, particularly in the healthcare industry. Attacks on the healthcare industry account for more than 50% of all cyber attacks. From an organisational perspective, there are of course many advantages to having access to modern software and system developments, and to living in a ‘data on demand’ culture. Organisations will benefit in many ways, particularly with the more recent developments in Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning. However, there is a feeling that data usage and access to data are not very strictly controlled. There are also concerns over the possible impact this may have. For instance, it may lead to criminal activity such as identity theft and victimisation.

With these points in mind, there is a growing motivation for industry to look at the benefits blockchain can offer in the shape of providing another layer of security and privacy to the organisation’s data and allowing the option to control data permission and use. This can provide an added layer of security which can work in harmony with the traditional cloud security systems and allow for a more secure and transparent way to handle data. The synergy between cloud and blockchain might be useful, especially as putting all data on the blockchain may place too heavy a burden on the blockchain in terms of processing, performance and scalability. Also, one must take into account the requirement of GDPR that those whose data have been collected by the organization must have the right of erasure. This prohibits the storage of personal data on a blockchain level. It might be useful in some cases to handle data off-chain and use blockchain as an immutable mechanism to capture details in chronological order and to authenticate access to data held off-chain in data lakes.

### 6.2.What Is Blockchain?

Blockchain is said to be one of the most disruptive computing paradigms after the Internet (Swan, 2015). The technology has advanced such that it is now more than just a means of financial and economic trading. Recently, different arms of industry have started to harness the technology to take advantage of its benefits and the many ways it can be applied.

The concept of blockchain was first circulated as a white paper (Satoshi, 2008), and created under the pseudonym Satoshin Nakamoto. As it was originally developed for use with a cryptocurrency (Bitcoin), blockchain is often referred to as Blockchain 1.0 when it is used with cryptocurrencies (Swan, 2015, p. ix). Blockchain 2.0 refers to the blockchain technology underlying smart contracts which go beyond just cash transactions, and Blockchain 3.0 describes blockchain technology which can be used in healthcare, government, intellectual property, etc. The healthcare industry is a good example of an industry in which issues surrounding privacy, security and access collide. It is also under pressure in several different directions, as there is a growing global demand for medical services as the elderly population grows and the number of elderly patients increases, an increase in the amount of data to be stored, an increase in data breaches, and so on. Blockchain adoption in the healthcare community is becoming widely accepted, as some surveys by leading industry providers indicate.

A recent survey (carried out by the IBM Institute for Business Value in 2017) of 200 healthcare executives (a mix of payers and providers across 16 countries) found that 16% were expecting a block-chain solution for healthcare to be deployed soon. This survey suggests that the percentage of healthcare executives who expected a blockchain solution to be deployed in their industry in 2017 is much higher than the percentage of executives from other sectors such as banking/finance and commerce who expected a blockchain solution to be deployed in their industry in 2017. This is despite the fact that blockchain methodology has been established in these sectors longer than it has been established in healthcare. [Figure 6.1](#chapter6.xhtml#fig6.1) describes the early adopters in the healthcare industry as ‘trailblazers’ and compares them to other healthcare institutions. It also serves as a timeline of how the healthcare industry will react to adoption.

To understand the use cases, it is necessary to analyse the healthcare sector and how the development of electronic records has not improved the interoperability between different devices. Essentially, the electronic data is sitting in silos. The IBM survey ([Fig. 6.2](#chapter6.xhtml#fig6.2)) shows the friction areas around inaccessible information (that is, the interoperability and security/privacy concerns regarding data).
