## Chapter 7

## Bring Your Own Device: GDPR Compliant or Headache? The Human Aspect in Security and Privacy

Jaime Ibarra Jimenez\* and Hamid Jahankhani^†

*Northumbria University London, UK*

*[\*jaime.jimenez@northumbria.ac.uk](mailto:jaime.jimenez@northumbria.ac.uk)*

^†[*hamid.jahankhani@northumbria.ac.uk*](mailto:hamid.jahankhani@northumbria.ac.uk)

## ABSTRACT

The world is facing an era in which technology has a crucial impact on the growth of businesses. It is claimed that in 2020 20 billion devices will be connected to the internet, therefore, data is crucial for employees, customers and organisations. The implementation of the European General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) gives the owner better control of their personal data. Consequently, organisations must be prepared to face cutting-edge threats to security in order to protect individuals against potential harm caused by unauthorized access to their data. Bring Your Own Device (BYOD) is a policy which provides some flexibility within organisations, and which results in better commitment in employees. This chapter analyses the impact of GDPR in BYOD architectures and proposes the integration of a multi-layer policy with an Information Governance Framework to ensure data privacy, focusing on the human factor when protecting personal devices.

*Keywords*: BYOD, GDPR, Blockchain, cyber security, mobile platforms, insider attack

### 7.1.Introduction

Since May of 2018, the European General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) has been implemented, and organisations keep struggling to adapt their procedures and core functions to achieve regulatory compliance. A survey of over 1,000 companies in the UK, Germany, France, and Italy before its implementation discovered that 60% of these companies were not ready for GDPR, whilst 44% showed concern about whether their company could comply with it (Jltspecialty.com, 2018).

One of the biggest concerns for organisations currently is the BYOD policy. BYOD allows employees to bring their own devices to work and to use them for professional purposes. Most companies allow the use of personal devices within the premises because this saves money. Allowing users to purchase their own devices makes a simpler network infrastructure (commonly wireless-based) a possibility, reducing the stress of IT administrators regarding network and endpoint management (McKinney and Pickard, 2016). Employees feel more comfortable increasing the productivity of the organisation by having the most up-to-date mobile devices and are able to continue working outside of work hours. Years ago, organisations were adapted to the Use What You Are Told (UWYT) principle. Electronic devices were provided by the company and were also customized according to their requirements and organisational goals (Wainwright, 2018). However, nowadays the world is facing an era when “millennials” are modifying the business landscape by having their personal devices connected at any time and at any place. These days, students who are still in high school already have the most up-to-date mobile devices, which are linked to their social media accounts. Moreover, they say that they do not have any concerns about sharing their personal information on the Internet. However, this is worrying for security experts because of the risks associated with this mindset. Security experts aim to train people to reduce risks based on social engineering techniques that could compromise the organisation’s productivity along with its prestige (Thomson, 2012). This is easily achieved in big organisations because they have the budget, governance frameworks, policies and controls to achieve compliance. However, this is not the case for SMEs, which often lack skilled cyber security personnel (McKinney and Pickard, 2016).

The BYOD policies implemented in most organisations are imprecise and immature in terms of security. This chapter analyses whether BYOD complies with the recently implemented GDPR, or whether it seems likely to cause trouble and concern for IT administrators and security experts, who need to ensure regulatory compliance. In addition, it shows the importance of the human factor when it comes to security and privacy. The rest of the chapter is divided as follows: [Section 7.2](#chapter7.xhtml#sec7.2) gives the reader a brief description of BYOD, along with the architecture commonly used in enterprise networks for personal devices, and the security concerns surrounding BYOD, [Section 7.3](#chapter7.xhtml#sec7.3) analyses the impact of GDPR on modern BYOD policies, [Section 7.4](#chapter7.xhtml#sec7.4) suggests practices and guidelines for achieving endpoint security in personal devices, [Section 7.5](#chapter7.xhtml#sec7.5) proposes a framework for the design, implementation and monitoring of a BYOD policy, and also discusses the importance of governance in achieving GDPR compliance regardless of the size of the organisation, and finally [Section 7.6](#chapter7.xhtml#sec7.6) concludes this chapter.

### 7.2.BYOD Architecture, Security Status and Challenges

BYOD started gaining popularity since 2009, and it is considered as a solution for business environments. It entails organisations allowing employees the use of their own personal devices for professional purposes. It is common nowadays that people interpret the phrase “personal devices” to refer to smartphones, laptops, tablets, etc. (Eslahi, 2014).

Years ago, before the massive growth of internet-based services, organisations used to provide personal devices to employees. This was known as *Use What You Are Told* (UWYT), and these devices were meant to be used only for professional duties. Computers were purchased and customized to help employees perform their duties and contribute to the accomplishment of the business’s goals. Furthermore, taking these devices outside the organisation was not allowed, making it harder for malicious attackers to steal personal data, because Internet use was not as frequent at that time.

Nowadays, because of the Internet revolution, it is easy to appreciate the fact that employees purchase their own devices for both personal and professional motives. Organisations have limited budgets, and therefore the BYOD policy has been implemented, allowing employees to use personal devices that satisfy their tastes. Likewise, network administration became easier for IT admins because it only requires the creation of configured network points at employees’ desks which adhere to the internal policies adopted by the organisation. In addition, more Access Points (APs) have been implemented in such a way that personnel can connect their wireless devices to the corporate network. Furthermore, these mobile devices are being used to perform professional duties during the commute between the organisation and any other destination and vice versa (Wainwright, 2018).

[Figure 7.1](#chapter7.xhtml#fig7.1) shows the general architecture for BYOD. It is also an overview of how personal devices get connected to a corporate network. The lower layer is the access network, where personal devices can access Internet services through Wi-Fi networks which can be personal or public networks. Likewise, personal devices can get Internet access using mobile networks. The transport network is known as the Internet, where ISPs control the traffic routing, and end users cannot take control of their information because in this layer the data is being transmitted. And finally, the corporate network is where the main servers are allocated and policies from organisations are enforced.

![image](images/fig7.1.jpg)

**Fig. 7.1.**Architecture of BYOD and connectivity to corporate networks.

The implementation of a BYOD policy seen from the technical perspective simplifies the network architecture, infrastructure implementation and management. Moreover, business software comes along with this solution to ease the network management for IT administrators (e.g. Active Directory). Analysing BYOD from the Human Resource (HR) perspective, it has been noted that employees are more satisfied as this solution allows them to engage completely with their professional roles, reducing stress, increasing productivity and therefore improving the organisation’s finances. Moreover, they do not have to budget for the purchase of devices that adhere to their internal policies (Ghosh *et al*., 2013). When their personal devices are used at work, professional staff can perform their tasks outside the office as long as they have internet connectivity. In addition, allowing the use of personal devices within the organisation attracts applicants who enjoy the flexibility offered. Nowadays, the “millennial” generation are more engaged with smartphones and use the Internet more frequently. High school and college students who are not afraid to share their information on the Internet are looking for flexible job opportunities.

### 7.2.1.*Current security models*

There are currently some BYOD models which are applied for security purposes. These are *Mobile Device Management (MDM), Mobile Application Management (MAM)* and *Mobile Information Management (MIM)*. The models are described down below with more of a focus on MDM, which is better known in the commercial market (Kale, 2013). The benefits to organisations of implementing these solutions within BYOD environments are the presentation of a stronger security posture to customers based on the importance of protecting information, as well as the protection and satisfaction of their employees, who enjoy having a flexible workstation that enhances productivity. The details of the features of various security solutions to BYOD environments are shown in [Table 7.1](#chapter7.xhtml#tab7.1).

**Table 7.1.**Features to consider when implementing secure BYOD environments.

![image](images/tab7.1.jpg)

### 7.2.1.1.*Mobile Device Management (MDM)*

Implementing MDM systems in an organisation allows the organisation to monitor in a remote manner the performance and functions of mobile devices. An MDM system is based in the client/server architecture, of which the main components are the agent and the server respectively. [Figure 7.2](#chapter7.xhtml#fig7.2) shows the general architecture of such a system, where an MDM gateway (relay server) is configured within the DMZ to enable mobile devices to get access to the corporate network whilst the server is monitoring their performance. The MDM agent is installed in the mobile device, and it transmits information about the user account and the status of the device whilst the server enforces the policies implemented to comply with the internal regulations from the organisation (Vignesh and Asha, 2013).

![image](images/fig7.2.jpg)

**Fig. 7.2.**MDM architecture.

### 7.2.1.2.*Mobile Application Management (MAM)*

IT administrators use this model to install, monitor, control, update, audit or remove customized applications created for the organisation in a remote manner. This feature allows IT administrators to take control of the applications allowed on each mobile device with the use of whitelists and blacklists (Kale, 2013). The main purpose of this solution is to control whether the applications installed on a mobile device fit with the policies of the organisation and to monitor in real time the performance of the customized applications. The solution balances three main features, which are performance, ease of use and security. In addition, customized applications and embedded systems are monitored to avoid exposing or compromising sensitive personal information from the current user/owner.

### 7.2.1.3. *Mobile Information Management (MIM)*

This model has great applicability in private cloud environments. The MIM system ensures the protection of and avoids any leakage of information, which is considered a crucial asset for the organisation. The model also demonstrates the limitations of installing trusted applications in mobile devices to control the data. The MIM solution comes across with the integration of MAM APIs into mobile devices, hence IT administrators can monitor whether information used by the user/owner is considered essential enough for the organisation to take the necessary measures to protect it. If the organisation protects the data, it will do so without getting involved with personal data.

### 7.2.2.*Security concerns*

Upon an analysis of the mind map shown in [Fig. 7.3](#chapter7.xhtml#fig7.3), it can be concluded that BYOD brings flexibility to organisations. This is accomplished thanks to the deployment of cloud environments, customized applications that can be installed on the endpoint devices, and the ability to allow employees to work remotely, saving them time. However, to reach the demanded levels of information assurance while avoiding any data leakage, strategic plans are required. These include resource optimisation and management, as well as the establishment of internal procedures and policies that can be controlled with suitable governance practices to keep the balance between flexibility, performance and security. As mentioned above, when BYOD is discussed, the use of wireless devices is also discussed, and so is wireless and mobile security. The protection of devices when connecting to public Wi-Fi networks, the encryption of sensitive information, the protection of phone and video calls against *eavesdropping* or *man-in-the-middle* attacks (MITM), and the protection of email and SMS services are all essential to the organisation. The high use of wireless personal devices increases in parallel their exposure to the cyber risks which are mentioned below:

![image](images/fig7.3.jpg)

**Fig. 7.3.**Implications of BYOD.

•*Social engineering* is when attackers take advantage of the lack of security awareness among employees to extract sensitive information.

•*Phishing* is sending emails with malicious links that could lead to credential harvesting or unauthorized malware downloading to users while pretending to be a known contact.

•*Spear-phishing* is the sending of phishing emails to a specific target (e.g. emails including the name of the owner).

•*Malware* is the abbreviated term for “malicious software”. Such software can be installed in a device to take control of it, to steal information or to launch future cyber attacks (e.g. trojans, worms, rootkits, viruses, ransomware).

•*Device theft* is considered a risk to the organisation despite it being out of the control of the owner. This is due to all the information stored in the device.

•*Insider threats* can happen because of frustrated employees or can be performed by cyber crime organisations. They occur when a person gets unauthorized access to the main computers used by an organisation.

•*Man-in-the-middle attacks* happen when attackers intercept messages between client and server in order to eavesdrop on information or manipulate it.

•*Shoulder surfing* is when an attacker is able to see the user typing out their credentials and acknowledging personal information such as banking or contact information on their personal devices. Despite being simple, it can cause great harm to organisations.

### 7.2.3.*BYOD security challenges*

There has been significant growth in the development of mobile devices in the last few years. Nowadays smartphones have features comparable to those of laptops. These outstanding features have enhanced functionality, therefore the use of smartphones by employees for professional purposes has been accepted by many organisations. In addition, these devices have become more accepted in the workplace as they now come with stronger security applications and features. Unfortunately, technological organisations are competing fiercely for market share and therefore, when developing devices and software applications, they tend to focus on innovation and ease of use rather than on security and reliability (Eslahi *et al*., 2014).

When talking about information security, it is necessary for cyber security practitioners, senior management and users in general to achieve security while maintaining performance and ease of use of computer systems in a professional environment. This is a complex endeavour. Following [Fig 7.4](#chapter7.xhtml#fig7.4), there are three components that must be appropriately balanced in computer systems, which are security, ease of use and performance. If software applications are developed to enhance business productivity and to improve organisational performance, their user interfaces must be easy to use, and during data processing they must follow the necessary protocols and functions to assure confidentiality, integrity and availability. For instance, if a system has more of the strongest security mechanisms, its performance is likely to degrade steadily, making the user interface less simple to use.

New electronic devices which can connect to *Internet of Things* (IoT) networks are being produced in great quantities. Mobile devices play a crucial role in managing these personal networks (e.g. autonomous cars, smart home devices). Currently, constrained devices on an IoT network tend to be in the form of hardware and are normally managed by smartphones using wireless communication (i.e., Bluetooth, ZigBee, Wi-Fi). However, this great technological advancement comes with minimal or no security features because of its electronical limitations, and thus, creates new opportunities for attackers to penetrate computer systems and succeed in causing personal identifiable information (PII) breaches, which in turn cause financial, technological and reputational damage to organisations. In addition, due to the increased use of mobile devices, organisations are dealing with the fact that confidential information is often delivered to devices that IT departments cannot manage properly, exposing the organisation to data leakage, theft and failure to achieve regulatory compliance. Attackers will try both simple and sophisticated tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs) to achieve their malicious objectives. Mobile devices will still be exposed to simple threats such as keyloggers, malware infection and vulnerability exploitation methodologies that could lead to the attacker gaining unauthorized access, compromising the user, the supply chain of the organisation he / she works in, the reputation of the organisation and the customer’s trust in the organisation. The next sections will discuss the impact of the European GDPR on BYOD environments, followed by guidelines aimed at teaching users how to protect their personal devices. Finally, a framework to enhance the security posture of organisations committed to the acceptance and use of mobile devices will be discussed.

![image](images/fig7.4.jpg)

**Fig. 7.4.**Features that need to be balanced in computer systems.

### 7.3.Impact of GDPR on BYOD Architectures

The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) is designed to enable individuals to better control their personal data. It is hoped that these modernised and unified rules will allow businesses to make the most of the opportunities created by the Digital Single Market by reducing regulation and benefiting from reinforced consumer trust. Privacy and data protection are fundamental rights protected by EU law. Privacy refers to the part of our lives that we as individuals want to control and keep to ourselves. The right to privacy is an umbrella concept that contains many meanings; it protects our communications, homes, bodies, lives, dignity, freedom, liberty and autonomy so that we can develop intimate relationships with others and achieve personal prosperity and wellbeing.

In the EU Fundamental Rights of Privacy which are covered in Article 7 of the Charter Fundamental Rights of the European Union, the respect for private and family life, home and communications is emphasised. Today, when ICT is increasingly being used, data collection and processing has become an important factor and a way of life. The Right to Data Protection was therefore developed to protect individuals from potential harm due to data abuse and misuse. In the EU, the Right to Data Protection is covered by Article 8 of the Charter; this article states that everyone has the right to the protection of their personal data. The right to the protection of personal data is furthermore enshrined in Article 16 of the treaty on the functioning of the European Union. In the digital age, new technology has been widely deployed in all aspects of life and many of these new technologies can invade privacy if they are misused or abused. They may cause harm to individuals or society even without us knowing it. However, we have become more and more dependent on such privacy-invading technologies and on the ever-growing data processing. Of course, data ownership, transparency and auditability will be one of the major challenges for EU citizens. In this regard, it is important to clarify individual rights that citizens are entitled to under EU Law. For this very reason, the GDPR has provided us with a robust legal compliance system (Shu and Jahankhani, 2017).

The GDPR requires that personal data be securely processed. This is not a new obligation when it comes to data protection, of course. However, the GDPR’s “appropriate technical and organisational measures”, which have been previously addressed under the Data Protection Act of 1998 (the 1998 Act), provides more specifics on what you have to do to securely process data and how to assess information risk so that appropriate security measures can be put in place. This is an important element when it comes to BYOD as it is now a legal requirement.

Article 5(1)(f) of the GDPR is concerned with the “integrity and confidentiality” of personal data and explains that data should be “processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security of the personal data, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage, using appropriate technical or organisational measures”.

Organisations are required to refer to the GDPR’s “security principle”, which is concerned with the broad concept of information security. The “security principle” requires that the appropriate security is put in place to prevent the personal data you hold being accidentally or deliberately compromised. This is important when it comes to BYODs. It is vital to know that whilst “information security” is sometimes interpreted to mean “cybersecurity”, which involves the protection of networks and information systems from attacks, it also covers other aspects including physical and organisational security measures. Therefore, it is important to consider the “security principle” together with Article 32 of the GDPR, which discusses the specifics of the security of your processing. Article 32(1) states that; “taking into account the state of the art, the costs of implementation and the nature, scope, context and purposes of processing as well as the risk of varying likelihood and severity for the rights and freedoms of natural persons, the controller and the processor shall implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk” (Shu and Jahankhani, 2017).

In addition to the six data protection principles, the GDPR Article 5(2) has “the principle of accountability”. According to this principle, the controller shall be responsible for compliance with the principles listed in Article 5(1) of the GDPR and shall be able to demonstrate its compliance with them. With so many rights given to data subjects and so much accountability on data controllers under GDPR, organisations in the EU and organisations outside the EU which process the data of EU citizens are required to keep all the compliance boxes checked.

Further areas to look out for when implementing the GDPR are as follows:

•Incidents: The GDPR will now make it a legal duty to report any incidents to the ICO within 72 hours. This legislates similarly to current working arrangements of contacting the ICO in a similar time period.

The potential financial penalties could be very high for incidents in which the regulations were not adhered to. Article 83 states the general conditions for imposing administrative fines. Paragraphs 4 and 5 state the limits of administrative fines that potentially can be issued (this is dependent on member state approval of what the maximum fine will be). The maximum fines for failing to comply with the regulations could potentially be 20 million Euros or 4 % of the organisation’s total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year.

Data subjects must also have fair processing information made available to them “at the time when personal data are obtained” (Article 13). Further to this, the fair processing information must include the following:

•“the contact details of the data protection officer”

•“the right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority”

•“the existence of automated decision-making, including profiling, referred to in Article 22(1) and (4) and, at least in those cases, meaningful information about the logic involved, as well as the significance and the envisaged consequences of such processing for the data subject”

Data subjects have the right to know what safeguards are in place for any personal data that is transferred to a “third country or an international organisation” (i.e. outside the UK). The applicable safeguards that can be used in international transfers are stated within Article 46.

Recital 47 states, in reference to the legitimate interests of a controller as a legal basis for processing a data subject’s personal data, that “given that it is for the legislator to provide by law for the legal basis for public authorities to process personal data, that legal basis should not apply to the processing by public authorities in the performance of their tasks”.

•Data Protection Impact Assessments (Article 35): Privacy Impact Assessments (PIAs) within the Act are named ‘Data Protection Impact Assessments’ (DPIAs).

There are limited differences between the two, except that the appointed Data Protection Officer’s (DPO) advice (currently, the SIRO’s advice) must be sought and, “where appropriate, the controller shall seek the views of data subjects or their representatives on the intended processing”. Recital 84 states that “where a data-protection impact assessment indicates that processing operations involve a high risk which the controller cannot mitigate by appropriate measures in terms of available technology and costs of implementation, a consultation of the supervisory authority should take place prior to the processing”. Article 25 states that data protection must not only be by default but must be by design. Privacy by design is a key element in BYOD implementation.

•Data Protection Officer Role (DPO): According to Article 37, Paragraph 1, the organisation must appoint a DPO.

The details of the appointed DPO must be published and submitted to the ICO. In some regards the DPO role has general similarities to the SIRO role. For example, all PIAs will need to have consultations with the DPO.

However, Article 38 states that “data subjects may contact the Data Protection Officer about all issues related to processing of their personal data”. It is unclear from this whether tasks such as subject access requests can be delegated. As the ICO would be the supervisory body in this respect, advice should be sought from them.

Similarly, guidance issued by the Working Party (EU Joint Committee of Member States’ Supervisory Authorities \[ICOs\]) about the role of the DPO is not clear. Guidance states that “the personal availability of a DPO is essential to ensure that data subjects will be able to contact the DPO” in Article 38, Paragraph 4, in regard to “all issues related to processing of their personal data and to the exercise of their rights under this Regulation”. The levels of expertise, skill, knowledge, etc. that are relevant to the role are stated in Articles 37-39 and Recital 97. It is also given that the DPO must be available to communicate directly with data subjects and the Supervisory Board (Shu and Jahankhani, 2017).

•Subject Access: Article 12, Paragraph 3, states that Subject Access Requests or SARs (as stated under Article 13) need to be complied with ‘without undue delay’ and within a month of receipt of the request (Article 12 does not state whether this is 31 days, or if organisations have until the same day next month to comply, e.g. from the 15th of Jan to the 15th of Feb).

Article 12, Paragraph 5 states that there shall be no charge issued to the requestor in complying with their SAR, unless requests from a data subject are ‘manifestly unfounded or excessive, in particular because of their repetitive character’. If a request is denied on these grounds, an unspecified fee may be charged (in relation to the administrative cost of dealing with the request). The request may be denied, but the controller must demonstrate that the request was excessive or manifestly unfounded.

The processes for providing the information to the applicant remain the same. When a large quantity of information on a data subject is being processed, the controller maintains the ability to ask the data subject to specify the information or processing activities to which the request relates. The fact that there can now be no charge for the first SAR made by a data subject has potentially large financial implications for an organisation.

•Processing Activities: Article 30 states that data controllers “shall maintain a record of processing activities under its responsibility”. An organisation currently undertakes similar programmes of activity through their information governance policy requirements. If these are followed, all data-sharing agreements and contracts should in theory be recorded and logged, however, in reality this is not done comprehensively in a consolidated repository or format.

•Strategic work to undertake in partnership with other organisations and potential future work: Article 40, Paragraph 1 states that the drawing up of codes of conduct in keeping with the regulations should be encouraged. Paragraph 2 states that “bodies representing categories of controllers or processors” should help prepare the codes of conduct.

In relation to the above, Article 41 states that compliance with the code of conduct must be undertaken by an appropriate body which has an appropriate level of expertise (expertise in this case is decided by the regulatory body — the ICO).

Article 42 states that data protection certification mechanisms for demonstrating compliance with the GDPR should be created and complied with. It is currently unknown what form any certification will take, however, the task of deciding competency for a certification body shall lie with the supervisory authority (the ICO).

•Other Considerations: Current legislation maintains that only the data controller for information may be liable for non-compliance with the Data Protection Act. Article 82, Paragraph 2 states that “a processor shall be liable for the damage caused by processing only where it has not complied with obligations of this Regulation specifically directed to processors or where it has acted outside or contrary to lawful instructions of the controller” — in effect stating that a processor is now equally liable, or entirely liable if, as stated in Paragraph 3, the controller “proves that it is not in any way responsible for the event giving rise to the damage”.

In such circumstances, Paragraph 4 states that either the controller or the processor will be held responsible for paying the entire fine, but Paragraph 5 gives recourse whereby the “controller or processor shall be entitled to claim back from the other controllers or processors involved in the same processing that part of the compensation corresponding to their part of responsibility for the damage”.

In general, it is very clear that accountability for security will provide adequate support so that matters are not overlooked and as a result the organisation’s overall security position will not become flawed or out of date.

An information security policy is an appropriate organisational measure to demonstrate what steps are required to comply with the “security principle”. Further to policy, organisations do need to consider security and other related matters such as the co-ordination between key people within the organisation. For instance, the security manager will have to know about the commissioning and disposing of any IT equipment, physical access to premises, equipment given to anyone outside the organization including computer maintenance, etc.

All this of course brings in additional security considerations and may influence the business continuity arrangements. However, information security policies provide pointers on how the organization can protect and recover any personal data being held. A regular check needs to be done to ensure that security measures remain appropriate and up to date.

Although technical measures play a key role in the protection of personal data, it is often the case that security incidents occur due to theft or loss of equipment or incorrect disposal of equipment. Technical measures here include cyber security, which is complex and ever-evolving.

From a security point of view, it is best to assume that an organisation’s systems are vulnerable and to constantly take steps to protect them through factors such as:

•The security of the network and information systems, including those which process personal data.

•The security of the data held within the organisation’s systems, including BYOD systems. These can be secured by ensuring appropriate access controls and data security policies.

•Online security, including the security of the organisation’s website and other online services, or of applications used by the organisation.

•Device security with a clear policy on BYOD.

All these need to link to the nature and practices of the business. For example, if the organisation is allowing staff to work from home, then measures must be introduced to ensure that this does not compromise the organization’s security, and these measures must be appropriate to the nature of the personal data held and the harm that might result from any compromise. The Cyber Essentials Scheme is a good starting point as it provides a basic set of controls, however, risk analysis should be also be looked at in parallel.

### 7.3.1.*Threats to personal data security*

Organisations adopting BYOD architectures need to be aware that they are collecting personal information about employees, customers, advisors and third-party consultants. That information might be names, contact details (e.g., phone, email, address), date of birth, national insurance number and critical information such as servicelevel agreements and non-disclosure agreements. Furthermore, organisations may occasionally require the collection of certain types of personal data for legal compliance purposes. Regardless of how it is collected, recorded and used — for instance, it may be collected using a computer or recorded on other media, which include hard copy pages and pictures from a CCTV — all this personal information must be handled properly to ensure compliance with the European GDPR.

In the United Kingdom, organisations should comply with eight principles, which are summarised as follows:

•Personal data shall be processed fairly and lawfully

•Personal data shall be obtained or processed for specific lawful purposes

•Personal data must be adequate, relevant and not excessive

•Personal data must be accurate and kept up to date

•Personal data shall not be kept for longer than necessary

•Personal data shall be processed in accordance with the rights of the data subjects

•Personal data must be kept secure

•Personal data shall not be transferred outside the European Economic Area (EEA) unless there is adequate protection

The three major threats to data security are data tampering (integrity), data loss (availability), and unauthorized access or leakage (confidentiality). Considering these threats risk affecting data security, they must be treated as main priorities for organisations. There are two main types of threats (Garba *et al*., 2015). Organisational threats occur when users abuse their privileges on computer systems and perform actions without authorization, or without having the legal rights to perform those actions. Systemic threats consist in the misuse of information by individuals who have legitimate access to it. These threats are also called insider threats when they occur in organisations.

### 7.4.Guidelines to Enhance Security Posture on Mobile Devices

The protection of mobile devices must be taken with the seriousness it deserves. This is because, nowadays, organisations along with their employees tend to use personal devices daily for professional purposes. Furthermore, new generations are becoming familiar with technology from an early age. For instance, children are using tablets and smartphones to play video games and download applications from marketplaces, exposing these devices to outsider threats and social engineering techniques. Malicious APIs uploaded on trusted and untrusted sources are likely to be the source of this threat. It is normal having meetings with stakeholders at places outside the organisation (e.g. cafeterias, restaurants) to create new partnerships between companies, and personal devices tend to get connected to public Wi-Fi networks. It is necessary for organisations to consider the protection of personal devices within their risk management framework, in light of the recently implemented European GDPR.

This section mentions security practices that protect mobile devices even when they are connected to mobile and public wireless networks. Regardless of the mobile operating system one uses (e.g. Android, Blackberry, Apple), these guidelines can be applied to any smart mobile device that has access to the internet and is used for both personal and professional purposes. It is important for the user to understand that using personal devices is commonly allowed in most organisations. Nevertheless, there are some exceptions (e.g., governments, federal agencies) where they work with UWYT policies because the sensitivity of the information they tend to manipulate requires higher levels of information assurance (Kale, 2013).

Now that the impact of the newly implemented GDPR mentioned above has been analysed and the benefits of implementing BYOD security architectures have been mentioned in [Section 7.2](#chapter7.xhtml#sec7.2), the implementation of the following security mechanisms and practices to protect mobile devices has been suggested.

### 7.4.1.*Strong passwords*

Nowadays it is very common that mobile devices which are used for professional purposes load default applications accessed by the user daily. For instance, users tend to immediately synchronize their smartphones to their e-mail and cloud-based accounts (e.g., Google Mail, OneDrive). Furthermore, most devices have a contract of access to 4G networks, with higher throughputs, allowing users to access internet-based services, download applications and documents, and upload files and folders to the cloud as well. The high rate of 4G devices acquired, and the high rate of cloud synchronizing that occurs, demands that the user have strong passwords. Despite having strong hashing algorithms and using salting techniques to strengthen passwords, if the mobile device is configured by the user to have passwords that are easy to guess/crack such as “Password” or “\[Name\]\[BirthYear\]”, attackers can apply old cracking techniques to retrieve passwords (e.g., John the Ripper, Hashcat).

Fortunately, on corporate networks there are software applications which are used to enforce strong password policies within an organisation (e.g., Active Directory). Nevertheless, as mentioned above, IT staff struggle to protect business data located in mobile devices. Strong passwords are recommended if personal services are going to be accessed on mobile phones. The UK National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), along with various security consultancy organisations, recommend that passwords should be created according to the combination of three random words that users can remember without doubt. In addition to this combination, it is important to use numeric and symbolic characters for password configuration. Nowadays, there is password enforcer software which makes users set authentication credentials that have a minimum length of 15 characters. The longer the password is, the harder it will be for attackers to crack it.

### 7.4.2.*Anti-virus software*

Anti-viruses are used in computers and laptops within organisations for detective and corrective purposes. They can detect threats and risks which are reported on exploit databases and download the latest updates to counteract the threat posed by viruses and malware. Anti-virus software can be downloaded to smartphones from marketplaces (e.g., Google Play, Apple Store) because it is common for attackers to develop malicious software for smartphones which tricks users and injects payloads that run in the background and perform unauthorized procedures. Applications considered attractive to users are exposed to cyber risks executed by attackers, allowing them to trigger rootkits, trojans or any other kind of viruses which can in turn allow them to perform information theft, file navigation, eavesdropping, etc.

### 7.4.3.*Authentication mechanisms*

As mobile networks and devices improve in terms of their performance and the service they provide to users, they demand more sophisticated security mechanisms for their protection. One of these mechanisms is authentication. During the rise of mobile networks several years ago, security was not necessary because the wireless transmission channels used in mobile networks were based on analogical technology as it had greater coverage, and these were used only for phone calls. Later, with the rise of 2G networks, multimedia messaging services (MMS) and internet services at lower speeds (e.g., 56 kbps), authentication mechanisms began to be required. The first authentication mechanism of this sort was phone locking on mobile phones using a hardware-based button. The user could control how long the phone would have to lie idle before they got locked out. With the rise of Apple and Android devices, authentication mechanisms got more sophisticated. It became possible to set a specific pattern which would unlock the phone, allowing the user to access the main windows. The pattern unlocking systems required the user to draw a specific figure on a nine-button environment.

Mobile devices have different authentication mechanisms. The first one is based on “something you know”, which, according to [Fig. 7.5](#chapter7.xhtml#fig7.5), can require the user to unlock the phone by: (a) drawing a pattern, (b) typing in a PIN number, or (c) inserting login credentials, in order to get access to the services the application offers. Login credentials are generally used to access services in BYOD environments. In addition, there is token-based authentication, which is commonly used for multi-factor authentication (MFA) purposes. For instance, some users receive a one-time passcode (OTP) via SMS, email or an application from the marketplace during the authentication process. This is called two-factor authentication (2FA) and is used to verify that the user legitimately owns the account they are logging in to. The latest authentication mechanism used nowadays on mobile devices is based on “something you are”. For instance, the latest smartphones come with biometric authentication such as fingerprint reading, facial or iris recognition or voice-based authentication (Samaras *et al*., 2014).

![image](images/fig7.5.jpg)

**Fig. 7.5.**Authentication mechanisms on smartphones. (a) Pattern, (b) PIN, (c) login credentials.

Upon analysing the authentication mechanisms, it can be concluded that the recommendation for mobile device users regardless of being connected or not to BYOD environments is to enable the latest authentication mechanism. Applications can also be purchased from the marketplace to add another layer of authentication to specific mobile applications. For instance, if a mobile device is hacked, the attacker would not be able to access a certain application or a certain piece of information if it is protected with another layer of authentication. This is because the attacker does not have the password, the temporary token, or even worse, the physical features of the owner that must be used for biometric authentication procedures.

### 7.4.4.*Remote control*

The implementation of BYOD security architecture and the MDM enables organisations to perform remote wipe or factory reset to mobile phones, but users can also take remote control of their mobile devices by registering them with the accounts associated with their respective marketplaces. For instance, to remotely protect Android devices, register the phone with a Google Account and use features such as *Find my Device*, which allows the user to locate the device through GPS services, play a sound remotely and remote wipe the phone to factory settings, deleting all the information on it, including any information in external storage.

### 7.4.5.*Importance of not rooting/jailbreaking the device*

Some years ago, the act of rooting mobile phones started gaining popularity, particularly in South American countries. This was because it gave users the freedom to customize their mobile phones to their tastes. One of the main reasons to root the device was to get access to applications from unknown sources for specific purposes, and to avoid paying for the benefits these applications provided. For Apple devices the process is called “jailbreaking”, and it was commonly used to connect the phone to the mobile network and to get access to phone calls, SMS and internet services. However, attackers nowadays take advantage of rooted phones because they can escalate privileges on these phones easily, taking full control of the devices in order to perform actions such as installing rootkits, using the devices within a botnet to perform further attacks, especially DoS attacks, and performing cryptomining in the background, thus consuming the phone’s resources. Moreover, rooting the phone also voids the warranty given when the user purchased the device. This leads to the user losing certain benefits. For instance, the provider will no longer troubleshoot problems with the device, or repair the device for free, as they ordinarily would during the duration of the warranty. Even though the user will have to pay to download some applications if they do not root or jailbreak a device, it is still best not to root or jailbreak the device, as doing so will remove a layer of security and the provider will no longer have control over the device. Due to rooting and jailbreaking, mobile providers have also had to dedicate more resources to customer service (Vignesh and Asha, 2015).

### 7.4.6.*Virtual private networks*

In recent years, there has been steady growth in the deployment of public networks, especially in metropolitan cities where users can connect their mobile devices to Wi-Fi networks at many places. Attackers can take advantage of these facilities to perform attacks that could lead to information leakage, eavesdropping and MITM attacks including session hijacking, data tampering and extracting sensitive data that could be critical for organisations. Using a Virtual Private Network (VPN) service, one can establish an encrypted session between server and client to assure data privacy and confidentiality. A VPN service can be purchased in the marketplace, or a dedicated VPN service can be configured to allow users access to the corporate network.

### 7.4.7.*Download applications from trusted sources*

With the increased demand for smartphones and the tough competition in the market, especially between Android and Apple devices, users are always looking for applications that can improve their lifestyles, such as fitness apps, budgeting apps, etc. Attackers are always looking to gain unauthorized access to mobile phones, take control of them and steal information that could potentially harm users. For instance, this information could be used to perform fraudulent transactions or to impersonate a user during a transaction without their consent. One way to accomplish these objectives is by developing fake applications and uploading them in the marketplace, or uploading them to the internet so that users can download them and install them manually. For instance, attackers started developing mobile apps claiming to be the popular video game “Fortnite” in order to insert malicious software into mobile phones. This malware stole information from unencrypted HTTP sessions. This campaign was targeted at Android devices because of the decision made by the provider to make the software available for download from the official website.

### 7.4.8.*Update systems to latest patches*

One of the biggest implications of bringing innovative products to the competitive market is the lack of security or the presence of bugs in these products. Mobile devices are not the exception. Organisations should place as top priority the setting of appropriate patch management procedures pointing out which updates are critical to security. This is especially true if there are valid proofs of concept that the exploitation of bugs and vulnerabilities by attackers can cause significant damage to the user or the organisation in general. In BYOD environments, IT administrators cannot control the personal devices of members of the organisations unless they have installed dedicated software compatible with MDM architectures on those personal devices; however, users should take full responsibility for the security of their mobile systems. Users cannot blame organisations that develop mobile operating systems or applications for security bugs uncovered after the release of these operating systems or applications, because a culture of secure coding is already being encouraged, and besides, because of deadline constraints and marketing purposes, developers are focused on making their products innovative rather than providing built-in security. Therefore, users should be trained to always download kernel, operating system or applicationlevel updates when they receive notifications about these updates.

### 7.5.Integration of a Multi-Layer Policy and the Information Governance Framework for a BYOD Security Framework

There are different security options for BYOD environments in various organisations, and each of them is designed for specific purposes. Most organisations, especially SMEs, are considered vague and unorganised according to security experts. This is because in SMEs cyber security is not fully considered due to financial issues or the lack of knowledge of personnel engaged with risk management procedures. Likewise, system administrators, who are commonly in charge of the security posture of the organisation, have frequently established few or no common policies and/or procedures to protect the personal data of employees, customers and third parties. Individuals should understand that cyber security does not only mean adding rigorous security technologies into the network infrastructure, it includes training employees to follow internal protocols to avoid risks caused by mistakes, internal threats and external attacks. Employees should be trained to respond properly to security breaches whilst assuring internal and regulatory compliance. The proposed BYOD security framework is based on the “Privacy by Design” principle, which considers the GDPR legislation along with the individual’s rights. It consists of two core elements, a multi-layer security policy and the Information Governance (IG) Framework developed during previous research for England’s National Health Service (NHS). The multi-layer security policy is formed by three layers of policies — Corporate Security, Application Security and Device Security policies — whilst this is supported by Information Governance according to [Fig. 7.6](#chapter7.xhtml#fig7.6).

**Layer 1 — Corporate Security**

Organisations must consider this layer in order to set the necessary terms and conditions with the employee prior to signing the respective policies regarding BYOD security. Policies and procedures are added to a checklist to be reviewed by executive management before they are implemented into the organisation. Implementation includes following protocols for internal compliance involving the protection of personal data during email usage, the usage of network services, communication privacy procedures and the usage of BYOD architectures. It is important to train users to back up their personal information and remove applications that could be considered a risk in the organisation. They should also be taught to avoid the usage of rooted or jailbroken devices and the consequences of policy violation should be explained to them.

The use of Access Control must be limited to a certain number of employees according to their roles and responsibilities, and it must be implemented in all the procedures established in the organisation (e.g., Incident Response, Business Continuity, Forensic Investigation, System Administration). Devices must be registered within the organisation and must not have access to the main corporate network due to confidential reasons. For network security purposes it is suggested that the implementation of isolated networks takes place to ensure sandboxing, meaning the isolation between personal and professional information (Zahadat *et al*., 2015). However, both personal and professional information can compromise the integrity of the organisation when involved in a breach. In addition, this layer suggests profiles which can be used to categorize employees in terms of privilege level:

![image](images/fig7.6.jpg)

**Fig. 7.6.**BYOD security framework.

•Standard User: A standard user is an employee at a junior level, who has spent little time working for the organisation. They may have undergone some training in terms of cyber security, but this training has not been extensive. They can bring their devices; however, they must sign a form stating that the devices will be used only for personal purposes, meaning no email synchronization or integration of corporate services or access limits within the enterprise network.

•Professional User: A professional user is one with experience and advanced security knowledge and expertise, commonly considered to be at a senior level or higher. Moreover, they are highly trusted and require the usage of personal devices in the workplace and at home. This is because they are likely to be sent to meetings with stakeholders and other organisations to establish partnerships, and meetings can be held at places where networks are not trusted by security experts. They use VPNs and cloud services to access confidential information.

•Guest User: A guest user is the new user in the network. Their devices do not have access to the corporate network. Organisations must also consider the configuration of guest wireless networks used only for web browsing purposes. These should have strong access controls, which can be established by rules at access points and proxies to prevent the leakage of network information that can expose the organisation.

**Layer 2 — Application Security**

This layer provides strong security for mobile devices such as smartphones through monitoring carried out by enterprise applications which assist the user in securing their devices. The application used for this purpose is the MDM, which has three main functions — control, monitoring and protection. Its main server can be configured and accessed from this application. The installation of the MDM allows for the implementation of various kinds of device control such as locking down, creating an SSL connection to the server, remote wipe, siren, data backup and policy enforcement on mobile devices. MAM is used to control specific applications on the device. It should be applied to control customised applications developed for the organisation, and should include patch management to correct coding bugs encountered by vulnerability testers and software developers. Furthermore, these customised applications must be developed properly to ensure GDPR compliance. To this end, the user must accept the terms and conditions set out by the application, which includes giving the application consent to run on their mobile device and accepting their responsibilities as a user. A good example of this is the use of cookies on websites. This is done in the name of regulatory compliance. MIM is the most important application, to be used when handling sensitive information. The installation of this application must be enforced mainly for professional users who have higher privileges within the organisation. The application must be implemented in smartphones, tablets and PDAs. In addition, customised applications should be developed with strong authentication mechanisms to validate legitimate users. The use of two-factor authentication, i.e., the generation of random tokens with every new session to avoid session hijacking, is suggested (Eslahi *et al*., 2014).

There should be external encryption software installed to protect data from external storage media. This is because, when a user installs an application from a marketplace, the application generally asks for permission to access some features in mobile devices such as:

•Account details

•Application information

•Phone calls

•Camera, gallery

•Network communication

•Location

•Storage

•Messaging

•Synchronization settings

•System Tools

•Bookmarks and web browsing history

The abovementioned features and credentials are sensitive, and when some applications request access to this information, the device is made more vulnerable to attackers as it becomes easier for details of the devices to be exposed and leaked. The MDM should monitor and restrict the application being installed and label it as a high-risk application if it requests access to lots of sensitive information. This is because the application could contain malware, or devices could be used to form a botnet for further attacks, or data could be used for information theft and privilege escalation within a corporate network. Therefore, MDM must warn the user before they install a high-risk application on their mobile devices.

**Layer 3 — Device Security**

Most organisations leave device-level security to the owner and the manufacturer of the device. Previously, device-level security policies included the certificate authority, data encryption and multiuser and rooting events. Nowadays, every smartphone comes with preloaded trusted CAs, and the removal of one can result in the user working online in untrusted networks. If a digital certificate is hacked, the chances of accessing the device is higher, and if the organisation is using the same certificate, the attacker can gain access to critical systems. Therefore, the device must monitor the CA credentials. The latest smartphones come with inbuilt encryption applications, ciphering data such as accounts, settings and applications. Moreover, some smartphones make it possible to encrypt the SD card inserted. In countries like Australia, USA and the UK rooting is considered legal, hence organisations must prevent the usage of rooted devices in a BYOD environment.

**Information Governance Framework**

It is a legal requirement for organisations to implement an efficient and effective agreement for information governance. These requirements are set out in the Information Governance Framework.

Organisations adopting BYOD environments are the data controllers for the personal and confidential data under their custody. Therefore, they have a legal responsibility to comply with the information governance requirements associated with this design. To ensure their accountability regarding information governance, organisations should consider that professional users must have access to a range of core support services. The elements of the framework are detailed below:

•**Core Element 1 — IG policy support:** Must be in place for the production and maintenance of local IG policies and procedures. Provides advice and support on the approval, ratification and adoption of IG policies by organisations. These must include policies on confidentiality, consent procedures for the use of personal data, responsibilities and requirements, human rights with regard to privacy, information security (paper records, access control for computer systems, mobile computing risk management), incident management and reporting, staff training and needs assessments.

•**Core Element 2 — IG Consultancy and Support** — Advice and support by phone and/or email on IG issues, including operational processes and new business initiatives. Advice and guidance about access and laws (including GDPR advice for regulatory compliance).

•**Core Element 3 — IG Training** — Training staff regarding IG, which includes the development and provision of training materials to support IG as required and communication methodologies to enhance teamwork and better relationships between stakeholders, customers, employees and third-party providers so as to achieve personal data security.

•**Core Element 4 — Compliance Support** — Advice and guidance for IG compliance. When following the IG framework, compliance support allows organisations to ensure internal and regulatory compliance, including compliance with the new GDPR.

•**Core Element 5 — Incident Management and Investigations** — Advice and support during the investigation of possible cyber security incidents and data breaches. Advising on incident assessment and reporting the incident to regulatory authorities (e.g., ICO in the UK). The reporting should be done by the CISO, the DPO and the involved personnel. Advice on postincident reviews and actions taken to protect the organisation’s and individual’s rights.

### 7.6.Conclusion

In this chapter, the impact of the European GDPR on “Bring Your Own Device” environments was analysed. BYOD environments are used by most organisations to save money while ensuring better commitment from employees. However, the increased demand for mobile device usage in professional workplaces has increased the risks of breaches and unauthorized access, as well as of insider threats, which could be accidental or intentional. The framework proposed involves the integration of a multi-layer security policy along with the Information Governance Framework, which enhances the security posture of organisations regarding the usage of personal mobile devices. Increasing communication between staff, stakeholders and third parties can aid in the implementation of preventive and corrective measures against data breaches. In addition, with the increased use of IoT devices, and the increase in the number of small devices connecting to the Internet, every organisation should train its employees so as to increase their awareness of threats and to impart basic skills in cyber security to them. This is especially unavoidable if the organisation chooses to offer flexibility by allowing the use of personal devices at work. Given the advances in technology, the adoption of policies, procedures, and guidelines which allow organisations to ensure regulatory compliance is recommended. The GDPR framework, for instance, is based on the “Privacy by Design” principle, and includes security guides to enhance mobile security and protect the rights of organisations and of individuals regarding their personal data. More generally, communication is essential if organisations are to respond properly to a security breach that could harm the individual. A quick and effective response to a cyber attack ensures business continuity, which is important in retaining customer trust.

## ABSTRACT

Over the last decade, the prevalence of new computing devices with greater processing power and ubiquitous internet-ready devices helped to facilitate the creation and sharing of vast amounts of data. This has brought increased risks to personal data and rendered previous regulations on data privacy less effective in the new digital age. The GDPR regulation was introduced across EU states on the 25th of May 2018 and brought radical changes that govern activities around the processing and sharing of data and how the protection of personal data is administered by various organisations. GDPR necessitates the re-assessment of existing frameworks in order to meet new requirements outlined in the articles and recitals of the regulation. This research addresses the existing challenges of integrating GDPR into incident response and breach notification plans, and proposes a conceptual Decision Support System (DSS) to address the challenges identified. Existing industry standard frameworks such as ISO27001, NIST, and SANS were analysed alongside Focus Group interviews with subject matter experts to gather feedback on the relevance and applicability of a DSS to meet GDPR compliance requirements. The findings of the study reveal a number of compliance gaps in existing incident handling frameworks which could be mitigated by employing decision support techniques as proposed in the study.

*Keywords*: GDPR, incident response, data breach notification, decision support systems

### 8.1.Introduction

An incident response plan is a formal document that outlines a series of measures to promptly identify and neutralise security threats and mitigate the associated risks to personal and sensitive information. It is typically established through technical controls, policies, procedures, and designated response teams with specific responsibilities. The proliferation of cyber attacks and important changes in regulation warrants a radical re-assessment of existing governance frameworks and security policies, in order to gain full visibility of data that traverse the internal and external sphere of an organisation.

Articles 33 and 34 of GDPR explicitly outline requirements for reporting data breaches within a specific timeframe and for organisations to demonstrate reasonable steps have been taken to secure personal data (GDPR, 2016). GDPR promulgates the foundation for a risk-based approach to assess the risk to personal data, and for privacy protection measures to be introduced by default when collecting and processing personal data. This requires organisations who are either controllers or processors of personal data to assess the risks relating to the rights and freedom of data subjects and formulate appropriate policies and security measures to protect personal data (Garber, 2018). This indicates that complying with GDPR necessitates a clear and consistent approach towards interpreting and integrating the relevant articles and existing incident response and breach notification plans.

The aim of this research is to investigate compliance challenges by formulating the following questions:

1.What are the main challenges and enablers of implementing GDPR into an incident response and breach notification plan?

2.What decision support process or system could be developed to address the challenges identified?

3.What method could be adopted to assess the relevance and usability of the design for meeting the new requirements of incident response and breach notification challenges?

### 8.1.1.*Background*

In recent years, the upsurge in cyber attacks and data breach incidents has become a phenomenon that represents an existential threat for organisations who fail to formulate robust security policies and stringent measures to safeguard valuable data. Appropriate preparation plans are imperative for effectively responding to the evolving threats that could cause irreparable damage to business operations and reputation. This helped to precipitate a paradigm shift in recognising the value of personal and business information, as well as the importance of adapting to the changing legal and regulatory landscape.

Despite this recognition and various measures taken by organisations to implement security policies via existing incident handling frameworks, new requirements for breach notification and communication in GDPR have created potential gaps in compliance that need to be re-examined. Moreover, there are no specific recommendations in GDPR that organisations can check against to verify they are fully compliant. According to Hedley and Jacobs (2017), verifying compliance will be done through either external audits or a process of self-assessment by individual organisations who interpret and implement relevant areas of the regulation into their existing incident handling frameworks with policies and procedures.

This indicates that organisations will need to justify and demonstrate to their relevant supervisory authority that stringent security safeguards are in place for securing personal data. The research director of Gartner, Mark Horvath (2018), elaborated that, even if appropriate security policies are established, organisations could still be held accountable under GDPR if employees intentionally or accidentally precipitate serious data breach incidents.

In 2015, a reported cyber attack on telecommunications group Talk Talk precipitated several deleterious consequences that included a rapid decline in stock market value, a loss of revenue amounting to £80 million, and the alienation of many of the customers affected. The Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) conducted subsequent investigations and a £400,000 penalty was levied on the company for failing to adequately secure their customers’ personal data (Ico.org.uk, 2018). Fowler (2016) noted that, under the stringent edicts outlined in the GDPR, the fines imposed could have amounted to approximately £70 million. The new mandatory 72-hour deadline outlined in Article 33 for reporting instances of data breach has left some organisations behind the curve in their efforts to establish appropriate frameworks and security measures for meeting compliance under GDPR (Mansfield-Devine, 2016).

The sophistication of new threats and the absence of appropriate response approaches and security policies can greatly increase the chances of a threat exploiting vulnerabilities in an information system with the result that personal data is compromised. [Figure 8.1](#chapter8.xhtml#fig8.1) illustrates a number of emerging threats that are contributing to the increased risks to personal and sensitive data.

### 8.1.2.*Aims*

The aims of this research are to examine the challenges that exist when interpreting and implementing GDPR through incident response plans, and to develop a structured process or decision support system to address the challenges identified. The research also aims to create an incident decision process flow to provide guidance for breach notification requirements. The objectives created for the research represent important building blocks for constructing and delivering the main goals of the research.
