### 9.4.1.*Examination process*

During this Process, a large number of techniques should be used to access, find and extract the potential digital evidence into a humanreadable format (Montasari, 2016a; Montasari, 2016b; Kohn *et al*., 2013). The Survey Digital Crime Scene Phase enables DFPs to find apparent pieces of digital evidence for a particular category of crime in a swift manner. It also assists them in ascertaining the skill level of the suspect, which in turn will allow them to decide what examination and analysis techniques are required in the next process of the SDFIPM, the Analysis Process (discussed later). DFPs must survey the digital crime scene to locate potential evidence, possibly within unconventional locations on the system (Montasari and Peltola, 2015). It is preferable to perform this Phase in a digital forensic laboratory (DFL), using the image (working copy) of the system acquired during the Acquisition Process \[8\], as it provides a controlled environment and the results can be repeated with another copy of the system. In cases where DFPs might need to perform this phase also on a live system, they must conduct field searches (Montasari, 2016a; Montasari, 2016d) by booting the system into what Carrier and Spafford (2003) call a “trusted environment”. DFPs must adapt their investigative techniques based on the specific category of crime to expedite the subsequent Analysis activities as there is often a large volume of data to deal with. For instance, in cases involving server intrusions, DFPs should search for apparent signs of a rootkit installation, examine application logs and also search for new configuration files. Another example (Carrier and Spafford, 2003) concerns analysing network traffic to learn more about an incident; the Survey Digital Crime Scene Phase might analyse traffic for the incident time frame and filter out certain ports and hosts. In other cases, as suggested in Montasari and Peltola (2015), the investigators should also analyse the “common” and “uncommon” locations on the system that might contain artefacts related to the suspect’s browsing activities. Unallocated file system space must also be extracted and processed for deleted files, and a low-level timeline of file activity should be examined to trace the user’s activities. Often, there are large volumes of data to be examined (Kohn *et al*., 2013; Ciardhuáin, 2004), and automated techniques should be employed using tools such as FTK (AccessData, 2018) or EnCase (Guidance Software, 2018) in order to support the investigators. Furthermore, a large number of techniques might be performed to process the obfuscated data. For instance, deleted or hidden data can be processed by utilising sound digital forensic methods, as File Allocation tables or disk indexing might be deleted in some investigations. Therefore, this Phase will enable DFPs to ensure that files that have been partially deleted are recognized from the original evidence. DFPs can also reverse-engineer suspicious executables and examine encrypted files (Carrier and Spafford, 2003). It might also be necessary for DFPs to examine the contents of every cluster (physical search) or every file (logical search) (Casey, 2011).

After all data including partially discovered files and folders have been made visible, data then needs to be harvested by giving a logical structure to the entire data set. The file and folder structure should be indexed to provide structure to acquired data. Raw data will be shown as information, and the partially deleted files which were processed during the Examine Acquired Data Phase will become visible to the degree that they were rendered visible. The result of the Harvest Data Phase is the production of a logical structured data set (Kohn *et al*., 2013) where the extracted raw data has now become structured information (Kohn *et al*., 2013; Cohen, 2009). Therefore, the harvested information can now be displayed by the original file systems such as FAT or NTFS. The data examined during the course of a DFI can be very large and therefore must be reduced to expedite the Examination Process. Identifying known elements can enable DFPs to reduce data. Metadata and unique identifiers such as MD5 must be used to remove known system files and other application data (Casey, 2011; Cohen, 2009; Beebe and Clark, 2005). The data that remains will be modified data or data that could be uniquely attributed to the users of a specific computer system. This will result in the identification of the potential digital evidence from data that has been examined, harvested and reduced. DFPs should also group together digital evidence with similar identifying patterns by focusing on the incident type. Digital evidence also needs to be restructured so that the investigation can be conducted more appropriately. If similar types of incidents or crimes have taken place in the past and are known to DFPs, they should then use the known classification in order to compare the current digital forensic data to the similar past incidents or crimes. The output of the Examination Process becomes the input to the Analysis Process, discussed in the following subsection.

### 9.4.2.*Analysis process*

Based upon the results of the Examination Process, DFPs must now be able to define what the exact characteristics of the incident are and who is to be held accountable for the incident. The Analysis Process enables investigators to reconstruct fragments of data based on their significance and determine a possible root cause of the incident (Montasari, 2016a; Montasari *et al*., 2015). Once DFPs have addressed what is possibly known from the digital evidence (Montasari *et al*., 2015), they must now be able to formulate a hypothesis of how the incident took place. To do so, they need to reconstruct a sequence of events which has resulted in the current state of the system under investigation. Investigators must thoroughly analyse and test data that was organised in the Examination Process against the hypothesis that they have formulated. The legal validity of the possible digital evidence must also be questioned by considering issues such as relevance, admissibility and weight as discussed in Montasari (2017b), Montasari (2016a) and Kessler (2010). Digital evidence should then be linked and attributed to the root cause of the incident by correlating the results of the digital crime scene with physical evidence. For instance, DFPs might need to correlate data center access logs to logins, linking online chat activities found on the computer with the activity of an undercover officer, and correlating activity on a compromised server with activity on the suspect’s home system and network activity recorded by an ISP. Subsequent to the attribution, investigators need to evaluate their findings to ensure that their hypothesis holds true. At this stage of the Investigative Process, backtracking from the Analysis Process to the Examination Process is often to be expected as the investigators acquire a better understanding of the root cause of the incident. The output of the Analysis Process becomes the input to the Interpretation Process, discussed in the next subsection.

### 9.4.3.*Interpretation process*

The main purpose of the Interpretation Process is to use scientifically proven methods to explain facts discovered throughout the Analysis Process within the context of the investigation (Montasari, 2016a; Montasari, 2016b; Palmer, 2001). During this process, investigators need to interpret the digital evidence to produce meaningful statements in the legal context for later reporting and presentation. They must be able to reconstruct the events associated with the digital investigation by using the results of the analysis techniques from the Analysis Process to put together the pieces of the digital puzzle so that an accurate reconstruction of events can be carried out. The interpretation of any evidence should depend on the available information regarding the circumstances surrounding the creation of that item of digital evidence (Valjarevic and Venter, 2015; ISO, 2015). DFPs must obtain information from individuals involved in the day-to-day operation of the system under investigation so that they can carry out a more effective interpretation of evidence. Moreover, investigators must consider information concerning the goal as well as the scope of the investigation. In cases where the contextual information changes, investigators might also need to change the interpretation so that it can reflect any such changes regarding the contextual information. DFPs must also utilise link analysis and timeline tools to assist them with the digital reconstruction. The interpreted evidence then needs to be classified and evaluated in order to ascertain the amount of trust that can be placed in it. The interpreted digital evidence should also be organised according to relevance in such a way that more important digital evidence can be differentiated from others. After completing this process, DFPs should now be able to determine how the digital evidence came into existence and what its presence denotes. The output of the Interpretation Process becomes the input to the Event Reconstruction Process, discussed in the next section.

### 9.4.4.*Event reconstruction process*

During this process DFPs need to reconstruct a possible event sequence which reflects the incident result as accurately as possible. In order to reconstruct the events, investigators must utilise the series of events that they have deduced from digital evidence. Event Reconstruction should not be established as factual; instead, DFPs should use this Process to explain how the incident might have taken place. During this Process, the investigation findings must be consolidated and refined prior to assessing the review results against the original hypothesis, which was formulated in the Analysis Process. This will be to determine whether the DFPs have acquired all the evidence required to support the original hypothesis. If all the evidence has not been captured, investigators will need to backtrack to the Examination Process, in which this Phase and subsequent Phases form a cycle that needs to be repeated until the DFPs can identify additional evidence and explain the incident. As an example, in cases where a server intrusion has taken place, this iteration involves DFPs linking the exploitation of a service that is open to attack with the installation of a rootkit and utilization of a network sniffer. If the source IP address of the network connections is investigated, this could result in the acquisition of additional digital evidence to examine. If there is no need to iterate to the Examination Process, DFPs must identify and address any areas of improvement. The output of the Event Reconstruction Process becomes the input to the Reporting Process, discussed in the next subsection.

### 9.4.5.*Reporting process*

DFPs need to compile, write and print out on paper a detailed and concise report during the Reporting Process. This report must contain conclusions that can be reproduced by independent third parties. Forensic reports that include opinions based on accurately documented digital sources are much more likely to withstand judicial scrutiny than opinions based on less reliable sources (Garrie, 2014). The report must contain the findings of the entire DIP in addition to the information about documentation, chain of custody, digital evidence preservation, authorisation and management. The report must be accurate, concise and clear and be restricted only to what is known (Beebe and Clark, 2005). Since a DFI might produce many incriminating items of digital evidence, investigators must ensure that all items of evidence are listed so that no valuable item of evidence is left out. The output of the Reporting Process becomes the input to the Presentation Process, discussed in the next subsection.

### 9.4.6.*Presentation process*

The output of the Reporting Process in the form of a well-written report must be presented to a wide variety of audiences such as courts, legal personnel, law enforcement, technical personnel and management. The report can be presented in the form of the expert testimony and can be accompanied by other formats such as the multimedia presentation and the deposition. During this Process, investigators need to prove their formulated hypothesis using supporting evidence. They must communicate their findings in such a way that facilitates future validation and that can be understood by both technical and non-technical audiences. In this regard, Beebe and Clark (2005) state that a presentation should be based on “careful consideration about how to best communicate information to various audiences”. Moreover, the presentation must also include relevant documentation and processes conducted during the investigative process, as well as any relevant physical evidence that can further consolidate the case against the perpetrator. It is also vital for DFPs to prove that the investigation was conducted in a forensically sound manner (Mumba and Venter, 2014). Furthermore, since the judge and jury or other interested parties are often nontechnical users, DFPs must ensure that in their presentation they avoid complex arguments, unless they also provide the audience with significant help so that they understand the technical points made. In cases where DFPs need to appear in court to give expert witness, they must ensure that they are fully aware of the jurisdictional legal requirements concerning the digital evidence. During the presentation, often the hypothesis is challenged by the defence lawyers through a contradicting hypothesis and supporting evidence. Thus, DFPs need to prove the credibility of their hypothesis and to be well-prepared to defend the hypothesis against criticism and challenge. In circumstances in which challenges are successful, investigators need to backtrack to the earlier stages to obtain and examine more evidence and develop a better hypothesis. If the decision is made in a court, it will be decided whether to convict the accused or to refute the allegations. If the decision is made in an organisational setting, it will be decided what disciplinary actions must be taken if the incident can be attributed to an individual. The output of the Presentation Process becomes the input to the Investigation Closure Process, discussed in the next subsection.

### 9.4.7.*Investigation closure process*

This process involves closing the investigation and applying the decision-making associated with it (Beebe and Clark, 2005). Lessons learnt must be captured, and the outcome of the investigation must be used to review the existing policies and procedures of the organisation. Moreover, relevant information concerning the entire investigation must be disseminated and communicated to all stakeholders. This includes communicating the need to return to a previous Process, deciding on the acceptance or rejection of the hypothesis or providing any reports or documents from the Presentation Process. The investigating organisation might decide to make some information available only within the organisation or they might decide to disseminate information more widely. The organisation’s policies and procedures should determine the details in this regard (Ciardhuáin, 2004). The investigating organisation must also record the investigation results, the case decision and all the evidence items. Such information will have an impact on future investigations and might have an effect on the policies and procedures of the organisation.

Thus, the accumulation and preservation of this information is a key part of supporting the work of DFPs and might be a productive aspect for the development of innovative applications that integrate techniques such as data mining and expert systems. Hauck *et al*. (2002) provide a detailed example of the dissemination activity in which they define a system named Coplink that provides real-time support for law enforcement investigators through an analysis application on the basis of a large accumulation of information from past investigations. An additional example is provided by Harrison *et al*. (2002), whose system is not real-time but instead delivers an “archival function” database to support investigators. Finally, during this Process, a decision also needs to be made to determine whether or not digital and physical evidence should be returned to the proper owner and what criminal evidence must be removed. The jurisdiction in which the investigation takes place and the type of authorisation determine whether or not the evidence should be returned, cleansed and reused or destroyed or whether the evidence should be stored for a certain period of time before any of the three possibilities can be applied.

### 9.5.Demonstration of the SDFIPM

This section follows the Demonstration activity of Peffers *et al*.’s (2006) DSRP, used in this research, and discusses the method employed to demonstrate the potential deployment of the SDFIPM. The Demonstration activity of the DSRP requires a researcher to apply the artefact in an appropriate environment such as “experimentation” or a “case study” to solve the stated problem (Hevner and Chatterjee, 2010; Peffers *et al*., 2006). Resources needed for the Demonstration activity include effective knowledge of how the artefact should be applied to solve the stated problem. In order to assess how the SDFIPM addresses the stated research problem, we adopt the case scenario approach whereby we apply the SDFIPM to a scenario and perform a walkthrough of the model. The approach followed is identified as being appropriate for evaluating “simulations” and “models” (Hevner *et al*., 2010; Peffers *et al.*, 2006; Balci, 2004). The Demonstration activity was carried out prior to the model being submitted to the experts for independent evaluation (discussed in [Section 9.6](#chapter9.xhtml#sec9.6)). A similar approach is adopted by other authors (Adams, 2012; Ciardhuáin, 2004; Beebe and Clark, 2005; Carrier and Spafford, 2003).

### 9.5.1.*Case study*

The following case study is based on an actual situation and is intended to demonstrate the potential deployment of the SDFIPM. It is modelled after Ciardhuáin’s (2004) scenario, which pertains to the exploitation of a vulnerability found in an online service operated by a bank:

This investigation started when Bank X in London (England) received an email claiming to have found a vulnerability in an online service operated by the bank. The email offered to provide details of the vulnerability in exchange for payment. On checking their logs, Bank X concluded that an unauthorised access had been made to their web server. The bank received further emails threatening to reveal the vulnerability to the press and public, including a link to a website which the suspect intended to use to disclose the vulnerability. Bank X reported the issue to the police in London who initiated the investigation. It became obvious that the compromised web server was located in Manchester (England) from Bank X’s headquarters and that the source of the emails was in Cardiff (Wales). Therefore, another police force, namely SWP (the South Wales Police), took up the case to start the investigation.

***Examination Process***

•This activity initially occurs when the bank examines their log files. It also occurs when the police examine the log files, the emails and the working copy of both the hard drive and the RAM images of the suspect’s system in the DFL. During the Examination Process, investigators process the deleted and hidden data to ensure that emails and log files are recognised from the evidence. Investigators also harvest data to provide structure to the data in which they are interested so that it can be mounted on the investigating machine. Since the suspect’s system contains a large amount of data such as known system files, investigators use metadata and unique identifiers to reduce the data by removing known system files and data from other applications. The investigators are now left with the log files and the emails that the suspect sent to Bank X. Now, the emails can be uniquely attributed to the suspect who has been the user of that specific system.

***Analysis Process***

•This Process initially takes place when Bank X’s system administrator, Mr. Thompson, and the incident response team, conclude from the log files that an unauthorised access has been made to their web server. Later on, this Process is conducted in a forensic laboratory by investigators who develop the initial hypothesis for the identity of the suspect and for the manner in which the incident has taken place.

***Interpretation Process***

•This Process occurs after investigators evaluate their findings in the Analysis Process and determine that their formulated hypothesis is true. During this Process, investigators interpret digital evidence to produce meaningful statements for later reporting and presentation regarding how the suspect made an unauthorised access to Bank X’s web server. As part of this Process, investigators classify and organize the interpreted evidence such as log files and emails according to their relevance in order to distinguish which digital evidence items are more important than others.

***Event Reconstruction Process***

•This process occurs when investigators reconstruct the events which led to the identification of the suspect and the subsequent seizure of the suspect’s computer. This entails the investigators iterating over the CDFIPM, and results in a more detailed hypothesis. Through this Process, investigators are able to explain how the suspect has carried out the intrusion to Bank X’s web server. Investigators consolidate and review their findings prior to assessing the results of their review against the original hypothesis that they have formulated. Through this assessment, investigators ensure that they have gathered all relevant evidence related to that attack to support their hypothesis.

***Reporting Process***

•This Process takes place when investigators compile a report based on their findings to be presented in a court.

***Presentation Process***

•This Process occurs five times during the entire investigation. This includes: when the bank’s IT Administrator presents the evidence to the management within the bank, when the bank approaches the MPS Police and presents their evidence to investigators, when the MPS Police passes the investigation to SWP, when evidence is presented to acquire a search warrant and when investigators present the evidence in court. The formality of the evidence increases as the investigation proceeds. Prior to presenting their findings to the court, investigators meet with the legal team to understand the presentation requirements. During the meeting, the target audience in the court is determined. Investigators also carry out the necessary preparation prior to attending court such as preparing expert testimony, exhibits and appropriate presentation aids.

•During the presentation in court, investigators are able to assist the judge and jury in understanding the technical points made by avoiding complex arguments and delivering their conclusion in a logical and structured manner. The presentation contains factual data that investigators have deduced. Moreover, investigators use the SDFIPM to enable the judge to comprehend the processes that they have followed during the investigation. In the court, the investigators have to prove and to defend the validity of the hypothesis as it is challenged by the court and the defence lawyers. Since investigators have followed a formal model which enabled them to carry out the investigation in a forensically sound manner, the opposite hypothesis is refuted. The court decides that the suspect has made an unauthorised access to Bank X’s web server and sentences him to prison.

***Investigation Closure Process***

•This Process takes place after a formal decision is reached by the court concerning the incident. During this Process, based on the outcome of the investigation, Bank X reviews its existing policies and procedures concerning its IT security. As there is no need to backtrack to the previous stages in the investigation, the bank management decides to accept the hypothesis. During this Process, the bank identifies the lessons learnt and the suspect’s system is returned to his employer’s company. The result of the case is recorded on the database for possible similar future cases.

•The final phase of this activity is Disseminate Investigation Results, where relevant information concerning this incident and its outcome are communicated to all stakeholders. The initial communication is carried out prior to the completion of the trial in order to remove the sensitive data from the disseminated information. The final phase, the Review Phase, discusses how the incident could have been handled better. One possible outcome is the installation of the central log server sooner than planned. The Review Phase includes a review of the investigation and identifies some new analysis techniques that are employed. The techniques are added to the official analysis procedures. During the analysis, new suspect files are identified, and they are added to the hash database so that they can be quickly found in future investigations.

This section followed the Demonstration activity of Peffers *et al*.’s DSRP (2006) and discussed the method employed to demonstrate the potential deployment of the SDFIPM. By using the selected method, we successfully applied the SDFIPM to a case scenario and performed a walkthrough of the model. This walkthrough mapped the model’s components to the corresponding activities carried out by DFPs operating in the three fields of law enforcement, commerce and incident response. Having completed the Demonstration activity, the next stage in Peffers *et al*.’s DSRP \[1\] is the Evaluation activity, discussed in the following section.

### 9.6.Evaluation of the SDFIPM

This section follows the Evaluation activity of the Peffers *et al*.’s DSRP (2006), that requires the artifact to be validated in order to determine: (1) how well it supports the solution to the stated research problem, and (2) whether it is necessary to iterate back to the Design and Development stage to improve the effectiveness of the artefact. Thus, to assess how the SDFIPM addressed the stated research problem, we involved the participation of the SDFIPM’s intended user community who could independently verify and validate the proposed model. This user community included DFPs operating within the three fields of relevance for this research, namely law enforcement, commerce and incident response, as well as experts in the domain of DF, legal practitioners and researchers in both academia and industry. Once the Evaluation Phase was completed, we were able to feed the results of the Evaluation activity back into the SDFIPM’s Design and Development Phase and amend the model accordingly. Similar approaches that involve using such an evaluation activity have been adopted in previous studies, for instance by Adams (2012) and Ciardhuáin (2004). The remainder of this section provides a summary of results in relation to the Evaluation activities performed on the SDFIPM.

### 9.6.1.*Methods of validation*

A major component of any forensic research is to demonstrate the validity of the results. The DSR studies are prone to the same types of errors as are any other qualitative studies, so ensuring validity is important. Therefore, to assess our model’s accuracy in meeting its intended outcomes, we employed a set of validation methods as opposed to relying on only one method. To ensure the credibility of the study results concerning the proposed model, we performed a triangulation technique to facilitate the validation of data. The triangulation consisted of combining five different methods to overcome the weaknesses or inherent biases and the problems that come from single-method, single-observer and single-theory studies. These methods enabling the validation of forensic artefacts included (Eddy *et al*., 2012):

1.Internal Validity — the model’s components are analysed and their accuracy is checked;

2.Cross Validity — results are compared with other models analysing the same problem;

3.External Validity — the model is used to simulate different scenarios;

4.Predictive Validity — the model results are compared with prospectively observed events; and

5.Face Validity — independent experts evaluate the model structure, its associated data and results.

In the context of this research, methods 1, 2 and 3 above have already been applied to the SDFIPM in the Design and Development stage of the SDFIPM, which is the middle part of the larger model, the CDFIPM, in Montasari’s study (Montasari, 2016a). See [Chapters 3](#chapter3.xhtml) and [4](#chapter4.xhtml) of Montasari’s research study (Montasari, 2016a) for more comprehensive details about the results of methods 1, 2 and 3. For instance, in terms of the Internal Validity method, the model’s components were analysed and justified in [Chapter 3](#chapter3.xhtml) (Design and Development), which addressed whether the model’s components behaved as intended and whether it had been implemented correctly. In relation to the Cross-Validation method, the model was mapped and compared with the existing models, which involved determining the degree to which they calculated the same results. Concerning the External Validation method, similar to [Section 9.5](#chapter9.xhtml#sec9.5) of this paper, in [Chapter 4](#chapter4.xhtml) (Demonstration) of Montasari’s research (Montasari, 2016a), the model was applied to different scenarios and a walk-through of the model was performed to simulate different types of real life investigations. Method 4, Predictive Validity, has been excluded from this research on the basis that this validation method would need to be carried out over a long period of time, thus being outside the timing scope of this research.

Face Validity (method 5), which is considered to be the strongest form of the 5 stated validation methods (Law, 2014; Eddy *et al*., 2012; Pace and Sheehan, 2002), is the topic of this section, where the external experts evaluate the model structure and its associated data, results and accuracy independently. This method is used to answer the following questions:

1.Does the model provide its users with both utility and usability?

2.Has the model been built right? and

3.Has the right model been built?

According to Pace and Sheehan (2002), the main validation method for models must include assessment by experts and peers. This argument is supported by other researchers in various scientific environments (Burgman *et al*., 2011; Czembor and Vesk, 2009; Ludwig *et al*., 2001). Moreover, in circumstances in which empirical data are scarce or unobtainable, expert knowledge and their input are often considered to be the best or only source of information (McBride and Burgman, 2012; Kuhnert, 2010; Sutherland, 2006). In these situations, experts can be requested to provide input for all the stages of the modelling process (Martin *et al*., 2012; Cowling and Pressey, 2003; Pearce *et al*., 2001). Thus, the remainder of this section draws upon the Face Validity method by recruiting external experts to answer the three questions above and to ultimately determine whether the SDFIPM has achieved both the ‘utility’ and ‘usability’ necessary for a model.

### 9.6.2.*Expert selection process*

Booker and McNamara (2004) define expert knowledge as the knowledge and expertise that qualified persons have acquired due to their technical practices, training and experience. Based on this definition, it is, therefore, reasonable to regard an individual as a ‘domain expert’ if he/she is familiar with the subject at hand and is accountable for the analysis of the issue and the provision of sound judgments. Moreover, according to McBride and Burgman (2012), the experts should be selected on the basis of explicit criteria in order to ensure transparency and establish that the results represent the full range of views in the expert field. The common metrics outlined in the literature for selecting experts include: experts’ qualifications, employment, memberships in professional bodies, publication records, years of experience, peer nomination, and perceived standing in their community (Czembor and Vesk, 2009; Drescher *et al*., 2008; Whitfield *et al*., 2008). Additional considerations that need to be made include the availability and willingness of experts to participate, and the possibility of conflicts of interest (McBride and Burgman, 2012).

The appropriate number of experts should depend on (1) the scope of the research problem (see below) and (2) the available timing during which the research is expected to be completed (McBride and Burgman, 2012). However, the literature on expert selection strongly suggests the inclusion of as diverse a range of experts as possible (Armstrong, 2006; Clemen and Winkler, 1999) by recruiting multiple experts in order to reduce the impact of individual mistakes and biases and to pave the way for assessments that are representative of the entire expert community (Fisher, 2009; Hokstad *et al*., 1998). In most scientific environments, as Martin *et al*. (2012) and Ludwig *et al*. (2001) point out, the breadth of research problems denotes that no one individual will be expert for all aspects of the problem. Hence, we identified and recruited a diverse group of experts with different skill sets for the Evaluation process. Therefore, since the intended applicability of the SDFIPM was aimed at three domains of law enforcement, commerce and incident response, we recruited experts operating within the stated fields to evaluate the model. This approach enabled us to ensure that the SDFIPM would undergo ‘utility’ and ‘usability’ testing by experts in relation to how ‘useful’ and ‘relevant’ the model would be to each of the experts’ particular domains of practice. Therefore, to acquire the needed expert coverage, we recruited a diverse set of eminent experts who could provide expert review and feedback on the ‘utility’ and ‘usability’ aspects of the proposed model. We based our selection of experts upon the common metrics found in the literature such as those presented in Czembor and Vesk (2009), Drescher *et al*. (2008), and Whitfield *et al*. (2008). The following selection criteria were considered during the recruitment process:

•geographical operation — DFIs and legal practitioners needed to operate within the UK as the model’s intended application would be aimed at the UK jurisdiction.

•period of experience and learning — the participants needed to have extensive knowledge and experience in the domain of DF for a period of at least 10 years.

•the manner in which the experience had been acquired — for instance, the experts’ experience needed to have been attained through practice and theory to ensure that the expert panel would consist of both theorists and practitioners.

•qualifications — the participants needed to have appropriate qualifications in relation to DF, information security (IS) or computer science (CS).

•reputation — the experts needed to have a solid standing in their particular domains of practice.

Therefore, we deemed the use of the following diverse set of experts to be beneficial in increasing what McBride and Burgman (2012) term as “the acceptance or perceived validity of the elicitation process”. This would ensure that different perspectives would be brought into the Evaluation Process. Experts (expert panel) who took part in the evaluation process were then categorized into three groups of (1) DFPs, (2) legal practitioners, and (3) researchers both in academia and industry. Experts from the panel were identified as representatives of their specific domains of practice based on their roles, responsibilities, experience and involvement within pertinent associations in the UK jurisdiction. The recruitment process for the expert panel was considered complete once numerous participants from each of the three fields covered by the research scope had consented to assist. The following are the profiles of the experts constituting the members of the three groups of the expert panel:

•A representative of law enforcement (MSc in Computing & Information Technology and EnCase Certified Examiner) with 25 years of experience as a police officer who manages the entire High-Tech/Cyber Crime team of the North West Regional Organised Crime Unit (TITAN), consisting of six police forces in Cumbria, Cheshire, Lancashire, Greater Manchester, Merseyside and North Wales;

•A representative of commercial practice with 18 years of experience as a Digital Forensic Investigator and a Forensic Triage Specialist who is the director of Digital Forensics for a large company;

•A representative of legal practice (LL.B) with 13 years of experience who is a self-employed barrister and who has worked on over 20 cases involving digital investigations;

•A Detective Sergeant of eForensics (BSc in Computing and Information Technology) who is a certified ENCE, a certified Security Incident Specialist, and a certified Forensic Investigation Analyst with 28 years of experience as a police officer who heads the Cheshire Police Headquarters (Cheshire Constabulary) High-Tech Crime Unit;

•A representative of commercial practice (MPhil in Operating System Anti-Malware/Security and an MSc in Internet Engineering);

•A Detective Constable of Digital Forensics at the South Wales Gwent Police High-Tech Crime Unit representative of law enforcement with 18 years of experience as a DFP;

•A Detective Constable of Digital Forensics at the South Wales Gwent Police High-Tech Crime Unit with 11 years of experience as a DFP;

•A representative of academia (PhD) who is a university professor and a prominent researcher with many publications on information security, biometrics and digital forensics. He has been the keynote speaker at reputable information security and digital forensics conferences;

•A representative of legal practice (LL.B) with 34 years’ experience of practicing law who is a Deputy High Court Judge and a barrister based in Exchange Chambers within Manchester, Leeds and Liverpool and the Chairman of the Northern Chancery Bar Association and a Trustee of the North West Partnership;

•A representative of academia (PhD) who is a university professor and a well-known researcher with various publications on digital forensic practice.

### 9.6.3.*Feedback formats and analysis*

In the first instance, the experts participating in the Evaluation process were requested to assist in this research via email. Once the experts were identified and their confirmation for participation in the Evaluation process was obtained, then in line with the best practices outlined in the literature (Morgan and Henrion, 2010; Rothlisberger *et al*., 2010; Cooke and Goossens, 2000), they were provided with relevant materials associated with the model that had been compiled into an appropriate, accessible form. These consisted of the UML Activity Diagrams of the model, the explanatory notes describing the model’s components, a questionnaire (see Appendix B), background information such as the aim and objectives of the research, and also a description of what they were requested to undertake. These materials had already been carefully piloted to ensure that the documentation had been compiled properly. It was important to ensure that the Evaluation questions had been formulated appropriately to reflect the research problem, identify potential issues with biases or question phrasing, and elicit feedback about any potential ways to enhance the quality of the process and of the knowledge that was to be extracted. The pilot process was conducted with academic colleagues who checked the compiled documents prior to their submissions to the experts for review. Once piloted and compiled, the documents were sent to the participating experts via email so that they could have sufficient time to evaluate them, raise any potential concerns, comment on any aspect of the model, and volunteer relevant information. Having acquired the experts’ feedback via e-mails, formal meetings were then held at the experts’ workplaces at an arranged date and time to discuss their feedback with them and to elicit further expert knowledge that it was not possible to obtain via e-mails. These meetings took place following focus group and interview formats as such approaches are recommended in the literature based on their advantages as follows:

•The interview and focus group formats take full advantage of the experience and skills of those participating by being more open than a narrowly-focussed survey.

•Experts have a stronger understanding of the subject matter as they can ask questions concerning the research rather than simply replying to a fixed set of questions.

•Participants are able to express and discuss views that are not likely to be identified by a simple survey. Such issues can be analysed in some detail during the interview or focus group.

•Experts are left free to express their views in whatever manner they feel is most appropriate.

Once all the data was collected, the participants’ responses were then subjectively analysed through a rigorous verification process and acted upon where necessary. In line with McBride and Burgman’s (2012) and Cooke’s (1991) suggestions, we checked for obvious errors or inconsistencies by comparing the expert’s responses to those of others in the panel. In comparing an individual expert’s responses with those of the rest of the panel, we looked for similarities, irregularities, biases, or strongly conflicting opinions in addition to varying interpretations of the information. When such irregularities or problematic responses were identified, we followed up on the conflicting feedback through further discussions with the experts. We then acted upon the acquired feedback which involved ‘addition to’, ‘alteration to’ and ‘deletion from’ the model. ‘Addition’ refers to a new component being added to the model, ‘alteration’ refers to the change in a component’s naming or order and ‘deletion’ refers to the deletion of a component from the model. The aforementioned three terminologies that have been acted upon are represented on the model’s UML Activity Diagrams using the following references:

1.Reference to Addition: ‘REF: ADD #n’, where ‘n’ represents the number of implemented ‘additions’.

2.Reference to Alteration: ‘REF: ALT #n’, where ‘n’ represents the number of implemented ‘changes’.

3.Reference to Deletion: ‘REF: DEL #n’, where ‘n’ represents the number of implemented ‘deletions’.

Both generic and detailed feedback are presented below in the form of quotes together with our specific comments in response to the feedback. We first provide the positive comments followed by a discussion of the more detailed feedback.

### 9.6.4.*General feedback*

*“I can see a lot of work has been put into this and you have covered everything I can think of, my only comment would be enabling your model to be interactive rather that a set procedure.”* (Law enforcement DFP and Case Officer)

*“The model is impressive in its detail and reasonably easy to understand and use. The author has clearly understood the practicalities of an effective and efficient digital investigation.”* (Legal practitioner, barrister)

*“With ACPO Guidelines, there is no defined structure to it, no defined path to it. What we need is that these methods have been validated scientifically. This is something you have worked out over long time. Your model has been peer reviewed both by practitioners and scientists even though we might choose it differently.”* (Law enforcement DFP)

*“This model is very timely and well-researched. It is my conclusion that you have gone deep enough into details of finding out what exactly is wrong with the existing models and what to do to improve them.”* (University professor)

*“This is sound standard for forensic service providers (FSPs). This is like UCAS was.”* (Law enforcement DFP)

*“Your model provides a concise guidance on the exact processes that examiners need to follow during any kind of digital investigation.”* (Commercial DFP)

*“It is necessary that the court understands the process that has been followed. Your model has done a great job as its processes are documented in a very rational way. A judge or barrister could pick up this model and work out what has been happening in a digital investigation.”* (Legal practitioner, judge)

*“What you have presented is actually good. You have done a great job; I feel that the model you have presented would accelerate digital investigations because it gives a common order of processes and activities that a computer forensic investigation requires.”* (Law enforcement DFP and Case Officer)

*“Your model is like modular plugin type for different fields.”* (Law enforcement DFP)

*“There is much in your model that covers cybercrime and such attacks that are not covered in LE.”* (Law enforcement DFP)

*“Sorry for the delay in replying. I have had a chance to look at your model and it is sound in its interpretation. How would you like my feedback?”* (Commercial DFP)

*“Your model reflects in part our Cheshire’s existing model, and I do not intend changing to anything other in the near future as this model simply reflects what we already have.”* (Law enforcement DFP and Case Officer)

*“I have had an initial look at your work and it looks interesting and a very comprehensive model.”* (Commercial DFP)

### 9.6.5.**Detailed feedback and responses**

**Feedback E-3:** “*Event Reconstruction is something we do not tend to practice as it is labour intensive. However, I would use this if the circumstances dictate.”*

•**Response:** Although Event Reconstruction might be labour intensive, it still must be part of any digital investigation so that it, together with the Analysis and Interpretation Processes, can enable DFPs to construct a full picture of the events that have taken place. If DFPs do not perform the Event Reconstruction Process, questions in relation to who, why, where, when and how will not be addressed properly. As a result, this can severely affect the outcome of the case in courts. However, in certain circumstances, Event Reconstruction might not be as necessary; for example, when the incident/crime is not classified as severe, and the investigation results are to be presented to the company management as opposed to a court. Thus, no further action will be taken in light of the above feedback.

**Feedback E-21:**“*Include team/investigation debrief in the investigation closure section.”*

•**Response:** This had already been covered under a different terminology ‘Conduct a Critical Review’ in the CDFIPM’s Investigation Closure Process. Since it appears that DFPs are more accustomed to the term ‘debriefing’ as this was pointed out also by a number of different experts, the terminology ‘Conduct a Critical Review’ will now be changed to Conduct a Team/Investigation Debrief (“REF: ALT #4”).

**Feedback E-23:***“‘Analysis’ should come before ‘developing hypothesis’. Although having analysis* + *hypothesis would be sufficient, you could always have a re-analysis in light of the hypothesis afterwards. In reality a competent investigator would always re-evaluate; so having a ‘re-analysis’ component would simply acknowledge that (& perhaps encourage/ remind less competent investigators to do so!)”*

•**Response:** The above feedback is aimed at the Develop a Hypothesis and Analyse Digital Evidence Phases of the Analysis Process. The ordering of the two Phases will now be changed and a new Phase entitled ‘Reanalyse Digital Evidence’ will be included after the Develop a Hypothesis Phase in the Analysis Process (“REF: ALT #5”) and (“REF: ADD #6”).

**Feedback E-24:***“What is meant by ‘reduce acquired data’? Why?”*

•**Response:** The above question was posed by a legal practitioner in relation to the Reduce Acquired Data Phase of the Examination Process. The following is the response that we provided and the legal practitioner’s further feedback.

The authors: “In terms of the ‘Reduce Acquired Data’ Phase, since a digital device can contain a large amount of data, most of which are not related to the case under investigation, investigators will therefore need to reduce data only to what they are interested in. Does this make sense?”

The legal practitioner: *“Yes, that makes sense. However, the fact that I (as a lay person) had to ask suggests it may be useful to provide a better explanation. An option would be to have a ‘Glossary of Terms’ at the end of the document — I think that would be really valuable, and I have seen them used a lot in other technical documents presented to the court.”*

The above comment had already been addressed in the Appendix section of Montasari’s (2016a) study.

**Feedback E-25**:*“There is no need to have ‘Consolidate investigation findings’ when you have ‘review investigation results’ immediately after it.”*

•**Response:** The Consolidate Investigation Findings Phase will now be removed from the Event Reconstruction Process as it appears to be repetitive of its following Phase, namely Review Investigation Results (“REF: DEL #4”).

**Feedback E-26:**“*After ‘Identify areas of improvement’, have a further action to act on any areas identified.”*

•**Response:** A new Phase entitled ‘Act upon Any Areas Identified’ will be added after the Identify Areas of Improvement (If Any) Phase of the Event Reconstruction Process (“REF: ADD #7”).

**Feedback E-27:***“In the ‘Presentation’ section, why is there a requirement to consider the appeal process at this stage?”*

•**Response:** The Consider Appeal Process had been included in the Presentation Process in order to enable investigators to make contingency plans in advance to take account of possible case rejection by courts of law where they would need to launch an appeal. Therefore, this Phase will remain in the Presentation Process, and no further action will be taken.

**Feedback E-28:***“Consider re-ordering ‘Presentation’ section as follows: Determine the target audience — Understand the requirements of the presentation — Consider (and apply) the legal jurisdictional requirements — Consider the appeal process — Prepare exhibits — Use appropriate presentation aids — Present the report — Prove/ defend the validity of the hypothesis — Decide the case”*

•**Response:** The ordering of the Phases in the Presentation Process will be amended as suggested above (“REF: ALT #6”).

**Feedback E-29:***“In ‘Investigation Closure’ section, ‘Record the case decision’ should come after accepting or rejecting the hypothesis and before the question of whether the evidence can be returned.”*

•**Response:** The Record the Case Decision will now be placed immediately after the Accept or Reject the Hypothesis Phase as suggested in this feedback (“REF: ALT #7”).

**Feedback E-30:***“If the evidence cannot be returned, have separate actions for (a) store, cleanse and re-use the evidence, and for (b) destroying the evidence — ask a question the answer to which would identify which of these 2 options would be followed.”*

•**Response:** The above comment refers to the management of evidence in the Investigation Closure Process. This is a very constructive piece of feedback which was brought to our attention as no explicit condition (question in the form of UML Activity Diagram notation) had previously been specified with regards to the sensitivity of digital evidence. Further clarification was needed in terms of the legal aspect of sensitive digital evidence. Therefore, further communication took place between us and the legal practitioner (judge) as follows:

Authors: “Thank you very much for bringing such an important issue to my attention. I am going to create further conditions as suggested. So, they will be like this: ‘Can the evidence be returned?’ If the answer is ‘yes’, the evidence will be returned. If the answer is ‘no’, the investigator will be provided with another condition asking whether the evidence can be destroyed. If the answer to this question is ‘yes’, the investigator will need to destroy the evidence. If the answer is ‘no’, the investigator could cleanse and reuse the device. From a legal point of view, is this a sound approach? And is this similar to what you thought?”

Judge: *“Yes. I don’t know whether you also need to include a more detailed guide for the investigator as to when each step would be appropriate. For example, presumably ‘sensitive’ information would not be returned, but would be destroyed. It may help investigators to have a finite list of which types of evidence would fall into each category; but I don’t know if this goes beyond the remit of what you are trying to achieve here. Another, perhaps simpler way might be this:*

—*‘Is the evidence sensitive?’ (And / or other terms that would cover all scenarios which you would decide whether to return, destroy or cleanse & reuse evidence.)*

—*Yes — it cannot be returned — Can it be destroyed? ……. (Cleanse and reuse, etc.)*

—*No — it can be returned.*

Based upon the above detailed feedback and further clarification, three new conditions have been developed that will be included in the Presentation Process to accommodate also for the ‘sensitivity’ of digital evidence (“REF: Add #8”). However, developing a fixed list of which types of evidence would fall into each category is outside the scope of this research and must be determined by the investigating organisations based on their own internal guidelines.

**Feedback E-31:***“Consider swapping order of ‘make recommendations’ and ‘develop a case study’ in ‘Future Readiness’”.*

•**Response:** The ordering will be amended (“REF: ALT #8”).

### 9.6.6.**Analysis of the results**

In relation to ‘utility’, this component of the Evaluation activity was intended to ensure that the proposed model had ‘serviceability’, ‘applicability’ and ‘appropriateness’ to the law enforcement, commerce, incident response and legal domains as stated in the research problem. The model was therefore subjected to an external, independent evaluation by the leading experts in its intended user community to ensure that it had been built right and that the right model had been built. The comments regarding the SDFIPM were very positive, and the feedback was both constructive and insightful. There were a total number of 31 detailed pieces of feedback in relation to the larger model, the CDFIPM, 11 of which related to the SDFIPM, including suggestions for new additions, amendments and deletions. Out of the 11 feedbacks for the SDFIPM, 2 new additions, 4 amendments and 1 deletion were made in and from the SDFIPM. Having made the new model subject to the experts’ scrutiny, it became clear that there did not exist any aspects of the SDFIPM that were not representative of the processes as carried out in the fields covered by the research scope. Similarly, there were not any aspects of the processes as performed in the stated fields that were not covered in the SDFIPM. In response to the question of utility (see the questionnaire in Appendix B), “Please rate the model on the scale of 1 to 10, with 1 being not useful at all and 10 being the most useful.”, experts provided the mean score of ‘9’. This suggests that the SDFIPM has achieved the intended component of utility required of a useful artefact. The following are some comments made by the experts in relation to the utility of the model:

•*“Much of your model covers most aspects in good detail of what is required but the order would change or be adopted to operational needs. But, all principles and processes are there in good details.”* (Law enforcement DFP and manager)

•*“You have identified the relevant problems with the current models and have provided detailed analysis. I believe that your model has made a significantly novel contribution in its current length and presentation. Congratulations on accomplishing such a daunting task!”* (University professor)

•*“This model allows a smooth transition from one phase to another during a digital investigation. If I were to use it, it would certainly give me a detailed advice about what to do with the evidence.”* (Commercial DFP)

•*“You have covered all avenues in different elements of digital investigations.”* (Law enforcement DFP)

•*“It is absolutely practicable and structured. You would not go wrong.”* (Commercial DFP)

•*“This model is very comprehensive; I can’t see any loopholes. Some issues are raised about detaining a suspect, where there could be multiple persons in a property with none saying who the suspect is.”* (Law enforcement DFP)

•*“I can say that your model provides transparency in acquiring produced result for each given process.”* (Legal practitioner, Judge)

•*“Because of its level of details, your model will facilitate collecting high quality evidence in a fast manner.”* (Law enforcement DFI)

With regards to the ‘usability’, this component of the Evaluation activity was intended to determine the ease with which experts in the law enforcement, commerce, incident response and legal domains can employ the SDFIPM to carry out those activities described by the model that relate to their practice. In response to the question of usability (see the questionnaire in Appendix B), “Please rate the model on the scale of 1 to 10, with 1 being very difficult to use and 10 being very easy to use”, experts provided the mean score of ‘8.7’. This also indicates that the SDFIPM has achieved the intended component of usability required of a useful artefact. The following are some comments made by the experts in relation to the usability of the SDFIPM:

•*“This model is clear in its layout and the majority of its terms, which largely enables the user to understand the steps taken during the investigation without assistance. Where some of the terms are unclear or technical, the assistance of the explanation of a digital forensic investigator would overcome any difficulty in comprehension.”* (Legal practitioner, barrister)

•*“It is important to have robust process behind the presentation of digital evidence because you have an adversarial system. Each seeks to undermine the evidence of the other if they can. Your model presents the forensic process very clearly; it is readily understandable to someone without technical expertise especially for jury.”* (Legal practitioner, judge)

•*“Your model has a very clear layout that covers all aspects succinctly.”* (Law enforcement DFI)

•*“I like the workflows as they are simple but effective.”* (Law enforcement DFI)

The aim of this subsection was to evaluate the SDFIPM in order to determine whether the model had been built right and whether the right model had been built and consequently to establish whether the SDFIPM had achieved both the ‘utility’ and ‘usability’ components. To this end, the model was subjected to an independent, external evaluation by its intended user community. From the positive feedback received and its analysis, it has become clear that the model has been built right and the right model has been built. It has also become obvious that the SDFIPM has achieved both the utility and usability required from a forensic artefact.

### 9.6.7.*Alterations made to the SDFIPM*

This subsection presents the modifications that were made to the UML Activity Diagrams of the SDFIPM in response to the feedback provided by experts in [subsection 9.6.5](#chapter9.xhtml#sec9.6.5). Where a modification has been made, this is shaded and provided with its corresponding reference (addition, alteration or deletion) from the feedback in [subsection 9.6.5](#chapter9.xhtml#sec9.6.5). The idea to modify our model in such a way is adopted from Adams’s (2012) study. The final version of the UML Activity Diagrams of the SDFIPM is presented in Appendix C.

### 9.7.Conclusion

### 9.7.1.**Research problem addressed**

Following the identification of three major issues with the previous DFIPMs, namely the lack of a model that has all three characteristics of being “comprehensive”, “formal” and “generic”, we formulated the following research question that we set out to address:

There does not exist a comprehensive model encompassing the entire digital investigative process that is formal, such that it can assist a court of law in determining the reliability of the investigative process followed, and that is generic, in that it can be applied in the different fields of law enforcement, commerce and incident response.

Based upon Peffers *et al*.’s DSRP (2006), the acquisition of two resources was sought in order to define the “objectives of the solution”. These included: “… knowledge of the state of the problem” and “current solutions and their efficacy, if any”. The knowledge of the state of the problem for this research was covered in the Introduction section, where the research problem was defined and the value of its solution justified. However, to address the two resources fully, further knowledge of the state of the problem was required and current solutions, if any, had to be identified. In order to acquire the two stated resources, previous models were critically reviewed and assessed against three different sets of assessment criteria in Montasari’s (2016a) research study, with the summary of this analysis being presented in this chapter. Through this assessment, the prevailing models that could contribute to the design and development of the proposed model were identified, and the necessary components that would constitute the basic structure of the new model were determined. Following the Design and Development activity of Peffers *et al*.’s DSRP (2006), the proposed model was designed and implemented based upon the information acquired through the critical analysis.

Once designed and developed, in accordance with the Demonstration activity of Peffers *et al*.’s DSRP (2006), we applied the model to a case study, thereby demonstrating the efficacy of the proposed model to solve the stated research problem. We then covered the Evaluation activity of Peffers *et al*.’s DSRP (2006), through which the model was subjected to a critical review and feedback process by the leading experts in its intended user community to determine how well the new model would support the solution to the stated research problem. To follow up on the feedback obtained from the experts, we returned to the Design and Development stage to make subsequent amendments, including new additions, alterations and deletions as shown in [Figs. 9.4](#chapter9.xhtml#fig9.4) and [9.5](#chapter9.xhtml#fig9.5) in their amended form and in Appendix C in its final version. This was to address the two components of ‘utility’ and ‘usability’ further by finding the answers to the two following questions: ‘has the model been built right?’ and ‘has the right model been built?’. All the acquired feedback was very positive, and there were no negative comments. When there was disagreement, we iterated back to the Design and Development Phase of the research, as stated, to make alterations based on the feedback in order to bring the model as close as possible (within the scope of the research) to its intended application. Having completed the formal evaluation of the model, we contend that ‘the new model has been built right’ and that ‘the right model has been built’ on the basis that its intended application has been observed, accepted and confirmed by the prominent experts in its intended user community. Therefore, the SDFIPM is complete, consistent, and accurate enough to fulfil the solution to the stated research problem, as defined in [Section 9.1](#chapter9.xhtml#sec9.1).

The last stage in Peffers *et al*.’s (2006) DSRP is the Communication activity, according to which the researcher needs to communicate the research problem and its importance, and also to explain the research artefact, its utility, usability and novelty, the rigor of its design, and its effectiveness to the intended user community. In relation to this research, we have made significant progress in this activity by attending various conferences, Forensic Expositions and Cyber Security Summits, and having extracts from our research study published in various peer-reviewed journals and conference proceedings.

### 9.7.2.*Research contribution*

This research has made a significant and novel contribution to the field of DF science by implementing a process model, the SDFIPM, that would assist DFPs in following a uniform approach. Our study has synthesized, harmonised and significantly built upon the existing models to produce the first process model that has all three characteristics of being comprehensive, formal and generic. No such model previously existed in the literature. The SDFIPM is scientifically rigorous as it assists courts in determining the reliability of the investigative process followed and generic in that it can be applied by DFPs operating in the three fields of law enforcement, commerce and incident response. The proposed model is inclusive of all the advantages of the previous models through their synthesis and harmonisation and contains purified terminology using the terms commonly agreed upon by DFPs. It is therefore argued that the SDFIPM would be a significant step towards the establishment of standards for the digital forensic investigative process. Every component in the model is well defined in terms of scope, functions and order. The model fully and thoroughly describes the flow of information in a digital investigation from the moment digital evidence is captured for examination until the investigation reaches its formal conclusion.

This study has also demonstrated how the digital investigative process can be represented through a proven formal notation, the Unified Modelling Language (UML). The representation of the SDFIPM via the UML Activity Diagrams will assist courts in properly understanding the digital investigative processes followed, a point acknowledged by the legal practitioners and judge who participated in the external evaluation of the model. Due to its level of detail and its step-by-step approach, the SDFIPM provides investigators with concise direction on the processes to be followed, enabling them to speed up the investigative process while minimising errors and negligence. Therefore, in the event of a challenge to the digital investigative process, there would be no doubt concerning the soundness of the processes followed. The proposed model also contains generic methods that DFPs can use to associate technology with non-technical observers. Importantly, the application of the SDFIPM could bring about the improved admissibility of digital evidence in courts, being a formal model with strong overriding principles resulting from rigorous scientific verification.

### 9.7.3.*Future work*

Although the SDFIPM is mainly aimed at the UK jurisdiction, it could easily be adapted to other jurisdictions. Without such modification, the model already has relevance to those jurisdictions which employ a similar legal basis for evaluating the digital investigative process. The SDFIPM focuses predominantly on Computer Forensics as opposed to other branches of DF. Although some much simpler models have claimed to be appropriate for various branches of DF, such a claim is not made in relation to the SDFIPM for accuracy purposes. However, it is argued that due to the SDFIPM’s detailed and generic approach, it could easily be adapted to cover any branch of DF. Although an evaluation of the SDFIPM has been undertaken by the High-Tech Crime Units (HTCUs) of two different police forces in the UK, experts in corporate and incident response environments, legal practitioners and researchers in academia, they cannot be representative of all intended users. Future work could include a more comprehensive trial by DFPs, experts, legal practitioners and researchers as part of a wider study. Similarly, although the case scenarios to which the SDFIPM was applied represent each of the three fields of DF to which the model is relevant, the SDFIPM would benefit from further case studies to identify task hierarchies. This would improve task development efforts and facilitate scenario development, assisting its users, researchers and tool developers in understanding how to take advantage of and apply the model. Finally, as with the future work, the SDFIPM must be validated through the Method Validation under ISO 17025 accreditation to determine its compliance.
