## ABSTRACT

Ensuring continuity of evidence in any investigation is problematic, even more so when multiple agencies are involved. Ensuring there is consistency between paperwork concerning the seizure of artefacts is difficult, and can often be scrutinized in court. The development of this prototype blockchain is for the recording of the transfer of evidence during an investigation, with the aim of providing a guarantee for the continuity of evidence. The implementation of the blockchain is completed using Hyperledger and is referred to in this paper as Blockchain of Custody, or BoC. To test BoC two simple mock investigations are carried out and then evaluated. The evaluation includes querying the evidence, access control, development, security, and auditing. The implementation of BoC is considered a success and the future improvements, disadvantages and advantages are discussed.

*Keywords*: Bitcoin, HyperLedger, blockchain, chain of custody, timestamp, legal assurance

### 10.1.Introduction

Over recent years the hyperbole surrounding Decentralised Applications (DApps) and Blockchain has distracted researchers from their rationales by making them consider new developments. Is the technology pushing change, or is change pushing the technology? Here we have taken the opportunity to investigate how blockchain technology can be implemented for the seizure and transfer of evidence, or, put simply, how a blockchain of custody would work. This proposal considers the development, the implementation, the benefits, the issues and finally the impact on Forensic Science in general.

There are many issues with how a current chain of custody for the collection of evidence is completed. In particular, there is one issue about safeguarding from tampering (ISO, 2017 (Section 7.11)). Chain of custody automation software is almost standard for accredited labs and is recommended in ISO (2017, 2013). However, there is room for improvement when it comes to transferring evidence to third parties and ensuring that the chain of custody is immutable and irreversible. This is the main motivation for this paper, to investigate the blockchain software development lifecycle facilitating the chain of custody procedures.

Blockchain of Custody (BoC) is a decentralisation application that provides an immutable and irreversible record of the chain of custody for evidence collected after any incident. It does not intend to replace evidence management software that provides much of industry standard and structure to generate reports and manage staff and facilities, e.g., Foreman (Lowman, 2018). Instead BoC intends to work with this software and improve the capability, value and quality of evidential-related material regarding the chain of custody.

### 10.2.Background

Whilst many marvel at the value Bitcoin, B, has bought to cryptocurrency, the biggest contribution to software engineering that Bitcoin has provided us with is decentralised applications or blockchain. Bitcoin (Nakamoto, 2008; Antonopoulos, 2017) and blockchain are inseparable; without blockchain technologies, Bitcoin would be unable to operate. Blockchain and consensus engineering are side products of Bitcoin. The blockchain is transparent, public, immutable, irreversible, secure, asynchronous, self-regulating and international. Briefly, Bitcoin users have a wallet, with which they can make transactions to other wallets securely using Public Key Infrastructures (PKI) encryption; this is facilitated by a distributed ledger, known as a blockchain. The blockchain is stored on multiple nodes in a network, each storing every transaction made between wallets. The confirmation of each transaction comes from the nodes, which check the validity of the transaction and then verify the transaction to all the other nodes in the network. The similarities between BoC and Bitcoin are as follows:

—Transactions: a transaction in Bitcoin represents the transfer of funds between two parties. Once this transaction has been verified it is added to the blockchain. BoC has transactions which record the transfer of artefacts between two parties and the blockchain can easily be modified to accommodate this type of transaction, see Greenspan (2015).

—Irrefutable: the motivation behind the validation of Bitcoin transactions is to ascertain that the spending party has the funds, and that there is no double-spending. Essentially, the motivation for validation comes down to financial accuracy. The motivation for the validation of BoC transactions are to ensure the integrity of the chain of custody.

—Longevity: in Bitcoin ledgers, the transactions are stored for the lifetime of Bitcoin itself. For BoC, all transactions of the chain of custody would also last for the duration of BoC, well beyond the time required for case information to be preserved. There is some concern over personal data being stored on BoC since it cannot be removed.

—Privacy: Bitcoin is public, so the ledgers can be seen by participants and non-participants of Bitcoin. BoC would be a private blockchain (Greenspan, 2015), often referred to as a permission blockchain, and would thus allow only authorised access.

—Data: Bitcoin transactions contain the users, the amount transferred, the timestamp and other meta-data. BoC transactions would differ and typically contain the receiver, submitter, manager, evidence ID, investigation ID and timestamp.

—Latency: the latency of blockchain verification in Bitcoin is such that it can take up to 10 minutes for Bitcoin to be mined and for this to be verified by a network of nodes; this latency is too long for the BoC application. This latency can be reduced to 10-20 secs, which is acceptable on a private blockchain, see Greenspan (2015) and Hyperledger Architecture Working Group (2017).

—Incentivisation: the incentive to set up a Bitcoin node is a reward of some value, albeit in the form of a digital crypto-currency. There is no value or reward in this BoC, however, typically there would be an incentive amongst regulators, e.g., FSR (Forensic Science Regulator, 2017), and accredited labs. If this was to be a national incentive, the nodes would be run independently by the regulators. This provides private transparency and the ability to see the chain of custody for each item of evidence.

—Disintermediation (Gaur *et al*., 2018): Many business and organisations rely on intermediaries, e.g. businesses rely on banks to complete transactions. It is necessary to trust one’s intermediaries. BitCoin overcomes this via consensus engineering and therefore removes the reliance on intermediaries. BoC would benefit from disintermediation, or not relying on intermediaries such as regulators or auditors. However, unlike the absence of regulators such as banks in the Bitcoin system, regulators would be integrated into the BoC system.

In summary, BoC is a system proposed, that, once updated, is immutable and irreversible. The system is implemented with blockchain technology, which is based on the Bitcoin technology. Its main contribution is ensuring that the chain of custody is immutable and irreversible and will add significant benefits to the integrity of all artefacts seized as items of evidence, both physical and digital, and therefore improve the overall quality of Evidence Management.

### 10.3.Blockchain of Custody, BoC

Evidential Continuity is part of evidence management and included in ISO17025 (ISO, 2017 (Section 7.11)). This means that to be an ISO17025 accredited forensic laboratory it is required, amongst other things, to have a secure information system that records, deletes, reports failures, ensures data integrity and has appropriate authorised access. ISO17025 compliance is an issue for all forensic laboratories handling evidence and allows the transparent audit of evidential continuity. These are usually only examined after the disclosure for a court case or audit. During the design and implementation of BoC the following are considered.

### 10.3.1.*Scope*

The scope of this evidence management system involves all stakeholders, but the system only records when evidence has been transferred between submitter and receiver. The details will include the unambiguous unique identifiers of submitter, receiver, investigation ID and artefact ID. The Business model involves the following stakeholders:

**Law Enforcement Agencies:** Police; Forensic Labs; Military; Security Agencies; Internal Quality Assurance Mechanisms; National Security Agencies; Expert Witnesses, and other government agencies.

**Legal Representation:** Prosecutors; Defence; Para-Legals; Internal Quality Assurance Mechanisms; Legal Mediator Assistants, and other business-related representatives.

**Audit Agencies:** Forensic Science Regulators; Independent Police Watchdogs; Legal Assurance Agencies, and other external agencies related to Law Enforcement and Legal.

### 10.3.2.*Transactions*

A DBMS has transactions to change the database from one consistent state to another. Partial transactions cannot occur, and transactions have to be committed. The transactions log, in a DBMS, is often used in backup instances or failures. Transactions have to pass the ACID test: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation and Durability (Haerder and Reuter, 1983). Some years later came OLTP and OLAP, which now dominate the data warehousing and data mining activities of organisations. Brewer (2000) highlighted these same issues with GraphDB. The problem was paradoxical, and the large databases could not address all three issues simultaneously. Much research has happened since 2000, and Brewer (2017) went on to elaborate on the advances in technology.

Transactions in blockchain and distributed ledgers are defined as the recording of the transaction inputs, transaction outputs, and amounts spent. A transaction does change the data in the blockchain. However, little is known about how consistency is applied to the blockchain. Whilst blockchain is decentralised under certain circumstances it can pass the ACID test (Verdian *et al*., 2018). This is important for such an application as BoC, in which consistency is required.

### 10.3.3.*No Wi-Fi, no reception*

Areas without Wi-Fi are common to crime scenes, e.g., underground. There are also issues with privacy on open networks, which are overcome by the encryption of the data submitted. In cases where there is no Wi-Fi access, the reliance on good old-fashioned forensics and physical paperwork will suffice and accompany evidence until a designated place with Wi-Fi access is reached and the blockchain can be updated. This is not unlike operations today, where internet access is prohibited due to network unavailability.

### 10.3.4.*Incentives*

The biggest implementation of blockchain is Bitcoin (Nakamoto, 2008). It is permissionless and secure; however, there are weaknesses. Sompolinsky and Zohar (2018) have discussed the arms race for ‘proofof-work’, the updating of the blockchain and the rewards received. Such incentives yield an uneven playing field created by nodes investing heavily in ASIC hardware to complete ‘proof-of-work’ and can lead to centralisation. As pointed out by Sompolinsky and Zohar, this will even out when the reward for block creation is withdrawn, and the focus is on transaction rewards. This does not affect permissioned blockchains, whereby control can be exerted over the network through consensus engineering. In permissioned blockchain applications where there are no tokens or coins, this is not a threat since there are no incentives for block creation and no reward for transactions.

### 10.3.5.*Permissioned blockchain*

The idea and advantages of permissioned blockchain (aka private blockchain) are discussed in Greenspan (2015). Permissioned blockchain (aka public blockchain) only allows authorised access, in other words, it is not permissionless. For BoC, permissioned blockchain is advantageous for the following reasons:

—It allows one to maintain control over transactions and how they are completed.

—The blockchain is only accessible by approved, trained and certified personnel.

—The blockchain has low latency. Permissionless blockchains, e.g., Bitcoin, have some latency between the timestamp of the transaction and the creation of the blockchain. This is to prevent node domination and is the result of the consensus algorithm, ‘proof-of-work’. With a permissioned blockchain, one can have control over the nodes, so competitive consensus algorithms are not required. Whilst consensus is required, the ability of a member of the blockchain to engage in node domination can be controlled.

—The members of the blockchain can be vetted. Vetting is an important process that is difficult in permissionless blockchains since anyone can join. In permissioned blockchain, members can be vetted and the issuance of keys can be controlled and managed.

### 10.3.6.*Tokens*

Blockchain is often incorrectly used synonymously with Bitcoin and therefore it is assumed that upon a transaction made on the blockchain an exchange of coins, or tokens, is required. Blockchain development can be completed without tokens; the question is, does the BoC application require them? Having a clear breakdown is not only important for designers and programmers, but also important for training purposes and ensuring that users follow procedures for updating the blockchain.

Typically, tokens are used in decentralised applications to prevent DoS attacks on nodes from disgruntled employees who have permissions to update multiple times. This could also apply to device breach, but this is unlikely since this would normally be reported and addresses associated with the device blocked. Tokens provide an additional level of security; however, the issuance of tokens would have to be centralised and updated accordingly. Re-distribution, re-use and the possible disposal of tokens is a concern, e.g. evidence store managers will have a surplus of tokens, whereas FRT members will have less, see [Fig. 3.6](#chapter3.xhtml#fig3.6). In order to perform a transaction, one would have to have a token of the minimum/smallest value. The value of the tokens can be controlled at issuance.

![image](images/fig10.1.jpg)

**Fig. 10.1.**Uneven token distribution: Where the evidence life-cycle ends, due to disposal or returns, there is an accumulation of tokens, represented by highlighted nodes in red.

[Figure 10.1](#chapter10.xhtml#fig10.1) illustrates the exchange of tokens between actors when exchanging evidence. For example, the path between vertexes 3 and 1 is directed and shows a flow of 10 tokens. [Figure 10.1](#chapter10.xhtml#fig10.1) indicates that there is a possibility of uneven token distribution. The distribution and issuance of tokens would have to be governed and completed by a central authority. This could lead to operational issues, e.g., the inability to submit evidence due to a token deficit. The issuance of tokens is also problematic and might have to be resolved by organisational restructuring, e.g., all Forensic Scientists might have to spend a day collecting tokens as a Custodian in the evidence store. It may seem possible to incorporate such measures into a BoC system, but these measures may be disagreeable to organisations in which the role of the user is less inter-disciplinary or in high demand.

Due to the problems outlined above, tokens will not be used in BoC. BoC is a not-for-profit permissioned blockchain application to assist in the recording of artefacts at investigations. Blockchain has a formula for cost, where *(Value created by blockchain – network operation costs > 0)* (Gaur *et al*., 2018 ([Chapter 10](#chapter10.xhtml))). However, when not-for-profit or public funds are used to cover costs the need and value of tokens diminish. When designing a blockchain application the need for tokens has to be considered and the important factors that play a role in this decision are as follows:

1.value of the token — is there any real value to the token;

2.purpose/funding of blockchain application — is the blockchain funded by the value of the tokens;

3.token issuance — how are tokens redistributed across all actors in the network;

4.uneven token distribution — does a particular type of user tend to accumulate tokens; and

5.organisational restructure — is organisational restructure required to redistribute your tokens.

### 10.3.7.*Hyperledger*

Participants, assets, transactions and events are the main components in a business network (Gaur *et al*., 2018 ([Chapter 6](#chapter6.xhtml))). These components can be described as follows:

**Participants:** Participants are the actors playing various roles in the business network, e.g., in BoC the actors are investigators, custodians, etc. These roles need defining and Use Case Diagrams are particularly important for identifying the participants. As pointed out in [Chapter 6](#chapter6.xhtml) of Gaur *et al*. (2018) there are three types of participants: individual, organisational and system.

**Assets:** Assets are the items of value to the network that are securely exchanged and recorded between participants. These assets need to be kept confidential, protected and secure. Much like data structures in databases, assets have properties and relationships, e.g., the ownership of an asset is a property of the asset.

**Transactions:** Transaction records change. Essentially, this is the asset lifecycle and the changing of properties, relationships and ownership are recorded and updated on the blockchain. In addition, the user that made the transaction is recorded, along with the timestamp when the transaction was made and finally, a unique hash code.

**Events:** Events represent a transition in the business network, e.g., when an artefact reaches a certain location.

### 10.4.Design

The design and development of blockchain applications is in its embryonic stages. There is no standard approach and it is proposed that using a modelling technique based on UML will help to provide a structured approach during design. The following sections explain the proposal and are centred around four aspects of blockchain: user modelling ([Section 10.4.1](#chapter10.xhtml#sec10.4.1)), data modelling ([Section 10.4.2](#chapter10.xhtml#sec10.4.2)), access control ([Section 10.4.3](#chapter10.xhtml#sec10.4.3)) and operational logic ([Section 10.4.4](#chapter10.xhtml#sec10.4.4)).

### 10.4.1.*User modelling*

The use case diagram in [Fig. 10.2](#chapter10.xhtml#fig10.2) identifies the roles of individuals and key processes required for the operation of a chain of custody, which is an important aspect of Access Control (as explained in [Section 10.4.3](#chapter10.xhtml#sec10.4.3)). The actors in the use case are generic and include a wide range of people in different organisations, e.g. Expert Witnesses are not included as a specific role, but can be accommodated in either Third Parties or Specialists. The issue here is that the attributes, which would be processed at run-time, allow a specific role certain access. The transactions carried out in the use cases have a direct relation to the transactions required in the blockchain, with the exception of Audit. In summary, the use case diagram helps a designer identify actors and transactions to add to the system.

![image](images/fig10.2.jpg)

**Fig. 10.2.**Use case diagram for BoC. Internal actors on right, external actors on left.

[Figure 10.2](#chapter10.xhtml#fig10.2) identifies five key use cases required: ‘Add new Investigation’; ‘Add new FRT member’; ‘Seizure’; ‘Exchange’; and, ‘Audit’. With the exception of ‘Audit’, each of these use cases requires a bespoke transaction and a flowchart detailing the sequence of events. ‘Audit’ is an exception, since it is querying the process and merely monitoring the blockchain, and since this is something that Hyperledger already provides. Of course, this is only a prototype. Future modifications may require updates to the blockchain when auditors view data, thus enabling an audit on the auditors.

### 10.4.2.Data modelling

[Figure 10.3](#chapter10.xhtml#fig10.3) illustrates the data requirements for this system. The class diagram does not include data attributes or methods since they are stored separately, the former on the blockchain and the latter in the system. It simply outlines the components required for the system and their relationships. Of particular importance is the generalised inheritence of the class ‘Person’, which has relationships with the classes ‘Custody’ and ‘Case’ (later defined as Investigation). The classes highlighted as external are entities outside the organisation; however, they are not external to BoC. The purpose of highlighting them as external is to demonstrate the exploitation of vendor-neutral representations with blockchain technology. Whilst each external organisation may have a different Management Information System, blockchain technology supplies a reliable, irrefutable and secure communication between any two organisations. This would be a significant challenge in system development and technology infrastructure. In summary, the classes identify the differences between assets, participants, transactions and information stored on the blockchain.

![image](images/fig10.3.jpg)

**Fig. 10.3.**Class diagram for BoC. The system includes external classes, which are accredited organisations that will have access to the permissioned blockchain. However, they have limited access. Access is controlled by an access policy at a policy enforcement point.

### 10.4.3.*Access control*

Access control provides participants with secure and authorised access to assets. During the embryonic development of access control, Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) (Ferraiolo *et al*., 2001) played an important part in authorising groups of users. Over time, these groups of users became dynamic and included attributes that informed authorisation. For example, a user may only be authorised whilst at work, or, whilst they have been delegated a task by a manager. Typically, more roles were added, which eventually led to a role explosion and complexity (Kuhn *et al*., 2010).

Many Access Control Models (ACM) have been proposed since Karp *et al*. (2009), however, spending some time finding the appropriate ACM for your system is worthwhile. This can often be dictated by the environment you are using, and in some cases, where there are no dynamic roles, RBAC would be perfectly adequate. This is not the case with BoC, as the roles are dynamic, e.g., the seizure of artefacts has to be delegated to the First Response Team, no one else can make the seizure since they are not clearly present. This has a dynamic role and access is dependent on the attributes of the participant and particular assets. It is these attributes that form an important part of the access control process. They are the reason why Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC) (Hu *et al*., 2014) has been chosen.

Essentially, there are three types of attributes when designing BoC, which are as follows:

1.Asset Attributes: These are referred to as object attributes in ABAC. In BoC there is only one asset, which is the artefact. The policy aims to protect artefacts from being accessed by unauthorised participants.

2.Participant Attributes: These are referred to as subject attributes in ABAC. In BoC there are many types of participants and their roles are dynamic. Initially, it is assumed that all participants are denied access to assets — this is a Hyperledger default. The attributes of each participant vary, and therefore, participants with the same credentials could have different authorisation. For example, consider two investigators, say A and B, and two cases, say 1 and 2. Investigator A has been assigned to manage Case 1 and, likewise, Investigator B has been assigned to manage Case 2. Investigator A can view the blockchain for artefacts submitted for Case 1, but not for Case 2. Conversely, the same applies to Investigator B.

3.Environment Attributes: These are attributes independent of the Asset and Participant Attributes, such as time, geo-location and threat level.

Use cases are recommended in Hu *et al*. (2014) to help in the development of Natural Language Policies. [Figure 10.2](#chapter10.xhtml#fig10.2) shows the use case and various access points. Access can be denied or permitted with the following privileges: read, write, update, delete and all.

**Conflict of Rules:** Access control lists have to be carefully implemented with consideration made to any demands in the transaction. By default, all participants have privileges denied. So, the access control list changes this default. However, care needs to be taken since privileges can contradict transactional access requirements. For example, consider artefact transfer. It is a key operation in the chain of custody and records the time of the exchange of the artefact. There are two definitions: the submitter, who, pre-exchange, is the current custodian of the artefact; and, the *receiver*, who, post-exchange, is the new custodian of the artefact. It requires a few rules, as follows:

1.The submitter can only read themselves.

2.The submitter of the artefact can initiate the exchange, no one else can do this on the submitter’s behalf.

3.The receiver has to exist.

4.The artefact has to exist.

5.The receiver becomes the new Custodian after the exchange.

Rule 1 is initially provided for privacy, and all submitters can only view themselves on the system. This puts a restriction on the access of the current user. The dynamic situation means that the receiver inherits new privileges upon becoming the new custodian of the object, e.g. the receiver can now exchange that artefact with someone else. Unlike relational databases, blockchain does not enforce referential integrity, therefore it is possible to exchange an artefact with a receiver that does not exist. To prevent this the transactional code will check two things: i) if the current participant is the custodian of the artefact that is to be exchanged; and, ii) if the receiver exists in the participant registry. The second of the two checks will always fail, since rule 1 in the list above only allows the current participant to read themselves, and therefore when access to the participant registry is requested, only the current user is included in it. Therefore, even if the receiver exists, rule 1 prevents them from being identified and the exchange will be denied (under these rules the exchange does allow the submitter to exchange the artefact with themselves).

Deconfliction of access control rules often needs to occur to allow some transactions to be completed correctly. There is a compromise, which is unusual for security and which could potentially create vulnerability. When a user accesses the system, it would be unusual to allow read privileges to other users.

Modelling access control is problematic due to the dynamic process, however, all possibilities still have to be considered when designing a blockchain application. Here we have opted for flowcharts and demonstrate access control by providing a single role example.

Flowcharts are often overlooked as simplistic, but many are used in proposing standard operating procedures (SOP), e.g., Mitchell *et al*. (2018), and these can provide a sequence of instructions that are followed. Of course, there are many criticisms of such a simplistic method; however, here the aim is to provide a sequence of events for each transaction identified in the system. Normally, this would be identified in UML by sequence diagrams; however, this would be misleading and incorrect since the methods and data are not encapsulated in a class. In the physical implementation they are separated.

### 10.4.4.*Operational Logic*

[Figure 10.2](#chapter10.xhtml#fig10.2) identified four transactions, which are discussed in more detail below.

**Adding a New Investigation:** Only managers can add a new investigation.^([1](#chapter10.xhtml#fn_1)) Managers cannot add a new investigation on behalf of others. Therefore, the current participant has to be a manager and can only add themselves as manager to the new investigation. Finally, the Investigation ID provided has to be unique and only then can the blockchain be updated. This procedure is illustrated in a flowchart in [Fig. 10.4](#chapter10.xhtml#fig10.4) (left) which shows a single update to the blockchain before the entire procedure terminates. Strictly, the access control list is less dynamic and more role-based for this procedure.

![image](images/fig10.4.jpg)

**Fig. 10.4.**Flowcharts for Adding a New Investigation (left) and Adding a Member of Staff to the FRT (right).

During the procedure for adding an investigation ID, the ID is checked to see if it already exists in the system. This test of the integrity of the data is unusual since in most data modelling techniques it is accepted that such items would be validated by the system, e.g., referential integrity provided by RDBMS. Hyperledger does this, however, it is worthwhile to remember that the data on the blockchain is just that, and the processes, functions and methods controlling that data are driven by the business logic provided by the designer and stored elsewhere. So, the final test in the flowchart in [Fig. 10.4](#chapter10.xhtml#fig10.4) accesses all the investigations from the asset registries and searches to see if the ID provided is unique. For the implementation in Hyperledger, this is included in the system since each investigation asset is unambiguously and uniquely identified, and therefore duplicate investigations are prevented. However, it is included here to emphasise the point of the separation of data and methods and is not akin to the object-oriented or relational database methods the designers may be used to.

**Adding a Member of Staff to the FRT:** Again, only managers of the Investigation can add members of staff to the FRT. Here the access control is a little more dynamic, and the update can only be executed by the manager of the investigation to which staff are going to be added. This prevents managers from updating the FRT via proxy and links authority to responsibility. Remember, once updated on the blockchain, this information is immutable and therefore it is important to get this accurate. The procedure is for the manager to log in and add members of staff by providing the investigation ID and staff ID. Firstly, a check to see if the manager is the manager of the investigation ID is completed. Secondly, a check to see if the member of staff selected exists and is qualified is carried out. If the first and second checks are compliant, then the blockchain is updated. Finally, the second stage can be repeated many times to add further staff. The updates are not completed in batch mode; each individual added to the FRT is updated as an individual on the blockchain. The blockchain is updated at the first opportunity possible and not left to batch mode, i.e., information is not stored for a given length of time before all the updates are made at once. This procedure is illustrated in the flowchart in [Fig. 10.4](#chapter10.xhtml#fig10.4), which shows possible multiple updates to the blockchain before the procedure ends. Access here is dynamic and dependent on user type and membership.

As in the subsection on ‘Adding a New Investigation’, there is a check to see if the current user is the manager. The ID of the user is checked against the IDs on an access control list. Those classified as managers in the list are given update, read and write privileges with regard to the Investigation asset on the blockchain. There is no referential integrity and this needs encoding, so a further check is carried out to see if the ID of the person provided exists in the appropriate registry. An update to the Investigation asset and the blockchain is completed. This can then be repeated for further FRT members. Each blockchain has a unique transaction code. The ID of the manager submitting a timestamp and the unique transaction code are used to identify the transaction during later audits.

![image](images/fig10.5.jpg)

**Fig. 10.5.**Flowchart for Seizure (left) and Exchange (right).

**Seizure:** Only members of the FRT can seize an artefact. The access control has to be dynamic. Potentially all users could seize an item, as long as they are a member of the FRT for the identified case. [Figure 10.5](#chapter10.xhtml#fig10.5) (left) illustrates the three stages of the seizure process. Each user would have their own device that would require some authentication and log in, e.g., a physical fingerprint and passphrase. Once logged in, the user can see the artefacts that they are the custodian of, other members of staff and the cases they have been assigned to. There is one additional piece of information that would show the users that they are a member of the FRT. When entering the case number there are two stages: i) due to human error if the wrong investigation ID is provided then access is denied and the user is required to enter the correct investigation ID; ii) if the user does not belong to the FRT of a particular case, then access to that case is denied and the user cannot seize any artefacts for that case. If the correct information is provided at stages i) and ii), the user can then update the artefact and the investigation and become the new custodian.

**Exchange:** Finally, we look at the exchange of an artefact between submitter and receiver. [Figure 10.5](#chapter10.xhtml#fig10.5) (right) illustrates the procedure the user has to go through to exchange an item. The submitter has to log in to their device and is only allowed to exchange items they are the custodian of. This is recorded as the user submitting to the blockchain, so there is no need to repeat this information in the transactional data. The submitter provides details of the Investigation and Artefact they are going to exchange. If these are validated as correct and belonging to the user, then further details of the receiver are provided and the update to the blockchain is completed. If the receiver does not exist then the submitter reenters the data. This update has additional information recorded by the system that includes: a timestamp (including the date), a unique identification (hash code) and the user who completed the transaction (in this case the submitter).

### 10.4.5.*Summary*

Data Modelling and Access Control lists are modelled above using a combination of class diagrams, use cases and flowcharts. The data modelling is abstract and the Blockchain application developed above does not enforce referential integrity, nor does it explicitly allow composite keys — not without some complications. This places some restrictions on the implementation of the blockchain. It is also why class diagrams are better abstraction tools than ERDs, which are typically used to model many of the databases that blockchain aims to be integrated with or even to replace. If an implementation is of a simple register of a manager assigning staff to an FRT, then there are some simple rules that are taken for granted in databases but that need consideration in blockchain. The manager would have privileges to add and remove members of the FRT. Submission of evidence can only be done by these members of the FRT since no one else has authorisation. There would have to be a check of whether the staff member existed and then it would have to be possible to add them to the group via a simple update. Only existing group members can be removed from the group. All these rules sound obvious and simplistic but need consideration and coding. As a result, there is a danger of data duplication, something that databases strive to prevent. Such duplication not only results in an increase in the amount of effort required but also in inconsistencies in data if not approached properly.

The design of the operational logic for the transactions is modelled using flowcharts. Having a clear breakdown is not only important for designers and programmers, but also important for training purposes and ensuring that users follow the correct procedures for updating the blockchain. The procedures followed by programmers are the same as the procedures followed by users. This provides some consistency and gives the additional benefit of allowing users to concentrate on the investigation instead of having to bear a cognitive burden when completing the form.

### 10.5.Results

The implementation of BoC was completed using Hyperledger Composer-Playground and Hyperledger Fabric. The programming language for data modelling was completed in CTO, the access control was completed in Access Control Language and the operational logic was completed in Node.js. The operating system was Ubuntu 16.04 LTS (64-bit).

Two mock investigations were carried out. These were small digital investigations in which between 2 and 10 artefacts were seized. The two mock incident scenes were conducted using BoC and the output is extracted from the blockchain and in JSON format. The details of the incident are included in [Table 10.1](#chapter10.xhtml#tab10.1).

**Table 10.1.** Case C111 & C222. Information about the cases.

![image](images/tab10.1.jpg)

From the results below the implementation of BoC was a success; however, problems were encountered. The first problem was using class diagrams to model the investigations, as typically the encapsulation of both data and methods is not possible with blockchain. The data, stored in registries, is on the blockchain, but methods such as transactions are not. This is why no data or methods are displayed in the class diagram in [Fig. 10.3](#chapter10.xhtml#fig10.3). However, other alternatives are also restrictive, e.g., ERDs are more restrictive with relationships. Class diagrams also allow the modelling to be more abstract from the physical representation.

A further problem that arose during the implementation was that a polymorphic method was required to capture the participant type at runtime. This would be required to access the correct and associated registries at runtime. In the design there is a separate registry for each specific role. This was necessary to implement restrictions on access, e.g., members of the legal profession can access the blockchain to inspect all transactions for the case, but are not allowed to exchange artefacts. Polymorphism is not possible, so an enumerator type was passed as a parameter in transaction-related methods in order to provide an indication of the registries required for inspection. This was considered a better solution than returning all the registries, which was the alternative but which had the issue of being inefficient.

As aforementioned, at least four transactions are required to make BoC possible. These are: the creation of a new Investigation; the addition of a new Member to the FRT; the seizure of an artefact; and the exchange of an artefact. These are discussed in the subsections below.

### 10.5.1.Creating a new investigation

[Figure 10.6](#chapter10.xhtml#fig10.6) shows the content of the blockchain after two investigations have been submitted. The transactions occur between lines 1-6 and 7-12 for investigation C111 and C222, respectively. These have been extracted from the blockchain and are in JSON format. The transactions on lines 3 and 9 show the unique ID for C111 and C222, respectively. The transaction ID generated by the system is on line 4 for C111 and the timestamp for C111 is on line 5. Likewise, the transaction ID and the timestamp for C222 are on lines 10 and 11, respectively. The two transactions are successes and can easily be retrieved from the blockchain. There is no record of who completed the transaction; this information was stored when the transaction was made and is also available from the investigation assets. From the transaction it can be seen that Information Managers ‘P111116’ and ‘P100001’ submitted Investigations ‘C111’ and ‘C222’, respectively. From the investigation assets the information for the Investigation ID, ‘C222’, and the Manager of Investigation (MoI), ‘P100001’, are shown on lines 2 and 3 respectively in [Fig. 10.8](#chapter10.xhtml#fig10.8) and are correct.

### 10.5.2.*Adding a new member to the First Response Team (FRT)*

[Figure 10.7](#chapter10.xhtml#fig10.7) shows the content of the blockchain after two transactions were made in order to add a new member to the FRT. The transactions for adding ‘P111110’ and ‘P211112’ to the FRT occur between lines 1-11 and 12-22, respectively. These have been extracted from the blockchain and it can be seen that both members have been added to the same investigation, ‘C222’. Again, the transaction ID and timestamps for each of these transactions are shown on lines 9-10 and 20-21, respectively. The two personnel added are from different roles and this is indicated by lines 8 and 19, which show that the first member belongs to the role, ‘Staff’, and the second member belongs to the role, ‘LEA’. This is the aforementioned parameter to extract the relevant Participant Registry at runtime.

### 10.5.3.*Seizure*

[Figure 10.8](#chapter10.xhtml#fig10.8) shows the data stored in the asset registry on the blockchain for the investigation assets after the completion of the seizure of all the artefacts.

[Figure 10.9](#chapter10.xhtml#fig10.9) indicates an individual seizure transaction (lines 1-16) and the resulting entry in the artefact asset registry (lines 17-26). This may raise some concern amongst readers since there is no time or date in the investigation registry or the artefact. However, [Fig. 10.9](#chapter10.xhtml#fig10.9) does not show the full picture; the blockchain is updated with each individual seizure, and only the individual records and not the transactions are viewed in the Investigation and Artefact Registry. Further explanation is required.

![image](images/fig10.8.jpg)

**Fig. 10.8.**The investigation asset registry for the item with Investigation ID ‘C222’. Note that all custodians are members of the FRT. This changes when exchanges occur. Nevertheless, when a seizure transaction is made, only members of the appropriate FRT can be custodians of artefacts. Some artefacts have been removed to improve clarity.

In the seizure transaction in [Fig. 10.9](#chapter10.xhtml#fig10.9) (line 11) the custodian is identified with the PIN code ‘0950’. This does not match the committed code in the final output and furthermore the person identified by the code does not exist as a person in the system. This is not a mistake. The user is logged in via their business network card, which is issued by the system and uniquely identifies them. In this particular case the business network card is for ‘S23’, identified by ‘P111113’. It is these values that are passed to the asset registries. If ‘P111113’ is a member of the FRT (clearly seen from [Fig. 10.8](#chapter10.xhtml#fig10.8), lines 8-9), then the update occurs to both registries. This explains the difference between the information in Figs. 10.8 and 10.9. Users cannot seize artefacts on behalf of other users.

![image](images/fig10.9.jpg)

**Fig. 10.9.**Individual seizure transaction and corresponding artefact.

[Figure 10.9](#chapter10.xhtml#fig10.9) does show when the transaction was committed to the blockchain. In the example, line 15 shows that the artefact ‘1636’ was seized at ‘2018-09-04T10:03:05.455Z’. So, all the information about the seizure of this item can be retrieved for internal or external audits. Simple generic queries can be set up to recall and organise all artefacts seized for an investigation.

There is also the issue of integration of systems across LEAs. [Figure 10.8](#chapter10.xhtml#fig10.8) (lines 18-24) shows an example whereby an external person is included in the FRT and demonstrates that they are able to seize artefacts, as shown by person ‘P211112’ submitting artefact ‘4695’. The subject of the integration of systems is discussed in the final section but raised here to show a plausible solution.

### 10.5.4.*Exchange of artefact*

After the exchange, the investigation and artefact asset registry are updated. [Figure 10.11](#chapter10.xhtml#fig10.11) illustrates the data stored in the investigation asset registry for the investigation ID ‘C222’. It is managed by ‘P100001’ (line 4), has four FRT members (lines 5-17) and has one artefact, ‘1636’, with custodian ‘P111115’.

![image](images/fig10.10.jpg)

**Fig. 10.10.**Blockchain recovery. Inspection of the blockchain.

![image](images/fig10.11.jpg)

**Fig. 10.11.**Listing of Investigation Registry from the blockchain. Some artefacts have been removed to improve clarity.

Only FRT members are allowed to seize an artefact; however, a keen eye will note that the custodian for the artefact, ‘1636’, is ‘P111115’ and is not a member of the FRT. [Figure 10.10](#chapter10.xhtml#fig10.10) shows who the *current* custodian is for each artefact, as does each artefact asset registry. Artefact ‘1636’ has been exchanged and the seizure of the artefact is recorded by the seizure transaction explained in the previous subsection.

[Figure 10.10](#chapter10.xhtml#fig10.10) shows the exchange when the user, ‘P111115’ (line 5), received the artefact. In the exchange transaction only the receiver is recorded, since only the current custodian can exchange an artefact, an artefact cannot be exchanged on behalf of someone else. [Figure 10.10](#chapter10.xhtml#fig10.10) (line 11) shows that the artefact was exchanged at ‘2018-09-04T11:30:03.572Z’ and includes the transaction ID.

Looking at the system, it can be seen that the transaction ID was completed by the user, ‘P111113’. By combining all the transactions for this artefact, a chain of custody can be reconstructed, i.e., by combining transactions in [Fig. 10.9](#chapter10.xhtml#fig10.9) and [Fig. 10.10](#chapter10.xhtml#fig10.10). Of course, this can be completed using a query on the blockchain to retrieve all the seizures and transactions for the artefact ‘1636’ belonging to the investigation ‘C222’ and displaying them in chronological order. Auditors can have read access to the blockchain and they can retrieve such queries.

### 10.6.Conclusions

The main contribution of this paper is twofold: i) blockchain engineering/modelling, and ii) prototype development of a decentralised application for evidence management. The two are entwined; however, it looks likely that the proliferation of decentralised applications is going to expand exponentially, and therefore methods are needed that can integrate and interact with all stakeholders.

Relying on UML-based design is problematic for decentralised applications, since whilst the implementation languages are object-based, the application is not. Our method has looked at use case diagrams and class diagrams to model the actors and data. The class diagrams are very abstract and do not include methods, but help identify attributes of the transactions, assets and participants. The transactions are then identified for the decentralised application and the sequence of events is modelled by flowcharts. Overall the design and implementation was a success. This has been proven by the completion of two investigations.

### 10.6.1.*Recommendations*

The gratuitous use of technology and the hyperbole surrounding BitCoin are not to be confused with blockchain development. However, blockchain has problems with disassociating itself from BitCoin. Excluding cost, new technologies should always bring improvements. BoC is an integrated system between all parties of an irreversible and immutable chain of custody for evidence management. In the process of designing and developing this blockchain application we have come up with several recommendations, which are as follows:

**Permanent Data:** ISO17025 (and GDPR to some extent) recommend that personal data be deleted. Of course, in legal cases, this is not permissible; however, once time spent has been completed, or acquittal been provided by courts or if information has simply not led to a court case, then there is the possibility of the disposal or return of evidence and the documentation related to it. Blockchain, by its very nature, does not allow the deletion of data — it is possible to delete data from the blockchain, however, there will be a record of this deletion and the previous blocks will contain secure, private and confidential data. It is the recommendation that personal data, e.g., the victim’s identity, is not stored on the blockchain in case a request is made for it to be deleted.

**Permissioned blockchain:** The auditing of organisations is integral to good evidence management. As shown from the results, auditors can access and view cases and view the records regarding the transfer of artefacts and evidence management. This can all be completed with transparency and low latency. Whilst there is more to internal audits than evidence transfer, this does allow instant updates of an important role in evidence management.

Many LEA will have their own DB for recording evidence management. From personal discussions, these can be different within the Departments of LEA, e.g., digital forensics may use a different DB to Forensics. If personal discussions are not enough proof, look at the wide range of software available: EvidenceOnQ, EvidenceGuard (CaseGuard, 2018), Forman (Lowman, 2018), Evidence Traq, Oracle’s Digital Evidence Management System (Oracle, 2017) and many more. BoC has an immutable and irreversible blockchain, and these are properties that databases do not have by default. That is the focus of the development of BoC. These databases are permissioned and require authentication and log in details. BoC is no different; it is permissioned, and under no circumstances should it be implemented as a permissionless blockchain application.

**Modelling:** Flowcharts display important interactions entered into by the users of the system. It is recommended that these be integrated into the training of individuals when implementing transactions.

**Audits:** BoC provides transparency, whereby an auditor can access all the transactions for a case without delay. It is recommended that auditors only have read access at all times.

**Tokenisation:** Not every blockchain application has to involve tokens or coins. The distribution, issuance and management of the tokens has to be considered. Finally, there is the value of the token. As discussed in [Section 10.3.6](#chapter10.xhtml#sec10.3.6), if the network operating costs outweigh the value generated by the blockchain then the cost of the network outweighs the benefit. The exception to this rule is when not-for-profit organisations are funding the blockchain; here, tokens become almost irrelevant as in the case of BoC.

**NPE:** Non-person entities have not been modelled; however, it is possible that NPEs could be necessary. NPEs are not associated with physical people, they are generated by the system, usually for administration purposes. In this case, there is a demand for NPEs, which could easily be added as another participant registry representing that role. Consider the issue of custody. Custodians are not always assigned 24/7 to artefacts; quite often artefacts are left in secure storage with no custodian. In such cases, there would be a problem with the current system. The principle of updating the blockchain every time an exchange is made may seem maddening. It may seem like quality overload is taking place without any value being delivered. This is not so. In evidence stores there are loopholes whereby persons who are not the custodian can exchange the artefact, leading to problems later on and thus devaluing the system. Here all artefacts have a unique custodian, and each time the Evidence Store Manager changes, so do the blockchain and the custodian for each item stored. This means only the custodian can exchange the artefact — it is a fundamental tenet of the system. So, going back to unmanned evidence stores, this would be where an NPE would be introduced. NPEs of evidence stores would not be allowed to update the blockchain except when an expected end-of-shift occurs. At this point, the NPE will be allowed to complete a special transaction that would allow all the items in the evidence store to change custody from the designated NPE to the designated Evidence Store Manager (now the custodian). This adds a further level of logical security. Whilst it cannot stop a physical breach, the blockchain will make it logically infeasible to exchange artefacts whilst the NPE is the custodian.

**Rescinding:** People make mistakes. If the seizure of an artefact goes wrong, can it be altered? Yes, it can be altered by giving the manager of the investigation delete privileges. An immediate request can be made, the manager can delete the request and all can get back to work. These errors are still recorded on the blockchain as transactions. The key here is transparency. BoC is about maintaining the auditability of actions, thus ensuring best practice. Therefore, the deletion of data records is not of concern, but when the deletion occurred or by whom the data records were deleted may be.

### 10.6.2.*Future work*

This paper covers the development of a prototype blockchain application using Hyperledger for a case study on evidence management. It is a beginning and, upon reflection, there are many improvements that can be made.

Firstly, the disintermediatory nature of blockchain allows multiple enterprise integration, or *interprise*. This has not been approached by this project, however, it is conceivable that international agencies could record transactions using multiple blockchains.

Secondly, combined with IoT and RFIDs, the tracking of evidence could become automated. This would require using different access control models, e.g., Xu *et al*. (2018), and could improve the automated control of events.

Thirdly, there is also a wider application of BoC to society in general. Where there are important transfers of artefacts between parties, and where no transfer of monetary value takes place, this model could be used. For example, BoC could be applied to conveyancy law, felony records, inmate records, or any other situation whereby documents are exchanged and a record of the change that has been updated by authorized personnel is required.

### 10.6.3.*Summary*

At the beginning of this chapter, it was judged that change was pushing technology, or that the tail was wagging the dog. In the past, the gratuitous use of technology to solve problems often proved to add little or no value, for example, online emergency services were used when a phone call was effective enough. Blockchain still has a long way to go to prove itself, however, in scenarios where there is a need to provide strict controls over the access to data, to provide a transparent and effective audit trail and to be secure, blockchain is a technology that should be considered.
