## Chapter 11

## New Issues in Cyber Security Forensics

Firas Hazzaa\* and Sufian Yousef^†

*Anglia Ruskin University, UK*

\**firas.hazzaa@pgr.anglia.ac.uk,*

^†*Sufian.Yousef@anglia.ac.uk*

## ABSTRACT

Cyber security is the term used to describe the processes and technologies designed to protect computers, networks, data and programs from unauthorized access, damage or attack. Many businesses pay lots of attention to security concerns. For these reasons this research has been undertaken. Ad-hoc networks are crucial enablers of next-generation communications. Such networks can be formed and reconfigured dynamically and they can be mobile, standalone or internet-worked with other networks. Mobile Ad-hoc Networks (MANETs) are established by a group of autonomous nodes that communicate with each other by establishing a multi-hop radio network and maintaining connectivity in an infrastructure-less manner. The security of the connections between devices and networks is crucial. The important challenges of supporting multimedia applications in an ad-hoc network are the security issues. In this chapter, a new and efficient media-aware security framework will be designed for facilitating various multimedia applications in ad-hoc networks over the Internet.

*Keywords*: cyber security, cyber crime, mobile devices, MANET, wireless network, DoS attack, forensics

### 11.1.Introduction

### 11.1.1.**Computer networks**

A **computer network** is a set of **computers** connected together for the purpose of sharing resources. In computer networks, computing devices exchange data with each other using connections between nodes. One example of a computer network is the internet, which has been developed over the last 45 years (Thomas and Robertazzi, 2017).

### 11.1.1.1.*Networks types and topology*

There are two types of network:

•**Wired Network**: A wired network is a set of PCs connected through wired links. Most of the wired networks use Ethernet cables to transfer data between connected PCs. One can use either routers or switches to organize the network, depending on its size (Cisco, 2016).

•**Wireless Network**: A wireless network is a set of connected devices that are not connected by cables of any kind. These networks use access points to get access to the network or use some wireless techniques such as ad-hoc and Bluetooth (Zheng *et al*., 2013). These networks usually are cost effective and easily deployed.

Also, there are two kinds of topology which can connect the networks. The two kinds of networks are infrastructure and infrastructure-less networks.

•**Ad-hoc Network**: An ad-hoc network is an infrastructure-less network. It is a crucial enabler of next-generation communications. Such networks can be formed and reconfigured dynamically and they can be mobile, standalone or internet-worked with other networks (Panaousis, 2012). For instance, the Mobile Ad-hoc Network (MANET) is the most important one of these networks.

•**Mobile Ad-Hoc network (MANET)**: A mobile ad-hoc network is a set of mobile nodes that communicate with radio links. MANET network infrastructure is not defined and there is no centralized administration that controls the other activities (Aarti and Tyagi, 2013). MANETs are established by a group of autonomous nodes that communicate with each other by establishing a multi-hop radio network and maintaining connectivity in an infrastructureless manner. They allow data, voice and video communications over a wireless channel (Thomas *et al*., 2010). The main role of MANETs is to enable wireless and mobile communication services without using the expensive service-provider network and without having a previously set-up infrastructure.

There are several uses of these networks in real life; for example, they are used in disaster and emergency operations.

The security requirements of wireless ad-hoc networks are very important. One of MANET’s big issues is that it is not a centrally-controlled network. Many applications on a network such as MANET need to be built with more care because the attacks on them may be internal or external. For example, connected vehicles currently connect to each other wirelessly with the Vehicular Ad-hoc Network (VANET). VANET is a wireless communication system that uses mobile cars as communication nodes to determine positioning and movement for the connected vehicles. Wireless networks like VANET validate every message circulating in their network without assessing the source’s quality or the content’s accuracy. As a result, VANET is inherently vulnerable to false messages being spread in the network by messages-poofing and denial-of-service (DoS) attacks (Sharma *et al*., 2017). So security concerns should be given further attention.

### 11.2.Cyber Security on Mobile Devices

It is expected that, in 2020, more than 50 billion devices will connect to the Internet (Hammi *et al*., 2017). Most of these devices should be wireless. 5G networks will make global life incredible, because they will enable the ICT to be faster, more reliable and more easily deployed. 5G networks consist of many types of networks. The significant parts of 5G networks are the wireless networks, such as mobile ad-hoc networks and wireless sensor networks. Houses, doors and windows are connected to the network; fridges, light systems and even personal coats are wirelessly connected to the network as well. For example, the sensor chip fixed inside a coat can automatically send the health information of a patient to the hospital if his situation is critical. Also, CCTV cameras and self-driving cars use wireless technology to connect with the network.

All of the above technologies will not be useful without security. Sometimes the absence of security may be a life or death matter. For instance, self-driving cars should be strongly protected against hackers, because any malicious breach would cause a disaster. According to Morgan (2017), the cost of cyber security reached $84 billion in 2015, and it is expected to reach $170 billion in 2020. So most businesses are paying lots of attention to security concerns. For these reasons we are undertaking this research.

Cyber security is the term used to describe the processes and technologies designed to protect computers, networks, data and programs from unauthorized access, damage or attack. According to the Telegraph, the cost of cyber attacks to UK businesses in 2017 reached $34 billion. To ensure cyber security, the corresponding efforts need to be made throughout an information system. The main elements of cyber security include applications security, information security, network security, disaster recovery and end-user education.

Unfortunately, conventional multimedia traffic management algorithms are developed mainly to guarantee delay while usually neglecting security requirements. A security-critical VoIP and multimedia service architecture is proposed, which jointly considers traffic analysis, security requirements, and traffic scheduling for multimedia applications. Many previous researchers (Nagendra and Sekhar, 2014; Ali *et al*., 2014; Binod and Hyuk, 2010) adopted security algorithms that were weak enough to deal with the constraints of the quality of service (QoS) in such a way as to make the delay within limits. Also, using multiple keys for encryption and decryption will make the probability of the encrypted data being decrypted by a hacker very low, because even if the hacker knows what the first key is, it is not likely that he also knows what the other keys are. Matesanz *et al*. (2012) shows the most common threats to ad-hoc networks and reviews several proposals that attempt to minimize some of these threats, showing their ability to protect these networks in light of their vulnerabilities and the threats that might arise. Some of these threats are described below.

*Address Spoofing*: This attack occurs when the malicious node intentionally selects an allocated or a free IP address. In the first case, the node takes an IP address which has been allocated to the victim, and once it has done so, hijacks the victim’s traffic. In the other case, the node allocates the free IP address to itself so that it can join the network. Once in the network, the node collects important information which can be used to execute some attacks, like denial of service attacks.

*Address Space Consumption*: This attack occurs when the attacker consumes the address space by demanding a huge number of IP addresses. The attacker could request the assignment of IP addresses to fake nodes so as to prevent other nodes from being configured and connecting to the mobile ad-hoc networks.

*Address Conflict Threat*: This attack occurs when the malicious node assigns an additional address to a client which is already in use. This would produce many problems in the mobile ad-hoc networks and lead to an address conflict (Sandoval and García, 2012).

*Denial of Service Threat*: This threat occurs when, in an auto-configuration process, the attacker acts as a requester and sends AREQ messages to several nodes simultaneously, causing an overload of traffic.

*Multiple Identities (Sybil)*: This kind of attack is possible when a repudiation system exists to state the legality of nodes in the network. The attacker could cause the isolation of valid nodes by creating messages to blacklist those nodes. Blackmail is a type of Sybil attack.

 
| Layer || Attacks |
| --- | --- |
| Application Layer || data corruption, viruses and worms |
| Transport Layer || TCP/UDP SYN flood |
| Network Layer || hello flood, black-hole |
| Data Link Layer || monitoring, traffic analysis |
| Physical Layer || eavesdropping, active interference |

Pietro *et al*. (2014) have surveyed emerging and established wireless ad-hoc technologies and highlighted their security/privacy features and deficiencies. They also identified open research issues and technology challenges for each surveyed technology.

Binod and Hyuk (2010) took the advantages of multipath routing which are useful for reliable MANET, and they proposed a basis for sending secure real-time streaming data over a multipath mobile adhoc network. Multipath routing can offers security for wireless ad-hoc routing and multimedia transfer. They considered digital signatures and encryption techniques. Their results show the good performance of the multipath mobile ad-hoc network. They also suggest the using of multicast, which is important in many video applications, in the future.

Emmanouis and Christos (2012) suggested a secure model for autonomous networks like mobile ad-hoc networks to create realtime communication in disaster rescue operations. Secure P2PSIP, intrusion detection and secure routing methods are vital parts of any secure model. The aforementioned concerns in the realm of emergency ad-hoc networks have been discussed. Emmanouis and Christos (2012) presented two additions to the IETF drafts and analysed them in relation to security power and scalability. The design of these extensions helps to meet the requirements of a mission-critical MANET within which rescuers can create links to communicate with each other by using lightweight devices such as PDAs. The situation concerning adaptive routing protocols and the use of IPsec to make them more secure has also been discussed.

These research studies have addressed some security issues for real-time traffic in MANET. However, they have not addressed the cryptographic issues in this network.

Sehgal *et al*. (2011) proposed an architecture in their research paper which states that self-organized distributed security could be provided by a five-layer security model, as well as authenticated and security-aware routing. After they carried out the simulation, they found that it provided security with negligible overhead.

A layered architecture can provide such advantages as modularity, simplicity, flexibility, and the standardization of protocols. The five-layer security architecture for MANETs incorporates the following layers: the Trust Relationship Security Layer, the Node-To-Node Security Layer, the Routing Level Security Layer, the Network Level Security Layer and the Application Level Layer. They expect this security architecture can be used as a framework when designing system security for ad-hoc networks.

Many previous research studies have also been conducted to address cryptographic issues related to real-time traffic. They could develop some algorithms to deal with real-time limitation issues, like delays.

Hu *et al*. (2009) propose a relay encryption scheme based on the threshold secret-sharing algorithm to enhance the data confidentiality, reliability and integrity in MANET. The basic idea is to distribute the whole encryption task to all the nodes along the route. Every node completes part of the encryption task instead of the single source node encrypting all of the data. They found that the encryption scheme can effectively alleviate the burden of the source node and reduce the transmission delay, besides, it improves the reliability of MANET.

Mohammed and Rohiem (2009) have introduced a Variable Mapping S-box technique with AES (VMS-AES) for the Voice over Internet Protocol (VoIP). A key is used to generate a parameter that is used to shift (remap) the substitution of the S-box randomly to another location depending on the initial key and the derived subkeys data. The results of this work could maximize nonlinearity so as to provide more resistance against linear attacks and to solve the fixed structure of the substitution function. They could also increase the overall security. Mohammed and Rohiem (2009) have also shown that seven rounds of encryption consume less power and execution time without affecting the security level. However, their findings have been criticised a long time ago, by Ferguson *et al*. (2001) and Daernen and Rijrnen (2002) who explained the possibility of saturation attacks on six and seven rounds of AES. They state that a seven-round attack can be mounted by adding one round before the distinguisher and two rounds after it. For these reasons their work is still unsuitable for the security requirements of wireless networks.

Another study on the topic has been published by Rahma and Yaco (2012). They proposed a symmetric dual key dynamic block algorithm (SDD) for digital video, which is a type of partial encryption technology. This algorithm meets the requirements of real time by combining a high level of complexity and a considerable speed. The proposed encryption algorithm SDD achieves better results than AES. It is faster by a factor of 13 times for encryption and faster by a factor of 9 times for decryption. It also has a high resistance to brute-force attack because two keys were used in the encryption process; however, it encrypts only selected parts of the data, which is considered a risk factor for a security breach. Also, in spite of the new features which have been achieved in their paper, there is still a lack of security analysis, which could have helped to prove its strength.

### 11.2.1.*Security and information protection*

1.Every wireless LAN implementation within UCSF must be done in accordance with a security plan. This plan must address the following issues at least:

1.Make sure that only authorized people can use it.

2.Prevent unauthorized users from being able to see confidential data appearing on the network, particularly UCSF passwords (Silver, 2017).

2.The Security Incident Response should include a wireless security response procedure.

3.Vendor default settings such as encryption keys and SNMP passwords must be changed regularly.

4.Wireless access point owners and managers are responsible for updating software.

5.Wireless networks which provide access to the UCSF campus network must limit usage to authorized users (Silver, 2017).

1.As of July 1st 2010 this option is mandatory for wireless networks comprised of three (3) or more access points.

2.As of July 1st 2010 this option is restricted to wireless networks comprised of two (2) or fewer access points.

3.Legacy host-based authorization systems utilizing the machine address code (MAC) may continue to be used until June 30th 2010. In the interim it is strongly recommended that the vpn@UCSF system be used to protect the communications of the wireless network user.

6.Encryption and Data Protection:

1.WPA2/AES-CCMP as defined by 802.11i is strongly recommended for departments that deal with highly sensitive information such as patient and HR/staff information. WPA2/AES-CCMP provides a higher degree of encryption protection for sensitive data being transmitted wirelessly.

2.WPA and WPA2 (RSN) as defined by 802.11i are the standard protocols for UCSF wireless security.

3.WEP on existing wireless access points must be updated to WPA or phased out by June 1, 2010. In the interim it is strongly recommended that the vpn@UCSF system be used to protect the communications of the access point users.

7.Wireless networks which do not support encryption and authentication:

1.Until June 30th 2010 it is strongly recommended that the vpn@UCSF system be utilized to protect communications to provide user authentication as well as data protection.

2.Starting July 1st, 2010 unencrypted wireless networks must restrict user access to the following:

1.Informational pages regarding network access, local service or customer support and helpdesk.

2.Access to vpn@UCSF or an ITS-approved authentication portal.

3.Access to a specific system or service for which the wireless network has been created so long as that system or service contains no restricted or private data.

### 11.2.2.*Voice over wireless networks*

The voice requirements in wireless networks are different from those in wired networks. In the wireless networks we must carefully investigate and analyse the problems associated with this integration. The transmission of a voice is a real-time application that is sensitive to requirements in term of delay. For example, in phone call conversations, the voice should reach the destination quickly and efficiently. If the voice is delayed, the quality of the call will be affected. This quality of the call will also be affected if security rules are applied. Furthermore, this problem will become worse in wireless networks because of the nature of wireless networks. Many researchers have paid close attention to real-time application in wireless networks. They have tried to address some of the issues concerning security and delay. For instance, Binod and Hyuk (2010) and Emmanouis and Christos (2012) suggested a secure model for autonomous networks like mobile ad-hoc networks to create real-time communication during disaster rescue operations. Secure P2PSIP, intrusion detection and secure routing methods are a vital part of any secure model. The design of these extensions helps to meet the requirements of a mission-critical MANET where rescuers can create links to communicate with each other by using lightweight devices such as PDAs. Liang and Han (2011) designed a new security framework to enable different multimedia services in an IoT environment. Also, they presented a novel media-aware traffic security style based on the proposed traffic classification to enable the supply of various multimedia services to customers anywhere at any time. Furthermore, they proposed the scheme’s basis and approach, that is, to perform a good trade-off between system flexibility and efficiency.

However, there are still some flaws in the real-time application of security and cryptography schemes. So, the question is: how does one transmit a voice securely over a wireless network without affecting its quality? As previously mentioned, the voice needs to be transmitted with speed and security at the same time, and this should be addressed in this research.

### 11.3.Wi-Fi Vulnerabilities

Wireless Fidelity (Wi-Fi) is the most widely-used network in the information technology field. It can be used indoors and outdoors, and it follows the IEEE 802.11 standard. There are two possible topologies that could form this network. The two resulting types of network are the ad-hoc network and the infrastructure network.

“**Vulnerability** is a cyber security term that refers to a flaw in a system that can leave it open to attack. A vulnerability may also refer to any type of weakness in a computer system itself, in a set of procedures, or in anything that leaves information security exposed to a threat.” (Wolfram, 2018)

“Security researchers¹ have discovered a major vulnerability in Wi-Fi Protected Access 2 (WPA2). WPA2 is a type of encryption used to secure the vast majority of Wi-Fi networks. A WPA2 network provides unique encryption keys for each wireless client that connects to it.

Think of encryption as a secret code that can only be deciphered if you have the “key,” and a vital technology that helps keep digital data away from intruders and identity thieves.

The vulnerability, dubbed ‘KRACKs’ (Key Reinstallation Attacks), is actually a group of multiple vulnerabilities that when successfully exploited, could allow attackers to intercept and steal data transmitted across a Wi-Fi network. Digital personal information that is transmitted over the Internet or stored on your connected devices — such as your driver’s license number, Social Security number, credit card numbers, and more — could be vulnerable.” (Norton, 2017)

### 11.3.1.*Threats and attacks*

•**Routing Attacks**: The routing signal is modified by unauthorized nodes and rerouted through an incorrect route in order to provide unauthorized data access to the attacker. Such attacks include breaking the neighbour, black hole, routing table poisoning, worm hole, and replay attacks.

•**Eavesdropping**: This is an unidentifiable, passive attack with no impact on normal system processing. The attacker aims to passively intercept data by breaking encryption, without altering the normal routing protocol (Goodrich and Tamassia, 2011).

•**Denial of Service (DoS)**: This attack aims to disrupt routing in order to prevent the network from functioning and providing normal service. The attacker sends a massive volume of simultaneous requests to overwhelm the server and hamper its response time by jamming its mechanisms, ideally halting the complete system.

•**Sybil Attack**: Fake identities are deployed (i.e. in nodes) to gain access to wireless sensor networks in these attacks (Suriya and Rajamani, 2015).

•**Masquerading**: Similar to a Sybil attack, masquerading nodes (presenting themselves as legitimate nodes) intercept data during the neighbour acquisition process, and they either modify or replay these messages.

•**Alteration**: These attacks involve unauthorized alterations to data and codes, falsifying the system integrity.

### 11.3.2.*Wireless sensor networks*

Nowadays, the world is rapidly moving toward becoming a wireless environment. In 2020 most devices will connect wirelessly. The most significant part of this technology is wireless sensor networks (WSNs). According to Matin and Islam (2012), a WSN can be defined as “a self-configured and infrastructure-less wireless network to monitor physical or environmental conditions, such as temperature, sound, vibration, pressure, motion or pollutants and to cooperatively pass their data through the network to a main location or sink where the data can be observed and analysed”.

Currently, many researchers are focusing on real-time Wireless Multimedia Sensor Networks (WMSNs), because they support many application layer services in order to solve real life concerns, such as health monitoring, transport management, weather forecasting and safety and security investigation (Elhoseny and Hassanien, 2018; Ehsan and Hamdaoui, 2012). A traditional WMSN consists of a variety of sensor nodes, including both simple and multimedia sensor nodes, and a Base Station (BS), as shown in [Fig. 11.1](#chapter11.xhtml#fig11.1).

![image](images/fig11.1.jpg)

**Fig. 11.1.**Traditional wireless multimedia sensor network (Usman *et al*., 2018).

WMSNs support the practical applications of advanced technologies for remote control, including IPv6 over Low power Wireless Personal Area Networks (6LowPAN), and for surveillance, within the Internet of Things (IoT) (Usman *et al*., 2018). WSNs, like MANETs, have major security issues. The fundamental problem is that there is a trade-off between security and performance. WSNs face the issue of node sizes undermining network functional effectiveness, particularly with complex data such as voice messages used in communication, as discussed in detail below. Extensive research is required to improve technology in this area, particularly given the importance of the applications of WSNs. The applications of WSNs include, but are not limited to, environmental monitoring, industrial machine monitoring, surveillance systems, and military target tracking (Yick *et al*., 2008). Each application differs in its features and requirements. To support this diversity of applications, the development of new communication protocols, algorithms, designs, and services are needed.

### 11.4.Security and Privacy Adaptation

### 11.4.1.**Network security challenges**

The recent increase in wireless portable users and data usage has placed a greater load on networks. Real-time applications over wireless networks often suffer from jitter, delay and packet loss. In future smart cities there will be a dense deployment of WSN with applications ranging from reserving water to public safety. As Hu and Cao (2017) said, “These WSNs and the Internet of Things (IoT) should be seamlessly integrated with future 5G networks. In cellular networks such as 3G, 4G and LTE, mobile devices are served by Base Stations (BSs) which cover a large area (about 1–2 miles). Due to many practical deployment issues, some areas have good coverage while other areas may not. As a result, the wireless signal strength of a mobile device varies based on its location”. IoT devices are an attractive attack target for cyber criminals: they often employ weak security measures, and their compromise can lead to privacy breaches and safety threats in the real world. Recently, several malware families were found to target vulnerable IoT devices (e.g., routers, IP cameras, and CCTVs) and to use them to form botnets for DDoS. It is estimated that some IoT botnets comprise more than one million infected devices. In October 2016, a botnet attacked the DynDNS service provider, taking down a large portion of websites in North America, including GitHub, Twitter, Netflix, and so on (Cheng *et al*., 2017). Also, the privacy of information that has been transferred into the network is repeatedly threatened by hackers. For example, man-in-the-middle attacks can reveal secure information by deceiving the users of the network.

Unfortunately, conventional multimedia traffic management algorithms have been developed mainly to guarantee delay while usually neglecting security requirements. According to Zhou (2010) and Zhao *et al*. (2009) applications and users can be sources of security threats. Liang and Chao (2011) claim that it is very important to adopt a security strategy to protect critical voice and multimedia applications.

AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) is the best cryptography algorithm used in computing to protect the confidentiality of data. There have been no successful attacks against AES since 2004. The United States Government announced in June 2003 that the block cipher AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) algorithm for a key with a length of 128 bits can be used to protect SECRET information, while TOP SECRET information could be protected with the same algorithm for keys with lengths of 192 and 256 bits. Many previous researchers (Nagendra and Sekhar, 2014; Nada, 2014; Binod and Hyuk, 2010) adopted security algorithms that were weak enough to deal with the constraints of the quality of service (QoS) in a way that keeps the delay within limits. Also, using multiple keys for encryption and decryption will make the probability of breaking the encryption on the data very low, because even if the hacker knows what the first key is, it is improbable that they will also know what the other keys are.

### 11.5.Security in Mobile Operating Environments

The **operating environment** consists of a user interface provided by an applications manager and usually an application programming interface (API) for the applications manager.

A recent study by Forrester (2011) predicted that by 2015, mobile banking will reach one in five adults in the United States, and for many customers, mobile banking will become the preferred channel for basic banking transactions. In Europe, mobile banking trends are similar to those in the United States — as many as 12% of European Net users do some mobile banking.

“But the growth in mobile devices has also driven the incidence of fraud targeting these devices. Whether simple rogue text messages, fictitious billing scams, or more malicious attacks using malware installed on the device, the number of attacks are now increasing alarmingly — by one account mobile malware increased by more than 45% in 2010. And with less education about mobile threats, users seem more inclined to fall victim to them.” (Byrnes, 2017)

### 11.5.1.*Mobile security vulnerabilities*

Mobile security involves several layers:

•Device operating system

•Browser

•Cloud

•Extended cyber enterprise (secure access to third-party apps such as Salesforce.com)

•App store

When we conducted the survey and in-depth telephone interviews late in 2011 for our “Leaders in Mobility Strategies” report, we found that 49 percent of the respondents had not yet developed a formal security policy on mobile devices and technologies — even though most of them were already on the mobility path and had adopted a bring-your-own-device (BYOD) model.

As illustrated in [Fig. 11.2](#chapter11.xhtml#fig11.2), mobile devices have unique security vulnerabilities that do not exist in other enterprise communication end points such as desktops or laptops (Rangaswami, 2012).

### 11.5.2.*Power in wireless devices*

Wireless networks have been a hot topic for many years. Their potential was first realized with the deployment of cellular networks for use with mobile telephones in the late 1970s. Since this time, many other wireless wide area networks (WWANs) have begun to emerge, along with the introduction of Wireless Metropolitan Area Networks (WMANs), Wireless Local Area Networks (WLANs), and Wireless Personal Area Networks (WPANs). The power consumed by individual nodes in each of these networks needs to be managed efficiently. Researchers have given significant consideration to energy-efficient schemes. These energy-efficient schemes, which are also referred to as “Green Computing”, are the products of one of the most essential areas of research these days.

However, there are still some flaws in energy consumption when it is applied to security and cryptography schemes. According to Masoud *et al*. (2015), the performance evaluation of a symmetric encryption algorithm like DES, Bluefish, RC6 or AES showed that the cost of implementing these encryption algorithms in smartphones is high. They state that high power consumption may prevent developers from employing cryptographic algorithms in the communication applications they have developed for smartphones. Also, they reveal the requirements of new power-saving ‘Green’ encryption algorithms. For these reasons, encryption algorithms are not only about security; power consumption should be taken into account when designing these algorithms for smartphones.

![image](images/fig11.2.jpg)

**Fig. 11.2.**Security risks and threats unique to mobile devices.

*Note*: The open source nature of mobile device operating systems is not necessarily a security threat. For example, Linux systems (which are open source) have proved to be pretty secure. However, device manufacturers could make insecure extensions to an operating system, which can open up new security vulnerabilities.

So, the question is, how does one secure the data in wireless networks without affecting the power of the nodes? As mentioned, the wireless nodes need to keep their power for as long as possible when implementing security enforcement. This issue should be addressed in this chapter.

### 11.5.3.*Limitations caused by energy consumption in encryption*

A data encryption algorithm would not be of much use if it is secure but slow in performance, especially because it is a common practice to embed encryption algorithms in other applications such as e-commerce, banking, and online transaction processing applications (Nadeem and Javed, 2005). The wireless device is limited in resources such as processing power, memory and power supply (from a battery). Battery technology is improving at a slower rate than other technologies. This causes a “battery gap”. This indicates that mobile devices normally operate on an economical power budget, and therefore, computationally intensive encryption/decryption algorithms and their related security parameters may not be supported. The key issue is that the processing in encryption algorithms consumes remarkable amounts of computing resources. This leads to battery power draining fast. That is the problem for mobile devices (Jiehong and Detchenkov, 2016). We also note that there are several applications such as wireless sensor networks in which the battery power limitation is extreme and recharging or changing drained batteries may be impossible.

Furthermore, there is a relationship between security and the power consumption. For instance, a higher number of rounds in AES encryption processes produces higher levels of security at the cost of additional power consumption. [Figure 11.3](#chapter11.xhtml#fig11.3) shows a general trend in the trade-off between vulnerability and power consumption with varying numbers of encryption rounds. Therefore, in order to design power-efficient encryption algorithms for wireless networks there is an **inherent need to understand the relationships between power consumption and encryption parameters**. Only then is it possible to optimize power consumption with respect to a security requirement.

Traditional cryptography deals generally with ensuring the security of the encrypted data. Several designs focus on security objectives while neglecting the QoS requirement. One main point is that the crypto-algorithms based on these designs usually do not account for physical constraints such as limited battery power (Chandramouli *et al*., 2006). It may not be possible to support a security requirement given the power budget. Then, the key questions are twofold: how does one optimize crypto-parameters for a given power budget? Therefore, the primary challenge in providing security in low-power mobile wireless devices lies in the conflicting aims of minimizing power consumption and maximizing security. In general, we can safely assume that by doing more computations one can achieve a higher amount of security.

![image](images/fig11.3.jpg)

**Fig. 11.3.**Trade-off between vulnerability and power consumption.

Many previous studies have addressed the issue of energy consumption in encryption processes. Khan *et al*. (2017) proposed a mechanism to reduce the cost of network coding by reducing the size of the data used for permutation. The basic idea is that the source permutes only global encoding vectors (GEVs) without permuting all the symbols in the message. This would significantly reduce the complexity and transmission cost over the network. Also, they suggest an algorithm for key generation and random permutation confusion key calculation. The proposed scheme achieves better performance in throughput, encryption time, and energy consumption. Zhang and Lin (2014), introduced a permutation coding scheme, called P Coding, which is a lightweight encryption method.

Also, there are some hardware solutions to address the high power consumption in encryption processing. However, Hamalainen *et al*. (2006) declare that a loop-unrolled and pipelined hardware implies a large area and high power consumption. Furthermore, these architectures cannot be fully exploited in feedback modes of operation. The hardware implementation has many limitations as well. Bansod *et al*. (2015) stated that the standard algorithms such as DES & AES have vast memory requirements and it would not be possible to implement them in the embedded system. So many research studies tried to use lightweight encryption algorithms such as PRESENT which should be more efficient in devices connected to wireless networks. However, there are many claims by other authors which suggest that these algorithms are weak against cryptanalysis (Lee, 2014; Faghihi *et al*., 2015) Several full-round attacks using biclique cryptanalysis have been introduced on PRESENT. According to Ramesh and Umarani (2012), “The last performance comparison point is the changing different key sizes for AES and UR5. In case of AES, we consider the three different key sizes possible, i.e., 128 bit, 192 bit and 256 bit keys. The simulation results are shown in Figure…. In the case of AES it can be seen that higher key size leads to clear change in the battery and time consumption. It can be seen that going from a 128 bit key to a 192 bit key causes an increase in power and time consumption of about 9% and going to a 256 bit key causes an increase of 17%. Also in the case of UR5, we consider the three different key sizes possible i.e., 128 bit, 192 bit and 256 bit keys.” The encryption and decryption processes consume a significant amount of computing resources such as CPU time, throughput, and battery power (Jiehong and Detchenkov, 2016; Ramesh and Umarani, 2012). [Figure 11.4](#chapter11.xhtml#fig11.4), for instance, shows the time taken to encrypt different images.

These research studies have addressed some issues regarding wireless networks; however there are still some clear gaps in their research. For example, the proposed mechanism to reduce the cost of the network may not provide sufficient security. As only part of the message will be encrypted, this might affect the security level. Researchers have tried modifying the transmission protocol using AES encryption, but they have not tried to modify the AES algorithm itself to make it cost-effective. For these reasons we are going to develop the current AES algorithm to make it cost-effective by keeping its power consumption low and its security at a high level.

![image](images/fig11.4.jpg)

**Fig. 11.4.**The amount of time needed to encrypt different images (Ramesh and Umarani, 2012; Zhang *et al*., 2014; Scarfone *et al*., 2007).

### 11.5.4.*Current state of security*

Security for a mobile environment today is much like it was in the early days of laptops. There is a sea of emerging mobile security solutions from both startups and more established software companies; we’ve published articles about several of these solutions on SandHill.com in the past few months. Organizations are trying to sort through the hype and figure out which products to use.

As companies learned over the years with laptops and desktops, a good mobile security strategy should be comprised of multiple solutions to provide in-depth security for the mobile device.

### 11.5.5.Secure access to applications

The security and management strategies for supporting a BYOD policy include an access-only approach to applications. This tactic prevents employees from downloading and storing any information on their mobile devices.

In addition, most of the CIOs we interviewed said their companies were looking at ways to separate corporate and personal data by implementing “container” structures on the devices. There are now several software companies with products enabling containment.

A **virtual desktop** is another structure which is used to contain information. This strategy eliminates the need for a BYOD policy and reduces device support costs while maintaining security and control. Currently software vendors such as VMware and Citrix and others are making virtual desktops more secure and therefore more organizations are following this strategy.

Using this strategy, a desktop in an employee’s home becomes the means of mobility. The employee accesses corporate applications virtually, and the company maintains control over the applications’ security. When the desktop shuts down, the connection to the applications is discontinued and no corporate data remains on the desktop.

“Smartphones and tablets are not yet powerful enough to handle this like desktops, but they will get there,” stated a CIO we interviewed in the study. “I believe the adoption of the virtual desktop strategy will rapidly increase as this technology and wireless technologies mature.”

However, a virtual desktop strategy has drawbacks even if mobile devices become powerful enough to handle it. It assumes continuous online availability, which is not assured in many locations, even in major metropolitan cities like New York City.

### 11.5.6.*Social media sites*

Allowing employees to access social media sites such as Facebook and Twitter from the company network is also a security risk. The challenge when employees go from an enterprise environment/network to another Internet site is that the company’s policies get replaced by the security vulnerabilities and lowest-common-denominator approach used by those sites.

Organizations need to make sure their company’s code of conduct for employee behaviour covers policies regarding accessing social media networks and websites through the enterprise mobile environment/network. Requiring employees to sign a code of conduct when hired is a common practice at many organizations (Paganini, 2012).

![image](images/fig11.5.jpg)

**Fig. 11.5.**Smartphone ownership rises in the USA, the UK, France, Germany, and Japan.

Companies and governments must be aware of the risks related to the careless use of powerful instruments. For instance, sensitive information could be exposed if the owners do not take the necessary precautions. The true revolution in the information technology world is the development and deployment of mobile systems, machines characterized by a processing capacity equal to that of a common desktop. This corresponds to a rise in smartphone ownership in certain countries, as seen in [Fig. 11.5](#chapter11.xhtml#fig11.5). People know our contacts (email, phone numbers) and manage our appointments, and when we surf on the web through these devices we indirectly provide them with information on our customs and traditions. A study reveals that Android-based smartphones suffered from more cyber criminal attacks due to their increased exposure to cyber threats. Due to how convenient they are, smartphones and tablets are becoming the preferred tools for browsing the Internet. The percentage of connections to the network from these mobile devices has increased significantly. This trend was evident in all countries, with the UK showing the largest increase in smartphone usage from 30 to 45% of the total population.

We have observed the increased attention of cyber criminals to the mobile sector. Cyber criminals often exploit security vulnerabilities in legitimate mobile apps, making data extraction and information gathering easier. The purpose is to steal information that is sensitive to the users such as banking credentials, but this is not the only purpose. Cyber espionage is another phenomenon that has exploded recently. Cyber criminals and government spies have discovered that it is really comfortable to spy on an individual by simply controlling his/her mobile device. Cyber criminals and government agencies are aware of the importance of information gained from mobile devices and are therefore showing high interest in the field. Hacker groups like Anonymous which target companies and individuals for various political reasons will pose a bigger threat to organizations that protect highly sensitive data. We have registered an exponential growth of malware designed to attack mobile systems and steal sensitive information which can be used to commit fraud. Don’t forget that hacktivism is considered one of the most serious threats by all the governments of the world.

### 11.6.Cross Border Security

**Wireless security** is the prevention of unauthorized access or damage to computers using **wireless** networks. The most common types of **wireless security** are Wired Equivalent Privacy (WEP) and Wi-Fi Protected Access (WPA). WEP is a notoriously weak **security standard**.

“The Government has set out a series of minimum cyber security standards which will now be incorporated into the Government Functional Standard for Security, obliging government departments and suppliers to comply. The Standards comprise 10 sections, covering five broad categories: Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover, and also set expectations for governance, such as obliging government departments to create “clear lines of responsibility and accountability to named individuals for the security of sensitive information and key operational services” (Mayne, June 2018).

One of the consequences of the rise of cloud computing — which in simple terms refers to using scalable computing resources as a service via the Internet — is that computer data are increasingly stored remotely (‘in the cloud’) instead of on users’ devices. This has significant implications for criminal investigation, particularly in cases where digital evidence is sought. Local search and seizure by the police will yield less and less evidence as users use cloud services such as webmail and remote data storage (Koops and Goodwin, 2014). This reinforces the existing challenges of cyber investigation, which not only has to deal with swift evidence-gathering due to the vulnerability of data loss, but which also has to find ways of remotely getting access to data, such as remote online searches or production orders directed at service providers. One particular challenge in cyber investigation is that such remote evidence-gathering powers may well extend beyond national borders. As remote access to computer data through remote cross-border searches and directly ordering foreign service providers to produce data are currently not allowed (Koops and Goodwin, 2014), states must resort to traditional procedures of mutual legal assistance, which tend to be relatively slow and not well-suited to securing digital evidence.
