## Chapter 12

## Ethical Considerations and a Proposed Support Process When Employing People With Autistic Spectrum Disorder in Cyber Security Roles

John Goldie and Hamid Jahankhani\*

*Northumbria University London, UK*  
[\**Hamid.jahankhani@northumbria.ac.uk*](mailto:Hamid.jahankhani@northumbria.ac.uk)

## ABSTRACT

There is an acknowledged global shortage in qualified and skilled cyber security practitioners, so much so that governments, employers and educational establishments are developing new routes and opportunities to encourage interest and applications from demographics that would not normally apply for cyber security roles. These demographics include women, young children and people on the autistic spectrum. The potential employment of people from this last demographic — people on the Autistic Spectrum — in cyber security roles will be the focus of this research. Two areas are of interest, the ethical considerations in employing people on the Autistic Spectrum and the identification of a strategy to support the employee and employer relationship. Both are discussed here. In Europe the shortfall is expected to be in the region of 350,000 employees by the year 2020 and in the United States the number is expected to be 1.2 million by the same date. This research looks at how specific autistic traits and strengths can be matched to cyber security vacancies and discusses ethical considerations and a potential support process. A qualitative research methodology was used to identify suitable traits and potential cyber security vacancies. Ethical principles and a proposed support process are put forward to allow potential employers and autistic employees to engage in equitable employment opportunities. The autistic demographic does indeed offer skilled and capable resources to help fill cyber security vacancies; however, work is needed to allow both sides to benefit from the opportunities.

*Keywords*: Autistic Spectrum Disorder, ASD, ethics, cyber security, training, employment opportunities, special needs, traits

### 12.1.Literature Review

Employers are competing against each other to attract potential employees who have the necessary qualifications, skills or aptitude to succeed in cyber security roles. This is due to shortages in the United States, where approximately 1.8 million vacancies are expected by 2020 (Frost and Sullivan Executive Brief, 2017), and in the European Union, where the expectation is that there will be unfilled vacancies totalling 350,000 until 2020 (Ashford, 2017). This means that employment opportunities in cyber security are excellent with benefits that include high salaries, work-life balance packages and further incentives.

Baker states, “It has been firmly established that the nation’s cyber workforce is lacking in numbers and in talented individuals needed to effectively operate in cyberspace. There is also undeniable evidence that the U.S. is trailing behind other countries in preparedness and sophistication in the cyber domain. While several directives, frameworks, programs, and initiatives exist that are designed to grow, train, and retain a skilled cyber security workforce, there are some gap areas where further focus could contribute to attaining measurable success.” (Baker, 2013)

Given the budgetary constraints that the government of the United Kingdom is currently experiencing due to the existing austerity measures, attracting qualified and skilled cyber security professionals could prove difficult. To alleviate this, various government departments have been and are running a number of initiatives aimed at identifying and encouraging potential employees. These initiatives include Cyber First (NCSC, 2018), Cyber Summer Schools (GCHQ, 2018) and Cyber Discovery (DCMS, 2017).

The cyber security industry is also conducting research aimed at identifying expertise within its own community to encourage professional development within the workforce.

Fontenele states, “One of the major challenges in current cyber security initiatives is to place skilled people wherever needed whilst reducing the overall knowledge gap. Thus, in order to orchestrate roles in such a complex and dynamic environment, a novel approach *to discover talent within the cyber security community is required.”* (Fontenele, 2017)

The Center for Cyber Safety and Education has recently completed a research paper *“Women in Cyber Security”*, which identified that 11% of the cyber security workforce are women. The paper concluded that women are underrepresented in cyber security roles and organisations needed to “take swift and considerable actions to engage, develop and retain women in the field or the global workforce gap will continue to grow year over year” (Frost & Sullivan, 2017).

Another demographic that is under consideration for providing potential cyber security employees is that of people with Autistic Spectrum Disorder.

The Israeli Defence Forces have used people on the Autistic Spectrum to good effect in intelligence analyst roles. Most notably, Unit 9900, one of Israel’s military intelligence units, has deployed male and female soldiers who have Autistic Spectrum Disorder in analysis roles where specific useful traits can be utilised to good effect (AIPAC, 2016).

Various United Kingdom government departments that have traditional information technology security and security service taskings are working with the National Autistic Society with the intention of identifying and developing opportunities for employing people on the Autistic Spectrum in cyber security roles within their organisations. The Cyber Security Challenge UK is a good example of this. It brings together the Information Assurance Advisory Council, CREST and the National Autistic Society to sponsor, develop and run “a series of national competitions, learning programmes, and networking initiatives designed to identify, inspire, and enable more people to become cyber security professionals. Established to bolster the national pool of cyber skills, it offers a unique programme of activities to introduce sufficient numbers of appropriately skilled individuals to learning and career opportunities in the profession.” (IAAC, 2017)

Evidently there is a potential resource available with people on the autistic spectrum. Research indicates that there are traits that may be suitable for use in fulfilling the requirements of cyber security roles. The following sections will identify these traits and potential opportunities.

### 12.1.1.**Autistic Spectrum Disorder**

### 12.1.1.1.*Basic brain anatomy*

Research shows that there are anatomical differences between neurotypical and non-neurotypical brains. The reasons and causes are not fully understood.

Autism may be the result of abnormal or damaged neurons (neural networks) in the brain. These neurons may be unable to establish synaptic connections or achieve neural synchronisation. A neuron is a nerve cell that specialises in sending signals or nerve impulses from one part of the brain to another or from the brain stem to the nervous system. This disruption may cause the cognitive, social and sensory issues exhibited by autistic people. Research to support this idea comes from anatomical (Courchesne *et al*., 2007), genetic (Geschwind and Levitt, 2007) and neuroimaging (Minshew and Keller, 2010) studies. Further research indicates that there may be much more densely folded grey matter in the rear regions of the brain, namely the left precuneus, left lateral occipital cortex and right temporal-occipital cortex (see [Figs. 12.1](#chapter12.xhtml#fig12.1) and [12.2](#chapter12.xhtml#fig12.2)).

![image](images/fig12.1.jpg)

**Fig. 12.1.**Neurotypical brain (Lal Mali, 2014).

People on the Autistic Spectrum and those with Asperger’s Syndrome have a range of potential issues ([Section 12.1.2](#chapter12.xhtml#sec12.1.2)), that could be exploited, either intentionally or unwittingly, by employer organisations or their employees. There are relevant laws, as documented below, that should protect autistic employees but unless there is an advocate or the autists themselves raise an issue, these laws may not protect the vulnerable employee. How likely it is that autists would raise any issues is not a matter that will be dealt with in this paper.

It should be noted that ethical research into autistic people tends to be conducted through parents, guardians or court-appointed deputies of the autistic person and is generally concerned with children (Mukaetova-Ladinska *et al*., 2012). Some autistic authors have highlighted this as an issue and suggest that more weight should be given to autonomy for autistic people, particularly when they have high-functioning autistic spectrum disorder.

![image](images/fig12.2.jpg)

**Fig. 12.2.**Areas affected by autism in a human brain (Haydn, 2013).

### 12.1.1.2.*Support processes*

There are potential issues associated with employing autistic people but there has been extensive work carried out by researchers, clinicians and charitable organisations in discovering and developing support processes and assistive technology tools. Some of these support processes are described and referenced here.

There are no official statistics in the UK relating to employment rates for autistic people, although the National Autistic Society has produced some estimates from surveys of autistic people. They are summarised in a report entitled *“The autism employment gap: Too Much Information in the workplace”* (National Autistic Society, 2018).

*“The Government wants to halve the disability employment gap. This would mean that 64% of disabled people would be in work*.

*60% of employers would worry about getting support for an autistic employee wrong*.

*60% of employers say they do not know where to go for support or advice about employing an autistic person.”* (NAS, 2017)

Employment offers social, psychological and financial benefits to all, including autistic people — for whom the psychological benefits may have a greater positive impact. Not least of these is the increased self-worth and autonomy that having a job can bring, which can lead to a feeling of contributing positively to society. There is also a decrease in the reliance on social and welfare benefits. There may be some issues associated with anxiety around integrating into the workplace and creating a new social network, although this can lead to psychological benefits once the initial anxiety and acceptance of change is recognised (Roux *et al*., 2013).

Gaining employment is seen as a rite of passage from childhood into adulthood and gives a huge psychological boost to everyone, including autistic people (Bennett and Dukes, 2013; Wilczynski *et al*., 2013).

It can be seen then, that there are improvements in quality of life, psychological and physical health, social standing and independence (both financial and social) associated with successful employment (Fleming *et al*., 2013).

Another issue is the interview process. There is evidence that interviews can be a cause for concern for autistic people. Researchers have identified that social difficulties can mean that the job interview can represent an intense challenge (Smith *et al*., 2014). This can lead to poor interview performance which results in a rejection; even in cases where the autistic person has the capability to perform the job.

The National Autistic Society, in the UK, advises organisations to make adjustments to their interview process and to consider using the following steps:

•*“Keep job description in simple English and focused.*

•*Weigh the qualities to indicate the main focus of the role.*

•*Be absolutely sure about what is essential and what is desirable.*

•*State that applications from autistic people and other under-represented people are welcomed.*

•*Avoid overblown statements about the company and the ideal applicant.”*

(National Autistic Society, 2017)

By implementing the suggested adjustments to the interview process, organisations may see an improvement in applications from autistic people and may then benefit from the skills and capabilities that they could bring to the role.

Socialisation is important, so it is seen as vital that both employers and colleagues of autistic people are willing to interact with them and develop support processes to ensure successful employment. López and Keenan (2014) conducted a survey that demonstrated that *“lack of appropriate understanding from employers and co-workers”* is one of the biggest barriers to successful employment.

Research in the United States has identified that socialisation issues can be a serious barrier to employment for autistic people (Chiang *et al*., 2013).

These socialisation issues can have a detrimental effect on work relationships when autistic traits and behaviours are exhibited (Test *et al*., 2014). These barriers may be ritualised and focused behaviour, inattention to duties, hyperactivity, irritability and shouting, all of which are unacceptable in the workplace and could lead to dismissal. These behaviours can, however, be triggered by misunderstandings in the workplace. Triggers could be sensory overload, misinterpretation in communications and unexpected changes to the work schedule or office infrastructure and facilities (Hurlbutt and Chalmers, 2004).

The lack of secondary school educational qualifications and work experience could have a negative impact on employment prospects for autistic people and even if a job is offered there could well be a mismatch between a person’s qualifications and abilities and the duties required by the role (Holwerda *et al*., 2012).

This is indicative of a lack of understanding from employers as to the capabilities of autistic people and supports the findings expressed in the National Autistic Society’s employment survey.

Prospects improve after a university education, whether the qualifications earned are undergraduate or postgraduate qualifications. This is predominantly true where extra transitional support or autistic mentors have been provided by the university or government agencies (Migliore *et al*., 2014).

This does not mean that a university education will guarantee improved employment prospects. Reports indicate that there are still high levels of under-employment and unemployment for graduates with autistic spectrum disorder, with some researchers finding that nearly 50% of autistic people were overeducated for the jobs they hold (Baldwin *et al*., 2014).

Studies show that having mentors during summer school periods can greatly enhance achievement for autistic students in their academic pursuits; especially when the student is encouraged to act as a mentor in the following summer school intake (Hotez *et al*., 2018).

Continuing support from vocational service providers could improve employment success. Indeed, research shows that there are definite benefits when provision is consistent (Howlin, 2013). Occupational therapists could provide the necessary vocational training and help to prepare autistic people to transfer into employment through a combination of support and advice to potential employers about any workplace adaptations. However, there is an issue with the lack of availability of qualified and experienced vocational OTs in the UK at present.

Support workers are employed to provide continuous support to severely disabled people in either voluntary or employed positions. Evidence suggests that having a support worker provides enough specific and intensive support to be of benefit to people on the autistic spectrum despite the initial increased costs. The support worker delivers long term benefits to the employee, employer and the government (in reduced benefits payments) (Howlin *et al*., 2005).

Support services have been shown to raise employment retention rates to nearly 90% for those autistic people who have access to them. This chapter will look at two approaches: TEACCH and Project SEARCH.

### 12.1.2.*TEACCH (Treatment and Education of Autistic and related Communication-handicapped Children)*

Mesibov and Shea (2010) state *TEACCH* “is a clinical service and professional training program, based at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, that has incorporated and contributed to the evidence base of autism interventions”. The late Eric Schopler, Ph.D., started the programme in 1972. The TEACCH approach is called ‘‘Structured Teaching.’’ Structured Teaching is based on evidence and the observation that individuals with autism share a pattern of neuropsychological deficits and strengths that we call the ‘Culture of Autism’, which includes the following characteristics:

1.*Relative strength in and preference for processing visual information (compared to difﬁculties with auditory processing, particularly of language).*

2.*Heightened attention to details but difﬁculty with sequencing, integrating, connecting, or deriving meaning from them*

3.*Enormous variability in attention (individuals can be very distractible at times, and at other times intensely focused, with difﬁculties shifting attention efﬁciently).*

4.*Communication problems, which vary by developmental level, but always include impairments in the initiation and social use of language (pragmatics).*

5.*Difﬁculty with concepts of time including moving through activities too quickly or too slowly and having problems recognizing the beginning or end of an activity, how long the activity will last, and when it will be ﬁnished.*

6.*Tendency to become attached to routines and the settings where they are established, so that activities may be difﬁcult to transfer or generalize from the original learning situation, and disruptions in routines can be uncomfortable, confusing, or upsetting.*

7.*Very intense interests and impulses to engage in favored activities and difﬁculties disengaging once engaged.*

8.*Marked sensory preferences and aversions.”* (Mesibov and Shea, 2010)

The support generated from this approach is aimed at the individual and involves the management of time, environment and sequences of events in order to facilitate clearer learning and making activities easier to perform.

The TEACCH program has proven to be effective and relatively easy to implement and has gained international support. In the UK, the National Autistic Society promotes its use and highlights that “*the TEACCH approach tries to respond to the needs of autistic people using the best available approaches and methods known so far, for educating and teaching autonomy. It is not a single method and can be used alongside other approaches. Our support uses techniques from the TEACCH approach, and we provide TEACCH training to professionals.”*

TEACCH values consist of the following:

***T**eaching — sharing autism knowledge and increasing the skill level of professionals and practitioners.*

***E**xpanding — increasing own knowledge to provide high-quality services to people on the autism spectrum and their families.*

***A**ppreciating — appreciating the strengths and uniqueness of autistic culture.*

***C**ollaborating and **C**ooperating with colleagues, other professionals, people on the autism spectrum and their families.*

***H**olistic — adopting a holistic approach, looking at the person, their family and community.*

Some of the TEACCH Autism Programme priorities are:

•*focussing on the person, their skills, interests and needs*

•*understanding the ‘culture of autism’ and identifying differences based on individualised assessments*

•*using visual structures to organise the environment and tasks when teaching skills*

•*being broad-based, i.e. support people at work, teach skills but also ensure that people are supported during leisure and/or social activities*

•*being flexible and teaching flexibility.*

*The TEACCH principles and techniques may always need to be in place for someone, but they may look very different at different stages of the person’s life.”* (NAS, 2018)

### 12.1.3.*Project SEARCH*

Project SEARCH is a transition programme developed to help youths with disabilities. It has been adapted to provide support to help young people with ASD to transition into employment and further education.

*“Key Project SEARCH programme components include setting a goal for employment, providing successive intensive internships in a community business, and assuring collaboration between school and adult services staff. Supports specific to students with ASD include providing intensive instruction in social, communication, and job skills; visual supports; and work routine and structure”,* (Wehman *et al*., 2012).

The high retention rates in employment for autistic people, identified through research, tend to indicate that providing support services is beneficial from a social, psychological and financial (both for the employee and the government — through a reduction in overall costs) viewpoint.

### 12.1.4.*Transition*

Transitioning from secondary school to further education and employment is recognised as a major milestone for autistic people in socially advanced countries around the world (Westbrook *et al*., 2015).The outcome is that autistic people achieve independence and employment.

It is recommended that these outcome-oriented transition services are made available as early as possible, with some researchers suggesting provision from the age of 14. This allows for longer individual preparation and could help to identify areas where further specific support is needed (Cimera *et al*., 2013). This research highlighted the increased wages and lowered costs for people who got early access to transition services.

### 12.1.5.*Assistive technology*

In recent years there has been an exponential growth in technology that can aid autistic people in improving life skills. These technologies include picture guiding, audio assistance, video modelling, virtual reality and robotics. Each of these technologies has been utilised in training autistic people to improve their social skills (DiGennaro Reed *et al*., 2011; Hopkins *et al*., 2011).

Internet-based training has proven effective in improving social skills relevant to employment, e.g. job searches and interviews. There is a programme that uses virtual reality to allow autistic youths to practice interview techniques. This has proven to be significantly effective (Strickland *et al*., 2013).

The use of technology to help people with disabilities has been proven across a range of physical and cognitive issues. Support can comprise of calendar entries to remind them of appointments or tasks that need to be completed. Communication can be improved through socialisation apps that ease misinterpretation between colleagues. Programs can be loaded onto tablets that allow for relaxation or rest when a situation is becoming stressful.

### 12.1.6.*Cyber security*

From the author’s perspective, the term cyber security refers to the security controls and countermeasures deployed at ingress/egress points in a network (or where network traffic passes a boundary) and where a resource requires greater protection. These security controls and countermeasures can be policies, processes, tools, software, hardware and firmware.

As such, these security controls and countermeasures are incapable of making ethical decisions and it is the human individual that has the responsibility of deciding whether any activity is ethically acceptable and should therefore proceed.

The advent of machine learning and artificial intelligence may render this stance as untenable in the future but at present both machine learning and artificial intelligence are driven by sophisticated algorithms and are not yet capable of making ethical choices.

*“The definition of computer ethics has various interpretations. One of the most oft-cited definitions is from James Moor: “A typical problem in computer ethics arises because there is a policy vacuum about how computer technology should be used. Computers provide us with new capabilities and these in turn give us new choices for action. Often, either no policies for conduct in these situations exist or existing policies seem inadequate. A central task of computer ethics is to determine what we should do in such cases — that is, to formulate policies to guide our actions.”* (Dittrich, *et al*., 2011)

The authors have been unable to find evidence of any prior research or published articles that specifically discuss ethics and cyber security in relation to security controls and countermeasures, although there is research available that examines how people use programs and malware to conduct attacks against targets. There is also a growing library examining ethics and cyber warfare.

To illustrate the point about cyber security elements being incapable of ethical decisions Stuxnet will be reviewed.

Langner states that Stuxnet *“marked a turning point in the history of cyber security — the arrival of the first cyber warfare weapon ever, known as Stuxnet. Not only was Stuxnet much more complex than any other piece of malware seen before, it also followed a completely new approach that’s no longer aligned with conventional confidentiality, integrity, and availability thinking. Contrary to initial belief, Stuxnet wasn’t about industrial espionage: it didn’t steal, manipulate, or erase information. Rather, Stuxnet’s goal was to physically destroy a military target — not just metaphorically, but literally.”* (Langner, 2011)

Here we have a software program specifically written to attack a given target. In and of itself the program is incapable of determining the ethical correctness of its purpose. The responsibility lies solely with those people that authorised its development and use.

Some commentators view Stuxnet as the first ethically developed cyber weapon in that it was designed to attack a given target with no collateral damage expected (Lucas, 2017).

There are various threat actors driving attacks against target organisations or individuals. Target organisations are constituent parts in the following fields: government, financial services, utilities, manufacturing, technical, military, security services, etc.

Threat actors can include sovereign states (Gutmann, 2010), intelligence organisations, hacktivists (Warren and Leitch, 2016), organised crime, hackers, etc.

Drivers for attacks from these disparate groups could be state espionage, corporate espionage, financial gain, political gain, publicity, fun, challenge, etc.

Each threat actor will have a different ethical stance or rationalisation for their activities. Each ethical decision will be made by a responsible individual and not by the tool employed to conduct the attack.

Ethics in cyber security has gained a greater meaning due to the diverse nature of the internet and the difficulties faced by any government in trying to prosecute threat actors based in another country, particularly when the threat actors may be part of the host nation’s intelligence services, and especially when the two nations may be geopolitically or ideologically opposed.

In 2015, the Office of Personnel Management, the US federal government’s human resources organisation, discovered it had been hacked and that 22 million records had been stolen; allegedly by Unit 61398, part of China’s People’s Liberation Army’s cyber espionage division (Koerner, 2016). To date, no evidence is available that the stolen data has been used maliciously. Which begs the question, “Why was the data stolen?” Could it be that the attack was a proof of ability or a warning from the Chinese to the Americans or an act of state cyber bullying?

Spoofing also presents issues in identifying a threat actor. If the attacker is able to effectively disguise the source of the attack or implicate another person or organisation, then innocent entities could be accused. This spoofing also allows states, organisations and individuals to claim innocence due to being framed. Plausible deniability, as Americans say.

In the case of the alleged attack on Sony Pictures by North Korea in 2014, Reuters reported *that “the results of a linguistic analysis of communications from the suspected hackers suggest they were more likely from Russia than North Korea”* (Hosenball and Finkle, 2014). In either case, neither country is likely to admit responsibility or extradite any potential suspects, due to the aforementioned geopolitical and ideological differences.

Sovereign states do not, technically, commit crimes, although their agents can be ordered to conduct activities that harm other states, organisations or individuals.

If one accepts that the points made above are correct, how can the perpetrators of these attacks be held legally or ethically accountable in the future? It is apparent that an international agreement is necessary.

There has been an attempt to implement an International Agreement to set acceptable parameters of cyber attacks. This followed the 2009 DDoS attacks against the Estonian government. This became known as the Tallinn Manual (named after the Estonian capital city where the Agreement was drafted, (NATO CCDCOE, 2013).

The manual was drafted by member states of NATO and had a US and Western European bias. This led to the proposals in the manual being rejected by China, Russia and Middle Eastern states.

Lucas (2017) states that *‘emergent moral norms’ sufficient to guide and govern the choices and actions of moral agents offer a hopeful prospect for obtaining some greater cooperation and constraint of activities as these choices and actions unfold in the cyber domain. One must be cautioned, however, that if the desired end is the governance of the cyber domain by means of an authentic moral point of view that is internalised, self-imposed and widely shared then we are still confronted with a profound obstacle. The prospects for attaining anything like an authentic morality or common ethos may prove all but unattainable in so diffuse, diverse and divided an environment as the cyber domain represents.”*

This leads one to the assumption that only a truly international and non-geopolitical and ideologically neutral conference will be in a position to develop a globally acceptable set of laws or ethics pertaining to cyber security matters.

Given the identified issues relating to cyber security-based international laws and ethics, how then can organisations implement effective moral codes to ensure that their staff use cyber security tools and treat their colleagues, stakeholders and customers in an equitable manner?

Interested organisations are holding workshops specifically aimed at cyber security ethics. ACM SIGCOMM’s “Cyber-security Research Ethics Dialogue & Strategy Workshop” in May 2013 is one example. The “workshop” embraced the theme of “ethics-bydesign”, and aimed to:

•“*Educate participants about underlying ethics principles and applications;*

•*Discuss ethical frameworks and how they are applied across the various stakeholders and respective communities who are involved;*

•*Impart recommendations about how ethical frameworks can be used to inform policymakers in evaluating the ethical underpinning of critical policy decisions;*

•*Explore cyber security research ethics techniques, tools, standards and practices so researchers can apply ethical principles within their research methodologies; and*

•*Discuss speciﬁc case vignettes and explore the ethical implications of common research acts and omissions.”* (Kenneally and Bailey, 2014)

The IEEE Standards Association is running “IEEE Project: 7000 — Model Process for Addressing Ethical Concerns During System Design”

The IEEE website has the following quote: *“Engineers, technologists and other project stakeholders need a methodology for identifying, analyzing and reconciling ethical concerns of end users at the beginning of systems and software life cycles. The purpose of this standard is to enable the pragmatic application of this type of Value-Based System Design methodology which demonstrates that conceptual analysis of values and an extensive feasibility analysis can help to refine ethical system requirements in systems and software life cycles.”* (IEEE SA, 2018)

Whilst the quote does not specify that such a methodology is needed in the field of cyber security, there is an obvious connection between security programming and ensuring that adequate security controls are embedded in systems during the development of software life cycles.

These workshops and projects indicate that interested global organisations are taking steps to develop and implement ethical processes. However, it is likely that these processes may take some time to be accepted and embedded into national and international organisations.

Another approach to embedding ethics which has been adopted by international and national organisations is for entities to publish “Codes of Conduct”. These are particularly deployed by vocational organisations that provide certification and training in Information Security.

These Codes of Ethics are high level aims that set out the organisation’s expectations of how their members/employees should act in relation to ethics — congruent to how organisations implement Tier 1 policies. If organisations combine these ethics codes with Corporate Responsibility processes and deliver training at induction and as part of an employee’s annual professional and personal development requirements, this should mean that ethical processes become part of the organisational culture.

To this point, the focus has been on implementing ethics as cyber security software, tools and processes are used. When teaching people ethical hacking, educational establishments demonstrate how offensive tools can be used to attack a target device or network. Then descriptions are given as to what “white-hat, black-hat and grey-hat” hackers are. The skills are already “out of the bag” so to speak. Surely there is a need to teach ethics before the tools and skills are made available, particularly when the student is a young child or an immature youth/adult or a non-neurotypical person, as in the case of autistic people.

Obviously, some organisations have a duty to conduct offensive hacking as part of their role (such as intelligence analysts). This would be made clear in contracts and terms of engagement and it is likely that crown immunity would apply. However, there is still a need to make students and employees aware of ethical guidelines.

Training people in ethics in advance of teaching the use of offensive tools will not necessarily deter criminal activity or those hacking for the challenge or the fun of it but it should give an ethical baseline to students and employees.

### 12.1.7.*Laws and ethics*

### 12.1.7.1.*Relevant UK laws*

Interestingly there are not many laws specific to cognitive and physical disabilities in the UK. The major law is the rather catchall Equalities Act 2010 (Equality and Human Rights Commission, 2010) wherein peoples’ rights to equality are guaranteed across the United Kingdom. Exceptionally, there is a law specific to autism in England. The Autism Act 2009 (UK Government, 2009) is the only conditionspecific law within the United Kingdom and demonstrates the level of importance that Parliament attaches to protecting the rights of people on the autistic spectrum. In Scotland, the Scottish Strategy for Autism was developed (Scottish Government, 2011).

In 2010 an Adult Autism Strategy “Fulfilling and Rewarding Lives” (NAS, 2010) was published. This was then superseded by “Think Autism” in April 2014 (NAS, 2014).

There are two further laws for consideration. The Children and Families Act 2014 “*supports young people in preparing for adulthood”* (UK Government, 2014) and The Care Act 2014 *“places a strong emphasis on preventing and delaying needs for care and support, making sure that there is appropriate information and advice for people, support for carers, and promoting integration between social care and health care services. It also places a duty on local authorities to promote a person’s well-being when carrying out any of their care and support functions in respect of that person.”* (UK Government, 2014)

### 12.1.7.2.*Ethics*

Ethics is a branch of philosophy that takes years of study to master and covers many different aspects from meta-ethics to normative ethics, which consists of areas such as virtue ethics, deontology, hedonism and consequentialism, to applied ethics consisting of areas such as bioethics, machine ethics and military ethics to moral psychology and descriptive ethics.

Clearly this section does not have sufficient space to deal with this level of philosophical ethics. Rather the section deals with ethics in a pragmatic way and looks at how policies and codes of conduct can provide support and guidance for organisations that are looking to employ autistic people in cyber security roles.

Embedding ethical and supportive governance processes into the business strategy may encourage relevant business units and employees to acknowledge and commit to the correct treatment of and engagement with their non-neurotypical workmates, thus establishing a set of guiding ethical principles for the organisation and workforce. This can also be considered as forming part of the governance processes established in an organisation. As such this would indicate that the Board and the executives of an organisation have responsibility for ensuring that ethical processes are embedded into the organisation’s culture.

Valentine and Godkin state that introducing ethical policies and continuing ethical training (specific to an employee’s role) by developing and implementing Corporate Social Responsibility processes will produce positive practices in the workforce and lead to higher retention rates and employee satisfaction (Valentine and Godkin, 2016).

Implementing policies and codes of conduct in a given field or organisation will provide guidance as to how organisations expect their staff to work in an ethical or moral way. However, this does not mean that the ethical requirements have been fully met if the relevant philosophers or experts have not thoroughly debated and proven the various aspects.

The approach of implementing codes of conduct in a given field or environment also ignores potential issues due to geopolitical or ideological differences on the international scene.

When considering a code of conduct for autistic people and their employers working in the field of cyber security one needs to consider autonomy and whether the participants fully understand the ethical requirements they are agreeing to. There needs to be an element of responsibility that will remain with those who authorise the activity. After all it has been established, in this research, that it is not possible to attach ethical considerations to the security controls and countermeasures that constitute cyber security.

It is likely that many of the autistic people who apply to work in cyber security roles will be high-functioning autists and will have the capacity to legally agree to adhere to a code of conduct but there may well be some people with special isolated skills or perceptual peaks that are able to carry out specific duties in a role, especially when it is an area that the autistic person enjoys and is focussed on, who may not have the capacity to make the required ethical declaration.

The codes of ethics published by ISACA (ISACA, 2018) and ISC² (ISC2, 2018) are excellent exemplars for information security and cyber security-based organisations but they do not provide adequate guidance when one considers that some of the people employed in the industry may be non-neurotypical and may not have the capacity to legally agree to requirements.

This section does not aim to address ethics from a philosophical perspective but from a layman’s viewpoint to try to determine how ethical considerations can support autistic people in finding employment in cyber security roles and how employers can engage equitably with potential new employees who are on the autistic spectrum.

Ethics is similar to the Hippocratic Oath requirements that physicians are constrained by — do no harm, respect the individual or group and act in an ethical way.

When ethics is considered from a practical standpoint the situation becomes more complicated; many differing arguments are put forward by interested stakeholders leading to complex issues that should be addressed by each individual stakeholder. Researchers have identified four specific categories of ethics that may pertain to autists and their social and employment interactions — personal, professional, regulatory and tangible (Brosnan *et al*., 2013).

The complexity of ethics could mean that organisations and their employees will pay lip service to ethical requirements and proceed with a nod towards laws and perceived morals, that is, trying to do the right thing. Whilst they may be well-intentioned, the potential for exploitation is apparent.

Stahl *et al*. (2013) identify different levels of ethical thinking*. “At the most basic level there is moral intuition which informs individuals with regard to what they perceive to be right or wrong. Where such moral intuition becomes problematic or contested, the second level, explicit morality, is needed so that clear statements can be made with regard to what is right or wrong. Ethical theory, the third level, seeks to justify such explicit morality. The fourth and most abstract level is meta-ethics, where ethical theories are reﬂected.”* (Stahl *et al*., 2013)

Embedding ethical policies and encouraging social responsibility may lead to employees taking the moral high road in working with both autistic people and cyber security tools.

Lucas (2017) states *“there are two possible strategies for the constructive role of moral considerations. The first involves exploring the relative advantages of morality as a form of self-governance in contrast to the constraints imposed by law. The second follows from the first and requires us to inquire more deeply into just what “ethics” represents as a kind of social institution and how it can plausibly claim to provide universal guidance for human conduct and the exercise of human (moral) agency. Both are important considerations in justifying claims for the efficacy of morality”.*

### 12.2.Methodology

### 12.2.1.**Qualitive review**

A qualitative research method was used to review secondary source information from peer-reviewed, respected journals, the Wellcome Collection Museum and Library and the National Autistic Society Library.

### 12.2.2.*Questionnaires*

Two questionnaires were developed, which continues the qualitative research methodology. Both consisted of open questions designed to elicit as much information as possible to detail what organisations were already doing with respect to autistic people and further to identify any ethical processes currently being followed and what support was under consideration or in place.

The open nature of the questions produced responses that were meaningful and salient to the responders and were therefore explanatory and rich in nature.

The questionnaires were also used to identify or confirm traits and strengths and potential cyber security vacancies at the employer organisations.

The first questionnaire was developed to gather information from The National Autistic Society.

The second questionnaire was developed to gather information from potential employer organisations.

### 12.2.3.*Case studies*

Finally, the case studies complete the qualitive research approach.

To ensure confidentiality and that data protection requirements are adhered to the name of the person discussed in this case study will not be divulged and random letters will be used to represent the individual in question. The letters JC will be used to identify the individual. The bespoke Managed Security Supplier (MSS) will not be identified.

Whilst attending an ethical hacking course in July 2017 an employee of a bespoke MSS met another attendee who had excellent programming, cyber security, vulnerability assessment and penetration testing skills but who had issues with communicating with the tutor and their classmates.

Through discussions during training modules and break periods it became apparent that JC was on the Autistic Spectrum. The MSS employee was able to encourage a tentative relationship to the point where JC accepted a business card and agreed to arrange a meeting between JC, his parents, a court-appointed deputy and the MSS.

The meeting established a willingness by all parties to enter into a short-term contract of employment for JC as a penetration tester. The initial, short length of the contract was to allow a sensible break if the agreement was unsuitable to either party.

It is noteworthy that JC was keen to have a level of autonomy in his role, although there was a legal requirement to agree to contractual and financial matters with the court-appointed deputy. All parties agreed to JC taking a lead in activities provided any legal issues were confirmed and agreed to with the firm of solicitors acting as JC’s legal deputy. This process took several months to sort out, mainly due to delays from the Court of Protection having to sanction parts of the contract.

JC received the same equipment, pay and terms and conditions as the other penetration testers at the company and where necessary adjustments were made to facilitate JC’s needs.

The role was home-based with occasional trips into the office to discuss requirements, adjustments or issues from JC’s perspective.

Initially JC was invited to visit the office so that he could be introduced to the environment and meet with some of the people he could be interacting with. During the initial meetings JC struck up a relationship with one of the team managers and it was agreed that JC would report to that particular team manager.

All the MSS’s clients were in the financial services domain so there was not any requirement to obtain security clearance — which could be an issue for anyone on the spectrum wanting to work on roles supporting government departments.

JC successfully provided vulnerability assessment and penetration testing services to the MSS and its clients for two years. One notable capability of JC’s was that they could look at a screenful of coding and almost immediately spot issues with either syntax, spacing or numerical errors. When asked how he was able to spot the mistake so quickly he said that the colours were different.

On a number of occasions support was required from the MSS in the form of report writing or accompanied attendance at meetings requested by the end client. There were two episodes of unusual interaction with colleagues; both of which were the result of misunderstandings — one employee was given training in how to interact with an autistic person and JC had an unexplained tantrum.

On the whole the relationship was successful and rewarding for both JC and the MSS.

Due to recent changes in ownership at the MSS, JC decided to leave his employment and move on to other activities. He was offered a continuation by the new owners, under the same terms and conditions that he had worked under for the preceding two years, but he was unwilling to stay.

At his leaving interview, JC stated that he had enjoyed the work and found that as he interacted more with his colleagues he noticed that his social skills improved so that he was more able to communicate with colleagues.

From an employer’s perspective the MSS was extremely satisfied with the quality of work that JC produced. Issues around reporting of findings were overcome when a team manager was able to build a good working relationship with JC. Some small adjustments had to be made to working practices but the benefits outweighed the costs.

The fact that JC was supported by a court-appointed deputy was an added complication but the only real negative was due to the time required to liaise with the deputy and the Court of Protection.

The role being home-based was a positive, as JC did not have to worry about unscheduled changes to the environment, workforce or duties which could have created an issue as change is recognised as a stress point for some autistic people.

Introducing JC to the office and keeping him informed of changes in personnel was a useful way of integrating him into the workforce and meant that any changes were forewarned and did not have a greater impact than they could have had.

Whether this approach would be acceptable in a government department or with a service management supplier in a central government contract, where security clearance is a requirement, is debatable as the processes around ensuring equivalency from a secure technical infrastructure in the home are complex and risk management of this will be a continuous task.

### 12.2.4.*Autistic savantism*

Professor Temple Grandin is a well-known scientist at Colorado State University, who works at reducing suffering in livestock. She is an accomplished author and gives speeches on autism and animal behaviour. She has Asperger’s Syndrome. She states that she thinks in pictures. She is considered to be a savant.

![image](images/fig12.3.jpg)

**Fig. 12.3.**MRI image of Grandin’s left medial temporal lobe (McGowan, 2013). Taken by Jason Cooperrider, University of Utah.

Grandin’s left medial temporal lobe — involved in memory — appears in pink in this MRI, shown in [Fig. 12.3](#chapter12.xhtml#fig12.3). The white crescent is her corpus collosum, a bundle of fibres that connects the two hemispheres of her brain.

Jason Cooperrider, who is one of a team of neuroimaging experts at the University of Utah who study brain changes in autism, carried out research on Professor Temple Grandin’s brain and reported that her brain is remarkable. The team scanned Grandin’s brain using three different methods:

•High-resolution magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), which captures the structure of the brain;

•Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), a method to trace the connections between brain regions;

•Functional MRI, which indicates brain activity.

The images revealed an unusual neural landscape that reflects Grandin’s deficits and talents.

Overall, the right side of her brain dominates. One theory of autistic savantism suggests that during foetal development or early in life, some developmental abnormality affects the brain’s left side, resulting in the difficulties that many autistic people have with words and social interaction, functions typically processed by the left hemisphere.

![image](images/fig12.4.jpg)

**Fig. 12.4.**Comparison of left ventricles in a control brain and Grandin’s brain. Source (McGowan, 2013) from Roen Kelly, Discover Magazine (2013), by Jason Cooperrider, University of Utah.

As can be viewed in [Fig. 12.4](#chapter12.xhtml#fig12.4), “*If brain tissue is damaged or does not develop fully, the ventricles — vessels filled with cerebrospinal fluid, shown in blue in this image based on neuroimaging work — expand to fill the space*. Temple Grandin’s enlarged left ventricle is a sign of abnormalities in her left hemisphere, which typically handles language, and may account for the difficulties she has with processing words. To make up for this, the right hemisphere sometimes overcompensates, which can lead to special abilities in music, art, and visual memory. Savantism is not well-understood, but between a tenth and a third of people with autism may have some of these abilities. Cooperrider’s team also discovered that Grandin’s amygdala, the almond-shaped organ said to play an important role in emotional processing, is larger than normal. This was not a surprising finding because among other functions, this region processes fear and anxiety, affective states often affected by autism. Her fusiform gyrus is smaller than normal — also not a surprise, since this region is *involved in recognizing faces, a social skill that autism may disrupt.”* (McGowan, 2013)

The two case studies seem to indicate that there are anatomical differences in brain structure in autistic people when compared to neurotypical brains as can be seen in the comparative brain scans shown in [Fig. 12.4](#chapter12.xhtml#fig12.4) above. Grandin’s brain scan shows marked differences in anatomical structure from the so-called normal brain. These differences could be caused by much more densely packed neurons in the highlighted area in Grandin’s brain scan. As the neurons are responsible for passing electrical impulses, this extra density may indicate that the electrical impulses occur faster and so allow for increased ability in particular areas. This can be called savantism, special isolated skills or perceptual peaks.

Also, the two subjects report that they experience their environment differently from how most people would experience it.

These differences could be advantageous in cyber security roles in that issues may be picked up more quickly. This may be particularly useful in combating an ongoing attack or in completing a forensic examination. Business-as-usual processes could also be more efficient and effective if the analyst was able to instantaneously spot errors or code in a particularly fast way.

If the supposition documented by McGowan (2013), “*Savantism is not well-understood, but between a tenth and a third of people with autism may have some of these abilities”*, is correct, then there could be between 70,000 and 235,000 autistic people in the UK with savant skills that may be useful in cyber security roles. Obviously not all will be useful in cyber security roles but this could indicate that there is a sizeable relevant skill set waiting to be identified and utilised in the autistic demographic.

### 12.3.Analysis and Critical Discussion

### 12.3.1.**Matching traits with opportunities**

The National Autistic Society provides support, information and services for autistic people (including those people with Asperger’s Syndrome), and their relatives and guardians in the United Kingdom. It is a leading charity that campaigns for a better world for autistic people. The Society describes autism as “*a lifelong, developmental disability that affects how a person communicates with and relates to other people, and how they experience the world around them.*” (National Autistic Society, 2017)

The Society has been working with interested organisations, educational establishments and potential employees to identify specific traits that can be utilised in the workplace or act as a base for further education and training.

### 12.3.1.1.*Traits and strengths*

Listed below are some of the traits and strengths exhibited by autists (National Autistic Society, 2016):

•Attention to detail

•Methodical approach

•Good memory for factual information

•Strong problem-solving skills

•Strong numerical skills

•Neuro-diverse thinking

•Pattern recognition

•Reliable

•Resourceful

These traits and skills have been recognised as a good fit for roles in cyber security, intelligence analysis or information security. There are many cyber security organisations including United Kingdom government departments that are actively assessing and recruiting autists to fill vacancies in these domains (IAAC, 2017).

Organisations that have expressed an interest in employing autists include, but are not limited to, NCSC, Microsoft, SAP, IBM, BAe, QinetiQ, NCC Group, Northrop Grumman and Thales.

### 12.3.1.2.*Opportunities*

Questionnaires were sent to the National Autistic Society and various interested employer organisations to try to ascertain requirements from the perspectives of support and employer functions. Results from the employer questionnaires seem to indicate that there are specific roles where autists are under consideration as potential employees. These roles include:

•Penetration testers

•Vulnerability assessors

•Cyber forensic analysts

•Network security analysts

•Firewall engineers

•Threat intelligence analysts

•Security Information Event Management (SIEM) analysts

•Security programmers

These roles all require a methodical approach, a good attention to detail and a level of tenacity to keep working at a mentally tiring exercise. Numerical and problem-solving skills are key to each of the roles, whilst pattern recognition and lateral thinking would be a distinct advantage.

Other roles were identified in the questionnaires but as they fall outside of the cyber security field they will not be documented here.

Note: As the majority of the questionnaire respondents are involved in activities that require security clearance, an undertaking (in the form of non-disclosure agreements) was given not to identify which roles are directly associated with individual organisations. In compliance with this undertaking, specific questionnaire responses will not be attached to this document.

A comparison of the traits and strengths and roles listed above does seem to indicate a useful correlation that could, with the implementation of appropriate support processes, lead to meaningful employment and mutually beneficial work relationships for both autistic people and employer organisations.

### 12.3.2.*Potential issues*

There are a number of traits that are exhibited by people on the Spectrum that should be considered by employer organisations to ensure an equitable relationship.

The National Autistic Society states *“Autistic people see, hear and feel the world differently to other people. If you are autistic, you are autistic for life; autism is not an illness or disease and cannot be ‘cured’. Often people feel being autistic is a fundamental aspect of their identity.*

*Autism is a spectrum condition. All autistic people share certain difficulties but being autistic will affect them in different ways. Some autistic people also have learning disabilities, mental health issues or other conditions, meaning people need different levels of support. All people on the autistic spectrum learn and develop. With the right sort of support, all can be helped to live a more fulfilling life of their own choosing.”* (National Autistic Society, 2017)

These potential issues could be seen as reasons to avoid employing autistic people but the research documented in this paper indicates that with some reasonable adjustments in the work environment and how communication is handled between the autistic employee and the organisation, a mutually beneficial working relationship is possible.

### 12.3.2.1.*Social communication*

Autists may be unable to process verbal or non-verbal language such as tone of voice, gestures and facial expressions. They can take as literal anything that is said to them, as some do not understand sarcasm or jokes. This processing of verbal and non-verbal language is a skill that most of us learn as we interact with each other and we can pick up on the different nuances that escape autists.

Some autists have problems with the spoken language but can express themselves very clearly in other ways, for example by using sign language or visual symbology.

The case study relating to JC shows that it is possible to implement communication strategies to enhance and support communication for the autistic person, the employer and their clients. Each individual is different so it is important that time is taken to identify the most appropriate strategy for that person.

### 12.3.2.2.*Social interaction*

Autists can find it difficult to form friendships and often have trouble reading others, that is, recognising feelings, emotions and intentions.

![image](images/fig12.5.jpg)

**Fig. 12.5.**MRI image detailing responses to the word ‘hug’ in a neurotypical and non-neurotypical brain. Image.

*Source*: Journal Plos.org.

This can lead to socially awkward events such as perceived strange behaviour, deliberate avoidance of groups (the desire to be alone) and the appearance of insensitivity and aloofness.

This is probably the most identifiable situation and is easily addressed by considering the work environment and letting relationships develop over time. [Figure 12.5](#chapter12.xhtml#fig12.5) shows how just hearing the word “hug” can have such a different impact on a neurotypical brain and a non-neurotypical brain (Ajakab *et al.*, 2013). Image A identifies the region of the brain that deals with social touching. Image B is the neurotypical control brain. Image C is the non-neurotypical brain (Journal Plos.org).

The images in [Fig. 12.5](#chapter12.xhtml#fig12.5) indicate very different responses in brain activity to the word “hug”. The autistic brain shows much less activity, indicating potential issues in social interaction, than does the control brain. This difference in activity has been shown to be replicated in other areas of the brain under stimuli in further brain scans, supporting conclusions that the autistic brain works in different ways to neurotypical brains.

### 12.3.2.3.*Honesty*

The often uncompromising truthfulness of autistic people could be a barrier to developing equitable social relationships.

Internally this situation can be supported by providing coaching and training for all employees although a strategy should be developed to mitigate any issues that may arise with client organisations who are not aware of the relevant circumstances.

### 12.3.2.4.*Routines and repetitive behaviour*

Autists can view the world as a confusing and very unpredictable place. To manage this some may adopt routines such as always arranging belongings in a particular way, or adopting rules to ensure they follow the ‘correct’ way to do things, particularly if they have been introduced to something new. As change can be an issue, repetitive behaviour can be a coping mechanism.

This repetitive behaviour could have advantages in a cyber security role that requires continuous monitoring or tool calibration.

### 12.3.2.5.*Focussed interests*

People on the Spectrum can develop focussed and often intense interests across a wide range of topics — anything from art, computers, history, politics to zoology. Some of these interests will be of interest to potential employers but the narrow focus could prove to be an issue.

Some autists have reported that these activities are fundamental to who they are and to their holistic well-being.

Managing focussed interests carefully could mean a beneficial increase in throughput or production but care will need to be taken to ensure there is no detrimental effect on the autistic employee.

### 12.3.2.6.*Sensory perception*

Autistic people can have a heightened or lowered perception associated with their senses (vision, hearing, smell, taste, touch), temperature and pain. Responses to these stimuli could be anxiety, panic attacks or hyper-focus.

Obviously, any extreme responses will be upsetting to all involved but simple measures may help to control external stimuli.

Heightened sensory perception could manifest as special isolated skills or perception peaks, which in turn may provide advantages in cyber security roles.

### 12.3.3.**Questionnaire response analysis**

### 12.3.3.1.*National Autistic Society questionnaire*

The NAS questionnaire identified autistic traits and strengths that could be useful in a wide range of roles including cyber security. NAS identified a wide range of roles, highlighting industries from the arts, libraries, administration, property management, information technology and horticulture.

Support strategies were identified and these strategies form part of the proposed support strategy proffered here.

From a law and ethics perspective the NAS discussed existing laws and policy requirements. Ethics related more to research ethics when clinical and social researchers were conducting autism studies.

The questionnaire identified a number of employer organisations that had worked with NAS in encouraging and assessing potential in cyber security work. These organisations include GCHQ, NCSC, BAe, NCC Group, Thales, Northrop Grumman, QinetiQ and UK government departments. This list informed which organisations received the Employer Questionnaire.

The National Autistic Society is a charitable institution that works specifically towards supporting autistic people. As such, there may be a natural bias in some of the responses received. As it is a single organisation, their views may not be wholly representative in the autistic environment.

### 12.3.3.2.*Employer questionnaire*

Eight employer organisations, from a total of ten, responded to the questionnaire; as the majority of them requested that available opportunities are not linked to their organisation and as some of the roles are associated with providing security-cleared services it was necessary to complete non-disclosure agreements to access the information. A decision has been made to retain confidentiality for all responding organisations.

The number of employer organisations which participated is small and may not be representative of the wider employment opportunities available. However, all those approached work in the cyber security domain and had previously expressed an interest in employing autistic people. The results could be improved by approaching more organisations for responses.

Potential vacancies are identified below. To maintain confidentiality the organisations will be identified using the numbers 1–8 in the following charts.

[Figure 12.6](#chapter12.xhtml#fig12.6) clearly shows there is great interest in employing autistic people in cyber security roles in the organisations that responded to the survey. Given the small survey size this may mean that the results are not representative across the industry. A larger employer survey is recommended to ascertain a more representative view.

[Figure 12.7](#chapter12.xhtml#fig12.7) indicates how the eight employer organisations are considering deploying autistic employees. Location is a consideration when employing autistic people as a changing environment could cause anxiety and lead to angry outbursts. If the correct support processes are put in place to mitigate this situation then any issues can be mitigated.

![image](images/fig12.6.jpg)

**Fig. 12.6.**Company-reported interest by cyber security role.

![image](images/fig12.7.jpg)

**Fig. 12.7.**Location preferences as expressed by employer organisations.

Where an autistic person is located could depend on the employer’s or their end clients’ requirements and this is something that needs to be taken into consideration.

The responses do indicate that employer organisations are considering some flexibility on deployment location.

[Figure 12.8](#chapter12.xhtml#fig12.8) represents whether the employer organisations have considered the different ethical options associated with employing autistic people.

The results seem to indicate that the organisations will rely upon existing relevant laws and their own policy document sets. The majority of the organisations highlighted their own Corporate Social Responsibility activities as being relevant. Only 25% reported that they had looked into ethical requirements, however, they did not stipulate how this was undertaken or what the results were. Less than half indicated that they were considering a mentorship scheme.

![image](images/fig12.8.jpg)

**Fig. 12.8.**What ethical considerations were discussed internally?

It should be noted that the responses recorded in [Fig. 12.8](#chapter12.xhtml#fig12.8) may represent the respondents’ own views or their knowledge of what support processes may be deployed within their organisation and may not represent what actually would occur if an autistic person were to be employed by the organisation.

Overall, the small survey responses indicate that there are cyber security roles potentially available to autistic people.

Further consideration by the employer organisations needs to be given to ethical considerations on how the organisation will support the effective introduction of autistic people into the workforce and what adjustments need to be made.

Research shows that providing mentors is a positive step, particularly when mentors are themselves autistic and have been involved with a previous iteration of mentorship.

Change can be an issue and the employer organisations have indicated a willingness to allow flexibility in location. Combining this with effective communication on any planned changes in personnel, office environment or duties should lead to an effective business relationship for all parties.

### 12.3.4.*Autistic brain structural anomalies*

While basic brain anatomy has been discussed in previous sections, [Fig. 12.9](#chapter12.xhtml#fig12.9) in this section details the differences between a “normal” brain and an autistic brain.

![image](images/fig12.9.jpg)

**Fig. 12.9.**Anomalies in brain activity and anatomy — Autistic brain vs. control brain (Yamada *et al*., 2016).

Research indicates that an autistic brain may have more densely grouped regions at the cerebral cortex and the cerebellum. This extra density can manifest itself in more folds in these regions. These folds can increase the surface area of the brain and bring neurons into closer proximity to each other.

*“The insular cortex comprises multiple functionally differentiated subregions, each of which has different patterns of connectivity with other brain regions. Such diverse connectivity patterns are thought to underlie a wide range of insular functions, including cognitive, affective, and sensorimotor processing, many of which are abnormal in autism spectrum disorder (ASD).”* (Yamada *et al*., 2016)

The extra surface area and the close proximity of neurons could mean that neurological signals pass more effectively and efficiently in the areas that have anatomical abnormalities. This could then mean that the autistic person can utilise these differences in more focussed ways, leading to peak performances in, for instance, identifying patterns useful in checking network security baselines, penetration testing, configuring SIEM tools, writing software codes, etc.

Neurons process and transmit electrical-chemical signals throughout the nervous system and can be found in the brain, spinal column and peripheral nerves. The potential cognitive phenomena exhibited by autistic people can manifest across a range of subjects or areas, such as mathematics, exceptional memory, increased perceptual capacity, visual acuity, languages, music and art.

Mathematics can be directly associated with cyber security skills when one considers elements such as logic, cryptoanalysis, statistics, algorithms and computation. Similarly, memory skills, perceptual capacity — where there is an ability to process large amounts of information — and visual acuity can also be utilised in cyber security roles.

### 12.4.Conclusions

As evidenced in this research, there are traits and strengths exhibited by people on the Autistic Spectrum that can be utilised effectively by cyber security industry employer organisations.

There are some potential issues that should be taken into consideration to ensure an equitable relationship. There is the potential for anxiety and disruption for the new employee, the existing employees and the employer.

Although unlikely, there is the potential for either deliberate or accidental exploitation of the individual, particularly when cyber security tools are deployed in furtherance of national interests. The natural inclinations of some autists could also mean that they become focussed on discovering vulnerabilities in a given system or network and will keep at it regardless of the time it takes or the effect it could be having on them personally.

By developing ethical policies and support processes, these issues can be avoided or mitigated. There are existing laws that provide a level of protection but adopting ethical and support functionality will mean that both sides will understand their responsibilities and build an effective and fair working relationship.

The anatomical differences in brain structure and the denser collection of neurons in the rear of the brain (which function by passing electrical impulses) seem to indicate that in certain circumstances it is possible for the autistic person to exhibit special isolated skills, perceptual peaks or savant capabilities. These abilities can then produce some remarkable skills that can be effectively utilised in cyber security roles.
