## Chapter 13

## An Ethical Approach to Understanding Cyber Security

Ojo Emmanuel Ademola

*Northumbria University London, UK  
[emmanuel.ademola@northumbria.ac.uk](mailto:emmanuel.ademola@northumbria.ac.uk)*

## ABSTRACT

The study of ethics in cyber security often raises more questions than it answers. A student may ask the question, “Why should I study ethics in cyber security?” As research becomes specialized and technical skill sets appreciate in value, ethical questions become more important to ask.

This chapter reviews the ethical aspects of cyber security. Ethics, in general, underscores various studies in which right is distinct from wrong. The understanding of these delineations evokes various ethical issues in cyber security, such as the morality of human behavior, policies, laws, and social structures. Considering theories of consequentialism and deontology, ethical analyses of cyber security, information privacy and ethics, and privacy issues in the digital age are performed through the use of relevant ethicallydriven cyber security case studies.

*Keywords*: ethics, digital age, cyber security

### 13.1.Introduction

An ethical approach to the understanding of cyber security in this digital age requires adaptability and continuous commitment as top priorities. A working definition of ethics that includes both consequentialist and deontological approaches to understanding the subject is emphasized. This definition also encompasses the introductory concepts that accentuate the issue of ethics in cyber security. Overall, the chapter provides a brief which is substantive enough to last the whole hour that a dedicated reader would commit to such an endeavour.

Retaining the highlighted comments about ethics or morals throughout this chapter, it is important to note other works that may provide help in understanding the ethical aspects of cyber security. The section titles in this chapter include:

•A Working Definition of Ethics

•Computer and Ethics in Cyber Security

•The Ethical Significance of Cyber Security

•The Undermining Ethical Issues in Cyber Security

•Cyber and Information Conflict

•Ethical View of the GDPR’s Cyber Security

•Ethical Issues and Data Privacy

•Ethics and Research in Cybersecurity

Significantly enmeshed in the literature of ethics, data protection, computer ethics, and privacy, as well as GDPR, this chapter provides a real, hands-on understanding of cyber security and its ethical implications for both scholars and practitioners.

### 13.2.A Working Definition of Ethics

As we transition and adjust to the cyber age, the use of data and its associated evaluation relates to the ethics of data use. The moral ecology of application systems that engage with data occurs across innumerable situations within any given cyber-algorithmic context or condition.

Abel (2010) acknowledges the connection between cyber security, global migration, populace conduct, and change, which underscores Edwards and Veale’s (2017) notion of ethical evaluation. These intertwined assessments illustrate approaches to moral views that relate to public sector engagement with machine learning, ambient intelligence (AmI), as well as variations in similar fields. Such connections underpin the ethical synergy of studying cyber security, which continues to gain traction globally.

Moreover, as deliberation and strategy continue, for example, in the United Kingdom (NCSS, 2016; see also Shafqat and Masood, 2016), the Netherlands (Kool, Timmer and Van Est, 2015), and France (CNIL, 2016), various positions on what constitutes “ethics” or “morals” of conduct emerge. Ethically, the simple thought of checking on “change” for instance, as a starting point, suggests above all else that something is “new.” Secondly, it could indicate that similarities are still present, and might also suggest the reasons, both noteworthy and immaterial, why more change has not occurred. It is a challenge to depict the physical and causal needs underlying the process of change.

Bühlmann and Hovestadt (2013) encourage the activity of singling out an instance and asking which ICT or IoT venture has addressed its brief most fittingly. This approach includes quantitative estimations that evaluate significance through the minimum number of standardized examples. Meanwhile, Schwab (2017) depicts the scene as a challenge when managing social change, the estimation of the mass, and the peripheral connections with subjective judgments. It is an evaluation of contrasts that can prompt moralistic declarations, which on a fundamental level, could present an opportunity for a distinctive notion of ethics. It looks to embed and actualize a network of actions, either socially or politically, as ethics remain an issue (Arendt, 1958).

Ethics on this note characterize a term by Gieryn (1983), “boundary work.” It originates from the Greek term *ethos*, as signifying “ongoing character and mien” in the plural, “behaviour,” and alludes to a person’s, community’s, or organisation’s exercises and lead. Conversely, the word “moral” originates from the Latin expression *moralis*, alluding to the best possible conduct of a person in a network or culture. Given the near and integrative vector of morals (which aims to extract from ethics and make them perfect), we discuss ethical issues in cybersecurity to address the level of society in which professionals engage with the subject of cybersecurity. We view this as constitutively pluralist and furthermore employ subjective methods for systematizing ethics as proposed in the literature (Benveniste, 1969; see also Lambert, 2001 and Lewallen, 2013).

There are numerous angles from which to consider the appropriate use of these two terms. One that appears to be critical to us is that, concerning cyber security, ethics or morals has less to do with something surely known. It might engage with the finding of a shared conviction or the insistence on not being entirely agreeable in professional circumstances. Such types of challenging requests we call “types of direct,” which can be encoded and deciphered in different behavioural contexts. Thus, there is space for interpretation about types of direct. In that sense, sets of principles give “focal points” through which we can consider the formalized ideas adopted as standards and measures. At the point when codes of behaviours are established, they are ordinarily rendered in wording that then claims a global legitimacy in the form of benchmarks, rules, and so on.

Such procedures of speculation are, apparently, extraordinary because of the gauges that result from those standards. The refinements with which we work include the following: A measure can constitute a framework (as in IT guidelines), whereas a rule comes from a full structure, or from a projective, perfect frame. These refinements are critical because, in cyber security and additionally in ICT, we have systems that are insufficient when viewed as frameworks.

“Frameworks” is a term suggesting rationales (components and sayings), whereas “systems” is a term suggesting coordination (particles, hubs, and dispersions). This distinction has significant ramifications for how we reason, survey, and assess frameworks and systems. “Implicit rules,” as we comprehend them, open up interrogative spaces in which to practice — either those that are endorsed normatively or those that are plainly obvious or “characteristic,” as propensities, traditions, or customs. Sets of conventional rules are consequently held on to because of the inconvenience that stems from “cyber-coding” such conduct to fit open spaces, where one’s custom is only one of the numerous conceivable ways to act. Haraway (2008) underscores that in spaces where coding or algorithms exist, an ethical view could be a propensity. Inherently, such a view could seem inconvenient when outlining an opening in order to understand an assertion. We should be cognizant, and give spaces a shape, keeping in mind the end goal.

Bühlmann and Hovestadt (2013) portray conventional rules as the state of probability for deciphering various practices without forcing a resolute pecking order. The paradigm moves crosswise over social laws because of the algorithmic conditions in cybersecurity that presently sort out life. In this manner, something beyond speed and frame-prescient apparatuses with which to quantify and study regulating methods of “quantitative institutionalization” is required. All things considered, Sharp *et al*. (2017) argue that it is not exclusively to represent moves in the association hypothesis, but in addition to having proper strategies, that emotionally supportive networks that draw in information must be consolidated into all choices. In this way, Harasim (2017) proposes an essential inquiry for morals in the working condition that discusses e-wellbeing, the populace, movement, security, correspondences, training, and research opt-in. It might be an analysis of how we create, utilize, and assess choice in emotionally supportive networks that draw in with information. The following inquiry might emerge: How can one turn the subject of cyber security into one with a reasonable response to ethics or morals?

### 13.3.Computers and Ethics in Cyber Security

Computers, cyberspace, and ethical analysis present a new infosphere when compared with any other utility. Considering the scope of this subject, “cyber” refers to computers and networks, focussing on the Internet, online, and web contexts as well as related technologies. Additionally, PCs, data morals, and different fields of connected ethics require ethical theories that soundly bring together deontological and consequentialist notions of ethics. Moor (1999) considers the hypothesis of just consequentialism as an underlying result of approaches inside the imperatives of equity, which makes just consequentialism a reasonable and hypothetically stable way to deal with the ethical aspect of cyber security. It is fundamentally a black box and could be unexplainable, especially when ethical issues reach a wrong conclusion. Considering ethical problems associated with computers and information ethics, ethical approaches are essential frameworks to justify the right outcome in general.

### 13.3.1.*Information governance and policy vacuum*

The flexibility of computers enables them to be utilized in novel and unexpected ways. The propulsion of computer innovation in the digital age leaves policy vacuums in its wake, and when necessary mechanisms do exist, they are regularly outdated and unable to be adapted. Fundamental objectives of cyber security include recognizing the need for appropriate governance and policy frameworks, illuminating related and reasonable perplexities, planning proper governance approaches, and standardizing appropriate ethics to justify applications.

Policies are standards ranging from formal laws to casual, verifiable rules for activity. Strategies suggest sorts of events that are at times dependent upon various circumstances. “Log out or switch off your system when you are done” is a command with less significant ethical value. “Try not to steal assets” is a phrase with clearer ethical substance. “Don’t eavesdrop on conversations” could be a policy with less immediate ethical consequences. Notwithstanding, when systems are extensions of strategies, they can assist with regulations to make the use of computers good for society. We can better understand a situation and respond appropriately. ### 13.5.1.*Hacking and computer wrongdoing*

In any organisation or association, ethics assumes a part and ought to be of concern with regards to cyber security. Specialist groups also accentuate what makes an ethical practice in IT.

Eminently, a substantial piece of cyber security is concerned with the insurance of computer assets and information against interception, interruption, modification, and fabrication. Such activities are frequently called hacking. Hacking, as defined in this section, is the utilization of computer aptitudes to increase unapproved access to information and computer assets. Hackers are exceptionally gifted computer clients that use their abilities to expand such access and regularly frame networks or systems with different programmer groups to share learning and information. Hacking is periodically recognized more adversely as the harnessing of unapproved access for malignant purposes: to take data and programming or to degenerate information or upset framework activities. Self-distinguished hackers, in any case, distinguish between non-malignant break-ins, which they call hacking, and malevolent break-ins, or cracking. Self-recognized programmers frequently legitimize their hacking exercises by insisting that they cause no harm and instead have a positive effect. The positive impact of hacking, they contend, is that it liberates information to the advantage of all and enhances frameworks and programming by uncovering security loopholes. These contemplations are a piece of what policies detail as the hacker ethic or programmer code of ethics, which is an arrangement of specific rules that guide the movement of numerous programmers. Such standards assert that data ought to be free, entrance to systems ought to be boundless, and exercises in the Internet do not cause harm.

It has been argued (Tavani, 2003; see also Spinello, 2010 and Quinn, 2014) that various standards of the hacker ethic lack credence for sustainability. The conviction that data ought to be free runs counter to the pure thought of intellectual property or licensed innovation, for instance, and suggests that the originator of data or designer of systems would have no privileges. It would also fundamentally undermine protection and the integrity of data, as data could be altered and changed freely by any individual who might access it. People can also deny having anything to do with a derailed outcome. Moreover, the good that hacking does in finding security shortcomings may not exceed the trouble it causes.

Some authors, like Yar (2013), have contended that both hacking and cracking have a tendency to be unlawful and may be considered a type of computer wrongdoing or cyber crime (see also McQuade, 2006, and Yar 2005). However, Tavani (2003) suggests two noteworthy kinds of cyber crime that harm computer security: cyber trespassing, which is the utilization of data innovation to increase unapproved access to computer frameworks or secret key ensured sites; and cyber vandalism, which is the utilization of data innovation to release programs that upset the activities of resources or degenerate information. There is also a third sort of cyber crime that occasionally incorporates breaks of security: cyber piracy. Cyber piracy, likewise, called digital theft, is the utilization of data innovation to duplicate exclusive programming or data or to disperse such information over a network.

Digital theft is altogether more common than digital vandalism or digital trespassing because it doesn’t require high aptitude, and various computer users find it morally tolerable to make copies of copyrighted software and data. Digital robbery incorporates breaks in security when it consolidates parts of copyright protections. Another sort of digital wrongdoing that combines breaches of security is deception, which includes false online identities or the adjustment of data. Computer blackmail may involve significant digital trespassing to gain passwords, automated identities, or other trade and access codes, as well as exhibitions of digital vandalism. Distinctive sorts of digital wrongdoing, for instance, child pornography or web-based harassment (cyber bullying), generally do include bursts of cyber security.

### 13.7.2.*The “security of processing”*

The security procedure is expressed in Article 32 of the GDPR, tagged as “Security of processing.” The article is short and simple; however, it contains some key information. (i)The pseudonymization and encryption of individual information: If an association is handling vast volumes of personal information or sensitive classifications, this is a significant advantage. (ii)The capacity to guarantee the progress of confidentiality, uprightness, accessibility, and versatility in preparing frameworks and administrations.

(iii)The ability to re-establish the openness and access to individual information conveniently in case of a physical or specialized context.

(iv)A procedure for routinely testing, surveying, and assessing the adequacy of functional and hierarchical measures for guaranteeing the security of every mode of data status within handling.

A review of the last three necessities has been kept together as they are related. What are the helpful tips one should follow when navigating an unfortunate situation? ### 13.8.Ethical Issues and Data Privacy

We now consider matters of cybersecurity, privacy, and ethics in this digital age. ### 13.8.1.*Privacy and its significance*

In western civilization, there exists widespread acknowledgment of the privilege to individual protection and the preservation of the right to be let alone. Privacy is hard to define, and numerous precise definitions have been presented. Frequently, the privilege of protection is distinguished by the right of people to control, access, or obstruct others from their private issues. Among a few definitions is that of Schoeman (1984, p.3), which underscores the ability that a person has to appreciate security in the sense that others have restricted access to data about them. It is a type of restricted access to the affections of their life or constrained access to their contemplations or their body. It is a definition, according to some commentators, for instance, Brey (2005), that asserts that the idea of security does not just apply to the preparing of individual data, but likewise refers to the perception of and obstruction of human practices and relations, the human body, and one’s home and personal assets. In other words, Voukko (2007) and König and Schallaboeck (2012) posit that privacy is held to be significant for numerous reasons to collaborate with Brey’s view.

Privacy often is esteemed as vital; it is thought to shield people from a wide range of outer dangers, for example, slander, mocking, badgering, control, shakedown, burglary, subordination, and prohibition. It presents protection as a verbalization of the central estimation of security, intended to shield individuals from a wide range of damage done by others. It has likewise been contended that protection is a vital condition for self-sufficiency. Without security, individuals cannot explore everyday life and build up their own identity since they would always be subject to the verdict of others. The privilege to security has additionally been asserted to ensure different rights, for example, the right to sexual articulation. Besides, protection has been guaranteed to have social incentive notwithstanding individual esteem. It has, for example, been asserted as fundamental for sustaining democracy because it looks after popular government.

The benefit to privacy should, however, be balanced against various rights and interests, for instance, the upkeep of open demand and national security. Security rights may similarly vacillate in different settings. There is, for example, a lesser want for privacy in the workplace or the overall public domain than there is at home. An essential standard used as a piece of security protection in Western nations is that of consent. It is customarily held that users should be actively told how organisations plan to store, use, or exchange their data and that users should be asked for their approval. People would then have the capacity to knowingly surrender their privacy to benefit their choices.

### 13.8.2.*Threats to privacy*

The continuing impact of Ubiquitous Computing (UC) and AI is a threat to ethical practices and confidentiality in cyber security. Both methods are pervasive. UC is an approach in data innovation that expects to move computer systems from a single workstation and install microchips into ordinary working and living conditions in an undetectable and inconspicuous way. AI is a propelled type of pervasive processing that joins remote correspondence and Intelligent User Interfaces, which are interfaces that use sensors and intelligent algorithms for profiling and recording, in order that the interface can adjust to client standards and adapt to various circumstances.

What is indeed happening to information in the cloud? Could IoT, AI, and the like yield more challenges to security? In AI situations, individuals may have many smart, networked PCs that know about their identity and needs and perform activities or provide data given their apparent needs. It has been argued (Langheinrich, 2001; see also Palen and Dourish, 2003) that UC has unique exclusive properties that possibly undermine privacy. These properties associated with UC are invisibility, memory amplification, sensing, and ubiquity. For instance, the persistent chronicle of individuals’ activities to make available logs of their past by accessing cookies or bookmarking.

With expert perception, one can add to the list to conclude that AI furthers the facilitation of similar properties. It extends the rundown of dangers associated with UC. What if the user profiling and the connectedness combine with the remote correspondence between smart items in smart cities? This question highlights the two advances and makes the protection of privacy a noteworthy test. As commentators have contended, UC and AI can make an interlaced society in which each human movement is recorded, and brilliant gadgets test individuals’ activities, aims, and musings. The distinction between the private and general social circle might diminish as many smart gadgets record personal information and interface with corporate or government IT infrastructures somewhere else. Real protection shields will be expected to prevent such situations. Hopefully, GDPR compliance will be pervasive and the ethics of learning cyber security advocated.

### 13.9.Ethics and Research in Cybersecurity

Researching cyber security has raised moral worries for nearly as long as the subject has existed. Be that as it may, a list of legal and moral vulnerabilities hangs over cyber security research. Then again, if a specific course of study is lawful but ethically dubious, researchers may carry out research in that area anyway without respect to moral considerations. Moral inquiries sneak past these legitimate issues and merit researchers’ consideration.

In other words, responsible research and innovation are interlaced in doing research. The subsidiary of capable study and advancement underscores the procedure that intends to guarantee that the results and methods of analysis are socially attractive, satisfactory, and maintainable. They are features essential to academic inquiries, for example, what are the benefits of the exploration, what are its dangers, what are the options, and who oversees the results of the examination? Researchers should consider those who must live with the outcomes. Scholars and practitioners must express their long-haul point of view and think on what will happen to their results outside of their labs. It is an approach that helps researchers to get better yields and limit the reactions to their results by envisioning their impact, reflecting on the reasons for the exploration, and connecting with the partners to influence the bearing of their research.

Nonetheless, researchers must frequently take the lead to change endeavors through the execution of seminars, workshops, insightful gatherings, and publications, meeting with policymakers, or educating the broader community on how research exemption influences them. The law can help to provide a sense of the interests relevant to cyber security and how privacy should intentionally guarantee security. Undoubtedly, such a legal approach will help cyber security researchers make decisions about their activities, considering broader ethical considerations. These contemplations ought to incorporate not just the clients whose exercises might be reflected in network information, but, additionally, the reputation of the researcher’s institution and the interests of analysts who have provided or might want to supply information. ## Chapter 14

## An Analysis of Data Mining Metrics to Identify and Evaluate Potential Radicalisation Utilising Social Media

Nishan Chelvachandran and Hamid Jahankhani\*

*Northumbria University London, UK  
\*[Hamid.jahankhani@northumbria.ac.uk](mailto:Hamid.jahankhani@northumbria.ac.uk)*

## ABSTRACT

The prevalence, and increased use and access, of social media platforms, have cemented their function in society as an interactive communications ecosystem, generating large quantities of data about users and their interactions on and between platforms.

Social media has evolved from its initial networking premise to the digital communications platform seen today. This evolution has occured through a synergic relationship with technology and its availability and development; both of which influence the other, leading to social media becoming an integral flagstone of social communication today.

The aim of this research paper is to analyse data mined from open source social media, in this instance to ascertain if a targeted behaviour can be identified from specific keyword usage. However, the keywords are those most frequently used in two datasets, consisting of data mined from Twitter, and religious quotes from extremist publications, where both the datasets themselves and the keyword metrics gained are discussed.

The results of the analyses show that it is difficult to attribute behavioural trends through specific keyword usage. Comparatively, the metrics from the extremist publications show language relating to religious ideology, whereas the Twitter data was more closely aligned with current and trending events. It was also shown that context has an important role in identification, and that an in-depth keywords-in-context approach to analysing the keyword metrics would be an interesting project for further research.

*Keywords* : social media, radicalisation, psychological traits, linguistic theory, data mining, Borum’s four-stage model, law enforcement Moghaddam's model, dataset

### 14.1.Introduction

The prevalence, and increased use and access, of social media platforms have cemented their function in society as an interactive communications ecosystem, generating large quantities of data about users and their interactions on and between platforms.

Social media has evolved from its initial networking premise to the digital communications platform seen today. This evolution has occurred through a synergic relationship with technology and its availability and development, both of which influence the other, leading to social media becoming an integral flagstone of social communication today.

The use of social media as an interactive information-sharing platform, to some, is an alternative to “mainstream media”, which can be seen to be censored or biased, whereas news on social media is unfiltered and more reflective of what is happening in the world. However, paradoxically, some users also feel that the lack of rules and viral algorithms are encouraging low quality and “fake news” (Newman, 2017).

The accessibility and availability of social media has also created a direct link to many users, who utilise the platforms to obtain news and information about the world around them (The Independent, 2015). This unfiltered direct feed to individuals has enabled extremists to propagate views and radicalise individuals, an occurrence that was previously more acute and less extensive before social media (Mughal OBE, 2016).

Facebook sees on average 1.37 billion active daily users and 2.07 billion active monthly users (Facebook, 2017). Many of these users will also use other social networking platforms and interlink accounts and posts, creating online personas and affiliations across varying niches of the social media ecosystem.

These platforms also provide a cursory method to network or build a network, communications within can be moved onto other platforms seen to be more private, such as ephemeral messaging applications (Torok, 2016).

### 14.2.Literature Review

The quantity of data generated and stored daily by Facebook alone is approximately 600TB (Facebook, 2017). The logistics, computing power and resources required to evaluate and monitor each data byte are considerable, and in any case the endeavour would be time prohibitive. However, if data mining techniques were used to analyse the Big Data sets in a targeted manner, they could prove to be power tools against the fast-evolving threat of cyber terrorism and affiliated radicalisation. If we were able to identify the risk factors and the methodologies used by extremists utilising cyber communications platforms, the potential threat could be mitigated.

Lara-Cabrera *et al*.’s (2017) research conducts a statistical analysis of risk assessment factors and metrics to evaluate radicalisation on Twitter. Focusing on the one social media platform, they use three different data sets: keyword-based metrics, perception of discrimination and declaration of positive and negative ideas about Western Society and Jihadism. Their work concludes that using their analysis, they were able to identify Twitter users that were radicalised or at risk of radicalisation based on the terminology used and ideas expressed. They also found that more radical users tended to write longer tweets, which contradicted the expectation that introversion would be an indicative personality trait of users who were or were at risk to be radicalised.

However, though the results are promising, they rely on several sets of keywords, which are limited by linguistic definition. Twitter itself is also a more streamlined social messaging platform by design, in that its purpose is to broadcast short, character-limited sentences written by the user, or tweets, on the platform, and so does not form part of a more complex communications platform. Automated users, or bots, can also be created to generate targeted tweets which in turn could be difficult to attribute to an individual.

The data that is generated by users on a platform, chronicling projected behaviours and interactions, is a resource of which the surface has barely been scratched. Algorithmic modelling approaches to big data analytics have seen an increase and are being used for various tracking and correlative analytics on communications platforms.

To analyse metrics for language or terminology that could reflect radicalisation, extremism or the exploitation of vulnerable people on social media, these terms first need to be defined. The guidance issued by the UK government defines radicalisation as “*the process by which a person comes to support terrorism and extremist ideologies associated with terrorist groups*.” (HM Government, orr. 12/03/2015, rev. 16/07/2015). It is the UK Government’s stance that it is possible to prevent vulnerable people from being drawn into terrorist-related activity through intervention. The “Prevent” strategy includes the identification and referral for appropriate interventions of those at risk of being drawn into terrorism. The intended aim of these interventions is to divert vulnerable people away from radicalisation (HM Government, orr. 12/03/2015, rev. 16/07/2015).

The “Prevent” strategy is also backed up legislatively through the Counter-Terrorism and Security Act 2015, specifically in Part 5, Chapter 1, which defines the general duties and powers of authorities to prevent people from being drawn into terrorism (HM Government, 2015).

The Terrorism Act 2000, Section 1, defines terrorism as “ *an action that endangers or causes serious violence to a person/people; causes serious damage to property; or seriously interferes with or disrupts an electronic system. And that the use or threat must be designed to influence the government or to intimidate the public for the purposes of advancing a political, religious or ideological cause”.* This legislation is also supplemented by the Terrorism Act 2006, Section 1, which widens the range of methods by which a terrorism offence can be committed under the 2000 act, by including the direct or indirect action or intention of the above described acts through a published statement (HM Government, 2006).

Extremism is defined by the UK Government as “vocal or active opposition to fundamental British values, including democracy, the rule of law, individual liberty and mutual respect and tolerance of different faiths and beliefs”. The definition used by HM Government also includes “calls for death of members of the armed forces” (HM Government, orr. 12/03/2015, rev. 16/07/2015).

While discussing legislation, it is important to point out the nature of surveillance. The terrorism acts above give definition to what acts constitute a criminal offence under UK law, however, much of the evidence required to corroborate and increase the guilt threshold from “reason to suspect” to “beyond all reasonable doubt” would often require targeted information and intelligence about the suspected individual. Under current UK legislation, this “targeted” approach, which will interfere with a person’s legal right to privacy, can only be warranted by a public body, such as the Court, or in matters relating to National Security, the UK Home Secretary. Targeted surveillance of an individual would include interception of communications and monitoring of an individual to gather intelligence on their habits and affiliations, with the purpose of collating evidence to substantiate the appropriate offence, as documented under the Warrant (HM Government, 2016).

It is for this reason that the “Prevent” strategy adopted by the UK Government relies on information on an individual and/or their activities by another party, or information gleaned from open source, publicly available information that does not breach the Data Protection Act (now the General Data Protection Regulation) or an interception of data, which would contravene the Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act, thereby making evidence used inadmissible in court. Therefore, the researcher decided to use anonymised data in the data analysis in order to comply with appropriate legislation, as the purpose of the research is to determine whether a proof of concept can indeed be gleaned.

Jurisdiction is defined by international law as “the limits of the legal competence of a state…to make, apply, and enforce rules of conduct upon persons” (Lowe and Evans, 2006). It also concerns “the extent of each state’s right to regular conduct, or the consequences of events”. The difficulty underlying jurisdiction in the context of offences purportedly committed in or utilising cyberspace is attribution. The operational mechanics of the internet give users the ability to disguise their identity and location; leading to inherent difficulties in determining, under current legislative thresholds, the perpetrator and originating territory or location. While it is agreed internationally that allied states need to share information appropriately to legislate within the confines of current legislation, there is little agreement about what information can and should be shared. Academics and the legislative community have made several efforts to conduct research studies, one of which is the “Tallinn Manual”, a 2-part book series which references legislation and defines jurisdiction utilising legislation used in air, in space, on land and at sea, as well as sovereignty and human rights (NATO Cooperative Cyber Defence Centre of Excellence, 2013; NATO Cooperative Cyber Defence Centre of Excellence, 2017).

The legislative conundrum concerning the jurisdiction of cyberspace means that traditional legislative definitions of crime and criminology do not fully fit with offences that culprits commit, or conspire to commit, online. Jahankhani *et al*. (2014) discuss the limitations of applying conventional legislative thinking and methodology to cyber criminality and proposes that there are two general categories of cyber crime: active and passive crimes. An active crime can be defined as that in which a criminal offence is directly committed by an individual using a computer, whereas a passive crime refers to the support and advancement of and conspiracy to an illegal activity.

Extremism is defined in a psychological context by Kruglanski *et al*. (2017) as “a *motivated deviance from general behavioural norms, and is assumed to stem from a shift from a balanced satisfaction of basic human needs afforded by moderation, to a motivation imbalance wherein a given need dominates the others”.* In essence, normal behaviour is that in which the needs of an individual remain relatively balanced and in sync with each other. On the other hand, an extremist mindset is one in which one given need dominates and outweighs all others, which in turns affects other thought processes and behaviours. This makes it difficult to model with traditional methodologies, given that behavioural traits can vary greatly depending on the individual when in a state of imbalance.

### 14.2.1.*Psychological traits and linguistic theory*

The definitions of terrorism and extremism describe a pattern of behaviour that leads to an intention being held or an action being committed that is contrary to the legislation. However, to better identify such actions or intentions in the remit of the Prevent strategy, it is prudent to consider any psychological research and markers, to assess if they could also play a part in the identification mechanism.

Radicalisation is a multi-faceted, complex phenomenon. As such, consideration should be given to how to approach the analysis and further understanding of causal factors. De Leede *et al*. (2018) discuss the caution required when translating research findings regarding increased vulnerability to radicalisation into policies and programmes, as “*labelling certain groups as more vulnerable to radicalisation can be counter-effective as it can increase stigmatisation and feelings of estrangement”*.

To make progress in developing a profiling methodology utilising the analysis of data generated on social media, psychological and social models must also be utilised to correlate data with behaviours for the purposes of profiling in a wider intelligence context. To understand patterns of behaviour drawn from an analysis of data, an analysis of the “Big Five Personality Traits” and demographic variables should also be considered (Pang, 2017).

Both Borum’s Four-Stage Model into a Terrorist’s Mindset (Borum, 2011) and Moghaddam’s Staircase Model (Moghaddam, 2005) propose an escalation of behaviour and trends, with each step leading to the next.

Borum’s four-stage model was developed as a conceptual model to give law enforcement officials insights into the process of radicalisation, albeit to be used as a simpler starting tool (Borum, 2011).

Moghaddam’s model is more descriptive in nature. It focuses on psychological over sociological factors, and outlines the route to extremism and terrorism as a staircase of stages, with fewer and fewer individuals progressing onwards as the stages increase. However, the model’s first stage assumes a personalised adversity to individuals. Research into this area highlights that there are a variety of reasons as to why people engage with extremist and radical narratives. However, it is recognised in Young and Rooze’s (2013) review that the model is useful in its metaphor of the staircase, as it highlights that there are a number of obstacles to overcome on the pathway to radicalisation, which prevents a greater number of individuals from becoming terrorists. It also recognises the role of morality in the individual’s path to terrorism.

In a research paper authored by Lara-Cabrera *et al*. (2017), five indicators were identified and categorised into 2 groups for the purposes of their research. These two groups are personality-related indicators and attitudes- and beliefs-related indicators.

•**Personality Related Indicators:**

•The individual is frustrated. This indicator was measured by considering swear words and the formatting of the sentence.

•The individual is introverted. This indicator was measured by sentence strength, the shorter the sentence, the more indicative of introversion.

•**Attitudes and belief indicators**

•Perception of discrimination.

•Expressing negative ideas about Western society.

•Expressing positive ideas about Jihadism, for example.

It is important to understand the underlying psychological and social behavioural indicators, so that a robust analysis can be completed.

### 14.2.2.*Social media and current events*

Social media platforms are considered an essential communication tool. Their virulence can be attributed to their ease of use and availability to complementary technology, such as smart phones.

Twitter is a social media platform with a unique model on which users post and interact with short messages known as “tweets”. These messages were originally subject to a character limit of 140 characters; however, in 2017, this was doubled to 280 characters. It is a requirement to “register” to the service to post a tweet; however, anyone can read public tweets, irrespective of registration. The platform was created in 2006, and rapidly gained popularity worldwide, with more than 100 million users posting 340 million tweets per day and handling an average of 1.6 billion search queries a day in 2012 (Twitter, 2012). By 2016, Twitter had more than 330 million monthly active users, and the company had 35+ corporate offices around the world (Twitter, 2018).

Social media has also become much more important as a news source in recent years, seeing almost a 20% rise from 2013 to 2016, with the use of print sources dropping back the same amount in the same period of time. TV as a news source has also seen an erosion from being the single most widely used source of news. Online sources (inclusive of social media) have overtaken TV in terms of reach, with at least 92% of the UK population having access to the internet (Nielsen, 2017).

The research conducted by Nielsen (2017) investigates how people find their news online, whether they go directly to a news agency or to a newspaper, to social media sources or to search engines. The results of the study state that while 47% of those surveyed say they go directly to the websites of broadcasters or newspapers, 20% find their news via various search methods, and 25% via social media methods. There is a suggestion that the digital delivery of ondemand news could lead to the formation of what is termed in the study as “filter-bubbles”, in that people will only get information from a few sources that would confirm their pre-existing views. However, the study goes on to suggest that people who obtained their news from utilising search engines or social media in a search capacity were more likely to consult different and more varied sources of news than those who did not. The results of their survey however do show a proportion of users who obtain their news from social media, without necessarily “searching” or corroborating the sources, and who trust the information they receive on their newsfeed or stream on their social media platform of choice.

### 14.2.3.*Wider relative research*

Research into the analytics of the keyword metrics of radicalisation on social media is relatively scarce; however, several wider research studies into radicalisation and the prevention of radicalisation have been conducted.

Lara-Cabrera *et al*. (2017) used risk assessment factors and metrics to evaluate radicalisation on Twitter. The study was focused on the statistical results of the data collected by analysing predetermined linguistic markers such as profanity, negative emotions and discriminatory terminology for certain behaviours, and comparing a dataset of tweets of ISIS supporters obtained from the group “Anonymous” and another dataset they compiled themselves of a random sample of Twitter users. Their research concluded that the tweets that they deemed to be more radical in nature contained more profanity and negative views about western culture and statistically were longer in length.

Torok (2016) discusses how social media has become a mainstream recruitment platform for radical extremists. The research discusses the psychological models mentioned earlier in this chapter as well as narratives from religious literature. They conclude in presenting the concept that there are three broad types of narratives that fuel violent extremism. The first occurs when a person’s grievances stimulate a strong emotional response to perceived injustices. The second occurs when the person sees jihad as an avenue to actively address these grievances. The third occurs when the person commits to jihad as a goal.

It has been noted by researchers that although the rise of online criminal and extremist activities has led to social media analytics being incorporated into security practices, these analyses have not become established in academic research or intelligence practices. A study by Yang Hui (2016) discusses collection methods and analytical tools for the study of social media for intelligence and to counter violent extremism. Multiple variances of analyses are discussed in this paper, and the paper finds that the technological capabilities of social media analytics are improving. There is a need for perspectives from social science to complement social media analytics in order to provide a wider contextual basis from which to discuss the results of analyses.

De Leede *et al*. (2018) authored an interesting study into radicalisation and violent extremism focusing on women and the development of their roles in society. These ranged from passive traditional roles in a Jihadist ideological construct to more active and operations roles. The study comprehensively reviews the pathways to radicalisation, considering socio-economic issues as well as ideological narratives. The study concludes with advice about the importance of a diverse, multi-faceted approach to policy implementation, and of investing in grassroots initiatives to communicate and liaise with individuals at a local community level, whilst avoiding the marginalisation and labelling that can adversely hinder prevention. These themes are echoed in the UK Government’s “Prevent” strategy.

Kruglanski *et al*. (2017) discuss the motivation factors underlying a shift towards extremism that are identified in the literature, giving examples of commonly reoccurring themes of *honour, vengeance, religion, loyalty to the leader, perks in the afterlife* and *feminism*, as detailed in assessments of specific cases in Bloom’s (2005) research. Kruglanski *et al*. (2017) acknowledge the appropriacy of these thematic indicators; however, they go further to explore an underlying theme, which they label *the quest for significance*. This is described as a fundamental desire to matter and to merit respect, which ties in with empirical psychological studies into universal human motivations such as the need for esteem, achievement, meaning and control. The paper goes on to discuss the manner in which this quest for significance could be triggered through a *deprivation of need*. This term describes how a perceived loss of significance by an individual can incite a desire to reinstate said significance by whichever mechanism. This is a technique used by recruiters looking to radicalise individuals, utilising, for example, the affront to one’s social/ethnic identity through the experience of Islamophobia. The paper suggests that individuals in this situation who are in such an aggrieved position could then find themselves being directed by extremist and radical narratives. They might allow themselves to be unwittingly recruited to sate the need for significance after their perceived loss.

Mythen *et al*. (2016) discuss and critique the understanding of radicalisation and its connection with “home-grown” terrorism in the UK Government’s “Prevent” strategy. The paper focuses on how specific understandings of radicalisation are constructed and operationalised in “Prevent”, and how these understandings align with the world views of political parties. The authors hypothesise that a continuous focus on the role of religious ideology in the radicalisation process, as assessed in the “Prevent” strategy, blocks the recognition of other important grievances experienced by individuals involved in violent extremism.

### 14.3.Research Methodology

### 14.3.1.**Datasets**

The aim of this chapter is to analyse keyword metrics used on an open source media platform, and to assess any correlation. The analysis is used as part of a mechanism to attribute radical and exploitative behaviour to particular individuals, or to identify users that maybe show signs of exploitation or who risk being exploited by such behaviour through their social media posts. The use of keyword analytics is nothing new, and indeed is used by most social media platforms through either the identification of certain sentence structures and themes, or through the reporting mechanism on the media platform, whereby other users can flag posts and content to administrators of the platform for review and removal. However, there is little published work and research into the keyword analytics underlying the behaviour of users and the wider social landscape.

While such behaviour and psychological profiling can be attributed to an individual, individuals may utilise multiple accounts in the online space which may not relate to their actual real-world behaviour. Wider online activity and behaviour can build useful context in a larger intelligence profile, but for the purposes of this paper, the researcher will retain a narrow scope for the data analysis, in order to further explore and answer the question relating to the keyword analysis itself.

To create a control and baseline for the analysis, datasets containing social media posts from known/suspected extremist users/accounts have been analysed. Also, for the purposes of context, a dataset of known extremist published material, which would share the same ideological profile as or have a similar ideological profile to the social media posts, would be analysed as well. The researchers assert that the analysis of the keyword metrics from these two data sets could be compared with the trends identified through the wider research in the literature review. Any correlations drawn or anomalies found could then be used to direct further research, and eventually to sculpt a mechanism to help further profile thematic behaviour. Radical Islamist Extremist posts and published material were used for this data analysis; however, it is the researcher’s hope that the same research methodology can be utilised. By changing the type of datasets used for the baseline and control, other targeted behaviours could be more readily assessed and analysed.

Both datasets were compiled by a US Department of Defence Research contractor, and as such, the sets used as secondary data have been deemed to be verified from a reputable source.

The first dataset is a compilation of religious and ideological texts used in ISIS English-based magazines, namely “Dabiq” and “Rumiyah” (Fraser, 2014; Wright, 2016). Both publications have been referred to as ISIS recruitment propaganda, given their ideological narrative. The former is more ideological in nature, and the latter is more urgent and deliberate in its directives (McKernan, 2016). The dataset obtained contains texts from 15 issues of “Dabiq” published between June 2014 and July 2016, and 9 issues of “Rumiyah” published between September 2016 and May 2017; a total of 2685 texts. As a baseline source for extremist terminology and keywords, the researcher believes this dataset to be extremely valuable.

The second dataset, provided by the same organisation, is a compilation of 17,000 tweets scraped from 100+ pro-ISIS user accounts on Twitter. The tweets are sourced globally and have been published since the November 2015 Paris terrorist attacks. The researcher’s intention for this dataset is to provide a wider context for the keyword analysis. If the keyword analysis of the publication’s dataset provides a baseline of the terminology, words and phrases regularly used in such a publication, then this can be compared with the terminology, words and phrases used in the tweets of user accounts associated with the extremist group used for this research.

By running analyses of these datasets, and by comparing the results of the datasets to each other and to the keywords and themes lifted from the research and critical literature review; the researcher should be able to corroborate the assertions made and discover potential further research avenues. The analytics of these datasets can provide profiling methodologies in a wider intelligence landscape.

### 14.4.Keyword Analysis

### 14.4.1.**Word count**

A key aspect defining the scope of analysis in this research is determining the type of analysis to be used, and which could be the best fit for the type of data to be analysed.

*“Data analysis is the systematic search for meaning. It is a way to process qualitative data so that what has been learned can be communicated to others.”* (Hatch, 2002)

A word frequency or “word count” analysis was conducted on the datasets to define the most frequently used words in the publications and the tweets in order to glean correlative patterns through appropriately weighting emergent themes. As defined by Pennebaker *et al*. (2003), word counts are based on the belief that all people have distinctive vocabulary and word usage patterns, with these patterns becoming what are often referred to as “linguistic fingerprints”. However, as highlighted by Carley (1993), there is an underlying assumption that words which are more important and have greater significance for the user would be used more often.

Miles and Huberman (1994) note that there are at least three reasons for word counting analyses, namely:

•To identify patterns more easily

•To verify a hypothesis

•To maintain analytic integrity

While this corroborates the reasoning for using this technique for the analysis of the datasets, as themes can be more readily identified in this manner, it should be also noted that there are weaknesses to word count analyses. As discussed in Leech and Onwuebuzie (2007), one drawback is that word count can decontextualize the word to a point where it is not understandable, and that in a sentence, the words before and after a key word would define the context of the phrase and the manner in which it was used, which is important when identifying and understanding themes. Another weakness is that users do not necessarily need to use a word frequently to portray important concepts.

### 14.4.2.*Keyword-in-context*

Another analysis technique that has been considered is that of “keywords-in-context”. This technique is a data analysis method that reveals how respondents use words in context by comparing words that appear before or after “keywords” (Fielding and Lee, 1998).

This analysis method provides greater depth and context to data, which may otherwise be less rich in information, and therefore, not as appropriate for use for this research. Results from a word count or a word frequency analysis, as discussed earlier, would provide the basis of further contextual research and analysis to be conducted on the resultant data. This would allow the researcher to delve deeper into the themes and behavioural psychological traits displayed by the users from these datasets.

### 14.4.3.*Data analysis*

The raw data of the datasets were compiled into a Comma Separated Value Microsoft Excel spreadsheet. The researcher then imported and transposed the datasets into Nvivo. The word frequency analyses of the two datasets were conducted separately, so that they could be appropriately compared.

For each of the datasets, two types of word frequency (or word count) analyses were run. The first was an “exact match” query, in that the frequency of each specific keyword would be counted and tabulated. The second type of query was with “specialisations”, which includes keywords of a similar meaning or definition into the count. The researcher conducted this second analysis with the intention of adopting some of the pros of a keyword-in-context approach. By counting other words with a similar meaning or definition and compiling them into the count, a level of context could be gleaned. It would also help dial back the potential for anomalous results.

### 14.5.Keyword Metric Results of the Data Analysis

The purpose for the use of the Religious Texts dataset was to act as a control and baseline for the keyword analysis. The two publications captured by researchers in this dataset are those that are named by so-called ISIS as their official publications, and are internationally recognised as being material that is authored by and for their cause. Therefore, the Religious Texts dataset was used to facilitate an accurate, pragmatic keyword analysis, and to see if the same thematic trends can be found in both theoretic and legislative terminology and these publications. This would provide a solid foundation for further research.

This dataset was obtained from a US Department of Defence Contractor. It contains 2685 religious texts scraped from multiple issues of 2 successive publications over a 3-year period. These quotes and texts are most likely representative of the arguments, themes and justification used within ISIS’s ideology.

The word cloud generated from the exact keyword frequency analysis of the dataset clearly shows the terminology and recurring themes present in the publications. Religious and violent themes are evident here, which were expected from an exact analysis of keywords found in a data source based on ISIS’s ideology.

Another word frequency query was run against the dataset, running exact matches with stemmed words, synonyms and specialisations. The inclusion of words with similar meanings and definitions would give a wider context to the keywords gleaned from the query, thus improving the results.

The results from the word frequency query with specialisations are similar to those from the exact match query. The “period” and “months” keywords are of interest, as this illustrates the use of and reference to key dates and timeframes; something which could be of wider interest in an intelligence context when comparing these details with posts on social media platforms.

The results of this query corroborate the assertions made previously in this paper that the word frequency query with specialisations would provide richer results with a degree of context for analysis. The word cloud also illustrates the increased diversity of the results, and together with the full set of results from which the sample was taken, would prove more useful in a subsequent and more detailed analysis of the results.

The purpose of conducting a keyword analysis on Pro-ISIS Twitter use was to provide a sample of tweets from known ISIS-supporting accounts, to assess if there were any trends or correlations that could be gleaned when the results of the keyword analysis of Pro-ISIS Twitter use were compared with the results of the keyword analysis of the dataset of texts originating from published propaganda.

The results from the exact match word frequency query illustrate the limitations that can occur with a narrow query scope. In this instance, as the data was captured from Twitter, and as the tweets themselves contain links to external sources, the keyword query has counted components of web addresses as keywords, such as “http”, “www”, and “com”.

The keyword frequency query shows more relevant data, with mention of key locations, as well as terminology relating to religion, war and terrorism. The word count for this query is ideal to visualise the results in their entirety for the analysis. While the web address anomalies still exist within this cloud, many other keywords can be noted from the cloud. Interestingly, the themes from this dataset vary from those from the dataset of religious texts. The exact match keywords identified from this dataset can be linked to current events, and themes linked to the ideological narrative. The religious texts gleaned from the publications refer to more religious themes, rather than the nature of or location of attacks.

However, in the vein of thought of extremism and exploitation, it could be inferred that the tweets discussing current events and providing an alternative narrative to that of the mainstream media could attract individuals looking for that very alternative narrative that they have been unable to find elsewhere, and thus that the social media platform could become the gateway for further exploitation and radicalisation by directing users to other propaganda sources such as the publications which have been collated in the first dataset used in this analysis.

A word frequency query with specialisations was again also conducted on this dataset. As seen with the previous dataset, this additional query does not result in a wholly new set of analysis results, but rather provides a depth of field or context to the results.

There are some anomalies that exist in the results, due to the inclusion of the “@”, a prefix for all Twitter handles, “2016”, the year from which most of the tweets were scraped by the originator of the dataset, and the web address components that appear in the previous queries. The results from this query begin to show a trend within this data set, compared with the exact match query, due to the wider context and grouping of words into a singular shared theme.

The word cloud for the word frequency query with specialisations shows the larger results of the query, and shows that the most frequent keywords that appear on the tweets relate to current events or trending topics on Twitter at the time of the post. It could be that these Twitter users are utilising the mechanics of the Twitter platform to maximise the visibility of their accounts and the other tweets they have written, to gain a larger audience and attract viewership from users that may not already be subscribed to a narrative which supports their ideological objects.

### 14.5.1.*Analytical comparison of the keyword metrics*

The analysis itself has provided clear fundamental support for the overarching theory hypothesised; that the use of keyword metrics to identify radicalisation and exploitation on social media for use in a wider intelligence picture is indeed possible. However, more indepth research into the keyword datasets is required. Whilst various compilations and datasets are available through some internet forums, online data repositories and indeed the “Dark Web”, verifying the authenticity and trust of an unknown source is difficult. The use of untrusted and untested sources could invalidate the results and findings of the analysis. However, verified sources for such data were available, although perhaps not as readily as the research first assumed. One of the biggest factors inhibiting such analysis of keyword metrics from these platforms was the ability to source viable datasets within an appropriate timescale. The sensitive nature of the subject matter within these datasets may also deter many researchers from further study into such an area.

The analysis of these datasets show that themes can be identified through the analysis of the keyword metrics. The dataset of religious texts, as expected, showed mainly ideological themes; religious contexts and references. The dataset of tweets showed mainly keywords relating to current events or trending topics. The word frequency with specialisations showed there is a greater repository of context underlying the initial statistics gleaned from the analysis. As a next step for further research, a keyword-in-context type analysis which involves reviewing the words before and after keywords to provide greater context in the results could be a suitable stepping stone to better understand the thematic mechanics of radicalised and exploitative themes, to create a more robust and overarching mechanism and framework to apply in wider targeted thematic analysis.

### 14.5.2.*Legislative and jurisdiction factors interconnected with the definitions of radicalisation and extremism*

Another factor when approaching research into radicalisation, extremism and exploitation is the definition of these terms. Geographical, cultural, political and socio-economic factors can change what language or behaviour would be apportioned in these categories. One of the biggest issues facing legislatures is that of jurisdiction, and the inconsistency of legislation that exists between nation states and jurisdictions. The very nature of social media platforms and their use of the internet is that while a user can be located in one jurisdiction, whereby the language used and behaviour displayed in their social media posts could be deemed acceptable; in another jurisdiction where the same posts are viewed, they may not be. There are also linguistic considerations to be made, in that translations of phrases may not correctly articulate intent or may have lost meaning in translation. For the purposes of this research, the researcher focused on the use of English language posts and translations. This research was also carried out with reference to the Tallinn Manual of Cyber Legislation and previous knowledge held by the researcher of the similarities in the legislation and jurisdiction of the five partner countries in the Five Eyes intelligence network and affiliated agencies. As such, the use of this accepted legislative similarity provided a suitable baseline on which the analysis of the data could be based.

### 14.5.3.*Analysis of the social media platform and policies, and their effect on current and future data capturing*

The Facebook Data Breach occurred when analytical and political consultancy “Cambridge Analytica” made use of user profiles and data misappropriated from the Facebook platform for their own commercial purposes. This saw an overhaul of the privacy policies used by Facebook, as well as increased transparency in the security and privacy settings available to users (Cadwalladr and Graham-Harrison, 2018). Due to Facebook being a closed platform, access to which is granted via a login wall, large data scrapes for the purposes of keyword analytics would prove quite difficult, as the process would rely on the users’ data and posts being posted as public. Anonymised data for academic research was previously available through Facebook and other research organisations with data sharing agreements with the platform; however, the data breach compromised the availability and use of such data.

The implementation of the GDPR has also led to the updating of data retention and privacy policies on such platforms, not only governing the data that is stored by service providers, but also making it more difficult for such information to be shared without an appropriate or proportionate cause. The nature of Twitter, which makes posts or “tweets” public as default, together with the quantity of “tweets” and the availability of the platform, mean that, for analytical purposes such as those described in this paper, large quantities of data can be obtained and utilised.

Many datasets did and do exist in online repositories, forums and exchanges on the dark web; however, their sources have to be authenticated to verify the validity of the research and the results of any analyses undertaken. The researcher found that other research organisations did hold verified datasets and were willing to share them for the purposes of academic research, as so little has been conducted on them.

### 14.5.4.*Review of the collated analytic data, psychological, social and legislative research*

Legislation and government guidelines provide a defined framework as to what actions constitute a criminal offence and can be defined as extremism. The dataset of extremist religious texts provides a baseline or justification for such actions, through ideological themes. What is interesting, however, is that the data collated from the Twitter dataset shows more frequent terms and keywords relating to current or trending topics on Twitter, rather than relating to the ideological themes found in the publications. Many of these tweets had links to external sites, and so, the researcher found that these tweets are using the mechanics of the Twitter platform to their advantage, maximising their outreach by linking tweets to trending topics without directly propagating ideological themes. A methodology to actively identify extremism and radicalisation on social media using keyword metrics is possible, however, further research needs to be conducted into the analysis of similar datasets. While legislation provides a definitive framework, the identification of behavioural patterns requires context to be taken into account during the analysis. A keywords-in-context approach to analysis could provide greater insight into the behaviours displayed through social media posts. However, the nature of Twitter creates a problem for such analysis. While its simplicity, accessibility and availability are reasons for the platform’s popularity, the character-limited posts mean that there will tend to be links to external sites, and the use of automated accounts means that a detailed analysis could prove difficult. Another social media platform, such as Facebook for example, would more likely provide more contextual data for analysis, as users with individual accounts and groups would more likely express views when there is no limitation. However, as discussed here, there is a legislative restriction on what data can be reviewed and analysed. For the purposes of academic research, however, anonymised data samples from the platform could be used for analysis to provide a potential proof of concept.

### 14.6.Conclusions

Whilst the research conducted in this project achieved its defined objectives, there were some limitations that were reinforced through the analyses, although these could be addressed in further research. The concise nature of the Twitter posts at the time of capture was restrictive, with the maximum character count permissible on the platform per tweet being 140 characters. This more recently doubled to 280 characters, so many tweets on Twitter are larger, in turn providing greater contextual data.

This greater depth of context in data could provide fruitful results for future analysis. While this research identified themes and trends expressed in known extremist material and tweets rather than seeking pre-set terms, it only scratches the surface of the behavioural and profiling data that can be gleaned for use in wider intelligence and law enforcement environments.

Verifiable datasets of such a nature for use in an academic environment are difficult to obtain. Many of the accounts that posted the tweets in the dataset were deleted by Twitter for breaching their “Terms and Conditions of Use”, however would reappear under a slight variation on the account name. However, the dataset used by the research accounted for these discrepancies.

Therefore, an area for further research could be the development of a dataset of datasets, whereby datasets from verified sources with data of such nature could be collated to ease and perpetuate much needed analytical research into such behavioural trends online and on social media.

More detailed keyword analytics methods could also be used on a wider range of datasets, again, to provide more context and to build a more detailed results picture from the available raw data.
